#6241. The 7 Best UPS Battery Backups

Keep your essential devices online and protected from the damaging effects of power outages and surges.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Between a modem, desktop computer, and network-attached storage (NAS), modern computing setups require a reliable power source to function effectively. If you work from home or own a small business, you know that nothing halts your workday and puts you behind like an unexpected power outage. An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) keeps your essential devices temporarily online, which provides a window for you to hit send on that last-minute email.

While a standard power strip or surge protector offers sufficient, albeit basic, protection, a UPS ensures devices are properly shut down and are protected from data loss. Beyond just keeping your devices running, the best UPS battery backups also shield sensitive electronics from potentially damaging power surges and fluctuations throughout the day. Read on to see our recommendations covering a range of needs and budgets.

To find the best uninterruptible power supply, we researched dozens of models from the leading brands in this space. Our selection process focused on several key features, including battery life, automatic voltage regulation (AVR), number of outlets, and other advanced features like power management software. After working from home and testing gear in our home offices for years, we understand the critical need for a reliable power source to keep devices online. Our personal experience and circumstances informed our choices, as we considered the models that could protect devices and provide sufficient battery backup during outages.

The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD offers a whopping 12 outlets, six of which can pull pure sine wave alternating current (AC) power from the battery. The six secondary outlets give you plenty of surge protection and power for non-essential devices, so you have a full power solution for everyday, and plenty of emergency backup power in an outage.

The battery backed outlets are clearly marked, so there’s no confusion. The shape itself also cleverly makes extra room for bulky power bricks in two spots, in case you have a couple of larger plugs.

The CyberPower model contains two USB ports—one USB-A and one USB-C—on its front, and an LCD display gives you detailed information on battery capacity and current load. An alarm sounds when something is wrong with either the device or your setup (like the battery is low or the UPS capacity is overloaded), plus there’s a button to mute the alarm as needed.

The CP1500PFCLCD also supports data line protection, so your devices stay safe from power surges that travel through Ethernet. The cord is a foot shorter than our top pick, but this model provides slightly more output capacity, so it’s worth checking out if you want a ton of outlets.

The Amazon Basics Standby UPS 600VA provides basic backup on a budget, but it lacks the more advanced features of other options. It has eight outlets total, including four battery-backed outlets to plug in devices like a modem, laptop, or NAS. And with an output of 360 watts, it’s the perfect option for home offices, with space to connect multiple devices simultaneously.

There’s a good amount of space between outlets on the Amazon UPS to easily accommodate two larger power bricks without crowding other nearby outlets. Additionally, it has a user-replaceable battery and supports power management software.

As we said, it lacks more advanced features, including AVR, but it’s still a solid, affordable option.

This CyberPower model offers everything you need in a powerful and reliable UPS. It includes 12 surge-protected outlets, with six of those backed by battery power. This gives you ample space to connect various devices, from your home office setup to more fun devices like your PlayStation 5, smart TV, or gaming desktop. The front of the UPS also features both a USB-A and USB-C port for connecting mobile devices.

An LCD panel displays information about battery and power conditions. If the power goes out, this model’s replaceable battery runs for up to 12 minutes at half load, giving you plenty of time to safely power down. It features simulated AVR, which corrects minor power fluctuations but may not be ideal for sensitive high-end gear.

This APC model features power management software and AVR and comes with an LCD panel, all of which make it another great advanced UPS for home offices and small businesses.

The APC’s power management software boasts several additional features, including the ability to remotely shut down your connected devices during an emergency. This prevents potential corruption or data loss. The device also supports a graceful shutdown feature, which automatically shuts down connected equipment if you’re unable to do it when the connected devices reach a predetermined power level.

The UPS offers both data line and coaxial line safeguards to give you extra peace of mind during power disturbances. An informative LCD screen on the front panel displays crucial information, such as battery capacity, load capacity, the number of power events that have occurred, and any system errors.

For added convenience, the UPS is equipped with both a USB-A and a USB-C port on the front to charge your phone or tablet in the same place as your home office equipment.

Most UPS devices take up a lot of floor or desk space. This one, however, measures approximately 4.1 by 10.8 by 5.5 inches, which is more compact than most for easier integration into your current home office.

Even with its smaller design, this UPS packs a punch with seven total surge-protected outlets, five of which offer battery power. It offers 330 watts of output power—perfectly suitable for a more modest setup.

The UPS automatically switches off from the battery backup when your power comes back on. And when the time comes, you can replace its battery instead of replacing the entire unit.

There are some trade-offs to the more compact design. For instance, more advanced models contain a few more outlets. You also miss out on an LCD screen and AVR. However, these compromises bring the cost down on this space-efficient UPS.

This CyberPower UPS easily integrates into a server setup because of its rack-mounting feature. The design makes it an excellent choice for small businesses that have a data center or server room, keeping the UPS close to the devices it’s protecting. It fits into racks as small as 14 inches in depth.

The device features eight battery-backed outlets and an LCD panel, which displays information on battery and power conditions. The screen also shows alerts about potential issues before they affect your devices.

Like other CyberPower models, this one supports management software for monitoring the UPS remotely. Other features include data line protection and an estimated battery runtime of 10 minutes at half load.

Most UPS models offer limited battery life, even at half load, which isn’t ideal for IT professionals or network administrators. This APC model, however, delivers impressive battery runtime, with up to 23 minutes at half load in the event of an outage. That’s almost double what other top models offer, giving you ample time to save your work and safely shut down your devices.

Beyond excellent battery life, this model comes with a number of advanced features, including cloud-based remote power monitoring, remote diagnostics, and email notifications with recommended actions. It also supports graceful shutdown.

All of these premium features mean this UPS costs more and is noticeably larger than other options on the list. That said, its combination of extended runtime and management features makes it a worthwhile investment, particularly for small businesses that want to protect their hardware and data.

A traditional UPS buys you a few minutes, just enough time to save your work and shut down. If the power's out for hours, you need something bigger. The Anker Solix S2000 is a portable power station that doubles as a UPS: Plug it into the wall, plug your gear into it, and when the power cuts out, it switches to battery power in under 10 milliseconds, fast enough for most home office setups.

And it can keep going for a long time. In our testing, the S2000 ran a refrigerator for just over 24 hours on its 2,010 watt-hours of capacity, and a typical home office draws far less. That's enough to keep a desktop PC and monitor running for several hours, or a modem and router online for more than a day. Its LFP battery is rated for 6,000 cycles before dropping to 80 percent capacity, so it should outlast several lead-acid UPS batteries, and it comes with a five-year warranty.

The trade-off is that it's far pricier than a standard UPS, and at 35.7 pounds, it's not something you'll want to move often. But if you live somewhere with long outages, it's the only pick here that can keep your WiFi running all night.

The UPS you choose should come with enough outlets to accommodate all the devices you need to plug in, with some room for additional devices in the future. Pay attention to the distinction between battery-backed outlets, which offer surge protection and battery power during outages, and surge-protected-only outlets, which, as the name suggests, only offer surge protection.

Every model we write about offers surge protection as a standard feature, even on outlets that don’t offer battery power. Batteries enable a UPS to power your devices once the grid fails. That’s why it’s essential to choose a UPS with enough battery-backed outlets to support the devices you want to keep online.

More advanced UPS models typically offer more outlets (and more that are battery-backed). For example, the more affordable Amazon Basics Standby UPS 600VA has eight outlets, four of which have battery backup, while the more advanced CyberPower CP1500AVRLCD3 has 12 outlets, six of which have battery backup. In addition to AC outlets, some UPS models have USB-A or USB-C ports to connect your smartphone and other devices. These ports easily charge your devices without taking up an outlet.

It’s also important to ensure replacing the battery on the UPS you choose is straightforward and easy. This simplifies maintenance and increases the device’s lifespan. Advanced UPS models typically include battery health monitoring features, so you’ll get a heads up when a battery nears the end of its life.

On average, UPS batteries last three to five years before needing replacement, though this lifespan varies depending on usage. Automatic Voltage Regulation, or AVR, stabilizes inconsistent incoming voltage. It converts fluctuating voltage from the power source into a steady, consistent output for connected devices. This protects sensitive electronics from power irregularities without relying on the UPS battery.

As a bonus, AVR reduces wear and tear on the battery, potentially extending its lifespan. Not all models include this feature, particularly those priced on the lower end.

During an outage, a UPS inverter converts the direct current (DC) stored in its battery into the alternating current (AC) that devices expect. Pure sine wave models output a smooth wave that closely matches utility power. The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD lists sine wave output on battery and is designed for active PFC power supplies. The APC BR1500MS2 lists sine wave output on battery with a transfer time of as little as eight seconds.

During an outage, a UPS inverter converts the direct current (DC) stored in its battery into the alternating current (AC) that devices expect. Power from the wall doesn’t just switch on and off. Its voltage rises and falls in a smooth, rounded curve called a sine wave, swinging from positive to negative and back 60 times a second.

Pure sine wave models output a smooth wave that closely matches utility power, so your devices run on battery the same way they run on the grid. Some models output a simulated sine wave instead, a stepped signal that switches between positive and negative voltage with brief rests at zero. That output works for basic electronics, but it could cause problems for more sensitive electronics, like audio equipment and desktop PCs.

Desktop PCs are the biggest concern. Most use power supplies with active power factor correction (PFC), a circuit that improves efficiency and helps the unit meet energy standards. On a simulated sine wave, some of these power supplies can shut down unexpectedly or run under extra strain. Most devices without active PFC, including modems and routers, can handle a simulated wave without trouble during a typical short outage.

For a gaming PC, workstation, or home theater system, a pure sine wave UPS is the safer bet. The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD lists sine wave output on battery and is designed for active PFC power supplies. The APC BR1500MS2 lists sine wave output on battery with a transfer time of as little as 8 milliseconds.

Having a display on a UPS may seem like a luxury, but it’s very helpful to have some kind of indicator to give you insight into battery status. Compact and budget models, like the APC BE600M1, typically stick to a few status lights that tell you whether the unit is running on wall power or battery.

An LCD screen shows measurements such as battery charge, how much power your devices are drawing, input and output voltage, and, most importantly, estimated runtime. That last one comes in clutch during an outage, since it tells you exactly how many minutes you have to save your work and shut down.

The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD's color screen tilts upward, so it's easier to read when the UPS sits on the floor under your desk, and the APC BR1500MS2 keeps a running count of the power events it has handled. And if your UPS lives in a bedroom, check whether you can dim or turn off the backlight. A glowing screen is useful during an outage, but less so at 2 a.m. when you’re trying to sleep.

A cable that’s at least five feet long offers greater flexibility in terms of where you place your UPS. A five-foot-long cable reaches wall outlets that are farther away and positions the UPS conveniently for your devices. You’ll have the freedom to place the UPS in the best spot for your setup, such as under a desk or in a server rack. Remember, a short cable potentially limits where you place the UPS, so it’s always a good idea to go longer, not shorter.

UPS models that support management software give you greater control over the UPS from a phone or computer to remotely shut down connected devices, and some support “graceful shutdown,” which automatically shuts down connected equipment if you’re unable to do it when the connected devices reach a predetermined power level.

Other features worth considering include an LCD display to monitor a UPS’s status, expandable battery capacity, and an audible alarm during power disturbances.

Setting up a UPS is straightforward: Simply plug the UPS into a wall outlet and connect your devices to the UPS. This plug-and-play simplicity means a UPS device is great for anyone, no matter their level of technical know-how. But be aware of the following safety guidelines before powering on a UPS in your home office.

Companies advise against connecting devices like copiers, laser printers, or space heaters to a UPS, as these can overload the device. Instead, use a separate surge protector.

Additionally, never plug a UPS into a surge protector or vice versa. It’s also important to avoid plugging a UPS into an extension cord because this can potentially overload the cord and create a fire hazard. It’s recommended to always plug your UPS directly into a grounded wall outlet. Doing so will ensure your UPS operates safely while providing the best possible protection for your devices.

Finding the right UPS battery backup largely comes down to the total wattage you need to keep your computer up and running while you save and shut down. Speaking broadly, we'd tell you that most home office setups with a desktop PC, monitor, modem, and router should look for a UPS around 600 to 1500 volt-amperes (VA).

To get a more accurate idea of what you specifically need, add up the wattage of all your connected devices, then look for a backup that can handle 120 to 130 percent of that load. That will give you enough time to shut down safely with some wiggle room in case you need to finish a task (or have something urgent come up before you can finish up).

Every system is different, but we'd expect a UPS in the 1000 to 1500VA range to keep your desktop and monitor running for about 15 minutes, which should be long enough to save and safely shut down. A smaller model can probably keep laptop-based setup for a similar amount of time, or power a modem and router for 30 to 45 minutes.

These are all broad estimates, though, and will vary based on what specific gear you're using. We recommend calculating your own power needs to figure out exactly how much time you'll have to shut down in the event of an emergency.

Yes, a UPS backup easily powers a router and modem, and this is one of the most common uses for a small unit. This type of hardware usually consumes only about 10 to 30 watts combined, which is relatively low when compared to computers or TVs. Because of this low draw, even a compact unit would be able to keep your internet running for 30 minutes or more during a power outage.

#6240. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column

The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 2:04 P.M.Moonset: 2:12 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

Fossil teeth from two caves in southern China are revealing that at least two lineages of early humans were present in the region around 184,000 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Homo erectus was adaptable enough to live in rainforests in what is now southern China and may have lived alongside Denisovans there, two new studies hint.

The research is based on the incredibly rare findings of nine fossil teeth from ancient humans — eight from H. erectus and one from a mystery human in the genus Homo. The teeth reveal that H. erectus lived in China much more recently than previously thought and that this population likely devoured tropical food found there.

"I think it's exciting because it means that there are two hominin populations occupying these rainforest conditions there at the same time," study first author Frido Welker, a molecular palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, told Live Science.

H. erectus is generally seen as the first human species to venture out of Africa, after evolving about 2 million years ago. It spread through eastern Eurasia, reaching China and Indonesia between about 1.6 million and 1.8 million years ago. It is one of the longest-surviving hominin species, and the last known record of it is from 108,000 years ago in river flood plains in Java, Indonesia. However, there was no physical evidence of H. erectus being on the Asian mainland more recently than 400,000 years ago.

But in two caves in Guangxi province in southern China, researchers have found thousands of mammalian fossils, accumulated there by porcupines that scavenged for and collected bones. The Baxian and Naxian caves are about 9 miles (15 kilometers) apart, sitting in a karst landscape of limestone formations that are prone to dissolving to create caves that would have offered crucial shelter for H. erectus.

The entrance to Naxian Cave, as seen by a drone, is the tall and wide opening of a cave that goes back around 330 feet (100 meters) to a fossil chamber.

Researchers found the nine human teeth among more than 18,000 fossils, including from apes, elephants, rhinoceroses and other ancient hoofed animals, Welker and his colleagues reported in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature.

Radiometric dating of the fossils and surrounding sediments by methods including assessing the decay of uranium, pins them to about 324,000 to 184,000 years ago. Eight of the teeth have physical features reminiscent of H. erectus, but the ninth is more elusive. It looks distinct from H. erectus, Neanderthals and modern humans, Welker said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Welker's team took samples from five teeth ‪—‬ four from the group that seemed to be H. erectus and one from the mysterious tooth ‪—‬ to see which ancient proteins were present, since DNA tends to degrade more easily than the proteins in an organism. (The study of these proteins is known as proteomics.)

The four similar ones had protein signatures that matched what had been seen before in H. erectus.

"The morphology is nicely confirmed by the proteomics," Welker told Live Science. Three of these teeth were from males, and the other was from a female, which the team was able to determine based on the presence or absence of amelogenin-Y, a protein coded for only by the Y chromosome.

Researchers investigating two caves in China have found nine human teeth, eight of which have been confidently identified as belonging to Homo erectus.

However, some parts of the protein signatures differed from what had been seen in other H. erectus remains in China, so the new specimens may be from a previously unknown H. erectus population that perhaps had a slightly different genetic makeup, Welker said.

The finding that H. erectus was present in mainland Asia until at least 184,000 years ago — rather than 400,000 years ago — fills a geographical and chronological gap, helping to explain how H. erectus was on Java 108,000 years ago.

"This brings the history of H. erectus in East Asia closer in age to the late Javanese examples, raising the possibility that these populations were connected through land bridges at times of lowered sea level," Chris Stringer, a paleoanthropologist at the Natural History Museum in London who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email.

John Hawks, an anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who wasn't involved in the study, previously believed that specimens from the past 400,000 years or so flagged as H. erectus were actually Denisovans ‪—‬ ancient humans who lived in Asia, disappeared around 30,000 years ago and belonged to the Homo longi lineage. But he told Live Science that the new morphological and protein findings provide convincing evidence that H. erectus did survive until relatively recently in some places.

The fifth analyzed tooth, known as PA1796, remains mysterious. The protein analysis revealed it was from a male, but it didn't show a recognizable signature in the protein sequence data. Therefore, Welker's team suggested it could be from another hominin species that was present in the region at the same time.

Welker didn’t want to speculate about which species it might be, but said: "Sequence-wise it doesn't have this Homo erectus substitution and morphologically, it doesn't look like an erectus tooth."

The tooth could be from a previously unknown human species, but many experts suspect it is from a Denisovan.

"With some of the new material probably dating to less than 200,000 years old, this already brings it close in age to known or putative Homo longi/Denisovan samples in southern China and Laos, implying potentially long overlaps between these species," Stringer said. "Tooth PA1796 could represent a longi/Denisovan, though it is relatively small in size, and relevant comparative data for longi/Denisovans is sparse."

The entrance to China's Naxian Cave, which has a small opening and goes back around 164 feet (50 m) to a fossil chamber.

Recent research suggests there was interbreeding between the H. erectus and Denisovan lineages, and the new evidence increases the likelihood that this happened, at least occasionally, Stringer said.

Any firm conclusions of who the tooth is from will have to wait for further finds of similar teeth elsewhere, Welker said.

Hawks agreed that the tooth is most likely from a Denisovan, perhaps from a divergent branch for which we don't have protein data. But it could also be from a novel H. erectus population or someone from the same population as the other teeth who, for developmental or genetic reasons, wasn't typical. "I would have liked to see additional comparisons in the paper to more Denisovan teeth," Hawks said.

In another paper, also published Nov. 18 in the journal Nature, Kira Westaway, a geochronologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, and her colleagues examined trace elements in the same teeth, as well as in animal teeth from the caves, to see what they revealed about the hominins' diet and local habitat.

Their analysis indicated that this H. erectus population found plants and animals to eat in tropical, rainforest-like ecosystems. Previously, it was thought that only our own species, Homo sapiens, was able to adapt to this type of environment.

"Rather than being confined to open woodland and grassland environments, H. erectus was considerably more ecologically adaptable than many of us have assumed," Stringer said.

"Being adaptable and being flexible are not traits that we associate with ancient human species — these are traits that we associate with H. sapiens," Westaway told Live Science. "Suddenly we're seeing H. erectus being able to survive in environments that we didn't think they could possibly survive in."

And given the mysterious tooth, it is possible that two different early human populations were this adaptable, said Welker, who was a co-author of the study.

A view from Naxian Cave in China, where Homo erectus teeth were found.

Westaway and her colleagues also looked at levels of the element strontium in the teeth, which can shed light on where someone grew up based on the unique strontium levels in water and foods they consumed as children. The team matched these strontium levels to another karst landscape about 200 miles (320 km) away, in the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

"It looks like H. erectus moved across large areas, traversing this karst landscape in the rainforests" ‪—‬ a finding that adds to our understanding of these ancient humans, Westaway said.

It's absurd that people often think of H. erectus as an unsuccessful species, she added. "We think they were the first to leave Africa, the first to use fire. It blows my mind because they survived six times longer than H. sapiens has survived so far, so I don't see them as unsuccessful."

Hawks' big question, however, is linked to modern humans, who were in the Chinese region from at least 45,000 years ago.

"Denisovan DNA is present in the peoples of Island Southeast Asia, so, modern humans must have run into Denisovans at some point," he said. "If H. erectus was enduring in the same area at the same time, might H. sapiens also have encountered late H. erectus?"

Researchers have zeroed in on a genetic variant in the human brain that came from Neanderthals, and it might protect us from schizophrenia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newfound genetic variant inherited from Neanderthals may shrink a part of modern-human brains without having any meaningful effects on mental ability, and it might also reduce the risk of schizophrenia, a new study finds.

"Genetic differences between Neanderthals and modern humans still influence our brains today," study co-author Hugo Zeberg, an evolutionary geneticist at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, told Live Science. Zeberg and his colleague Svante Pääbo detailed their findings Nov. 16 in the journal PNAS.

Before they went extinct around 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals were among the closest relatives of modern humans. More than a decade of research has shown that Neanderthals and modern humans once interbred. Most people not of sub-Saharan ancestry living today possess about 2% Neanderthal ancestry.

Neanderthals' skulls were larger and more elongated than modern humans'. One reason for the differences has to do with the occipital lobe, the smallest of the brain's four lobes, which sits in the back of the skull. The occipital lobe houses the visual cortex, which helps process signals from the eyes. This area was relatively larger in Neanderthals than it is in modern humans.

In the new study, the researchers analyzed modern-human genomes for genetic variants that are related to occipital lobe size and were also likely inherited from Neanderthals. They discovered one such variant associated with the DAAM1 gene, which a 2019 study linked with brain development. This genetic variant was found only in modern humans outside Africa and was seen in five Neanderthal genomes.

Curiously, the Neanderthal variant the scientists detected in modern-human genomes led to an approximately 0.05-cubic-inch (0.85 cubic centimeters) reduction in occipital lobe size per copy of the variant in an individual. This means that the Neanderthal gene was linked to a slightly smaller brain size in modern humans.

A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk.

This effect is the opposite of what experts expected based on Neanderthals' large skull size, Tony Capra, an evolutionary geneticist at the University of California, San Francisco, who was not involved in the research, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

However, it's important to remember that this one gene variant "does not reflect the full set of variations that might have been present in Neanderthals that might have affected the shape and size of their brain structures," Capra noted.

Zeberg and Pääbo also discovered that having two copies of the DAAM1 gene variant was associated with a nearly 10% reduction in the chances of having schizophrenia in modern humans. But there was no apparent link between the variant and intelligence in modern humans.

"A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk," Zeberg said.

Symptoms of schizophrenia can include altered perceptions of reality, such as visual hallucinations and problems with processing visual signals. This makes it "tempting to speculate" that this Neanderthal gene variant's effects on schizophrenia might be associated with the visual cortex. However, there is currently no evidence for such a link, Zeberg said.

Future research along these lines could analyze how other Neanderthal genetic variants influenced modern humans, Capra said, "to see if they had a consistent effect on us." Looking into Neanderthal variants that are missing from modern-human genomes could "show us what makes us modern humans as opposed to them," Capra added.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6235. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night."

Trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over."

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly."

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”

#6234. From Noah’s Ark to Oak Island: In 1976, We Named the 7 Great Quests of Man. Bigfoot Still Hasn’t Called Back

Some quests got closer. One got debunked. And one may owe its modern revival to this very magazine.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

“A quest is a search and an adventure,” reads the opening salvo of the September 1976 Popular Mechanics cover story, “7 Great Quests of Man.” Admittedly, this is a somewhat muted, almost “Maid of Honor Reads the Webster’s Dictionary Definition of Love for Her Toast”-esque opener to place beneath such a grandiose headline.

In defense of that half-century-old article, finding a really great opening line for a story can be hard. That’s as true now as it was 50 years ago. At least the author didn’t take the easy way out and just start it by quoting somebody else instead.

But what of the “Great Quests” themselves? Have any of them been conquered in the last half-century? Have any of the tools and technologies developed since 1976 brought us a smidge closer to solving these age-old mysteries?

To mark the 50th anniversary of the “7 Great Quests of Man,” we took a look back at the quests that captivated readers in 1976, and how close we’ve come to bringing them to an end since then.

The first Great Quest on the list is one of the oldest, the search for the lost continent of Atlantis. The earliest extant record of the story of Atlantis was penned by Plato, who put the words in the mouth of his interlocutor Critias in a pair of dialogues written around 360 B.C.E.

By 1976, Atlantis was having a moment in the sun (one whose rays could presumably reach its watery depths). Paranormal phenomena researcher Charles Berlitz’s book The Mystery of Atlantis was back on bookshelves in a new paperback edition, and on television, everyone from Leonard Nimoy to Jabberjaw was seemingly in search of the sunken continent.

In “7 Great Quests of Man,” after dismissing the claims of a psychic who said Atlantis would rise again, we actually offered up a different theory: that Atlantis had already been found back in the 1960s, and it was actually a volcanic island called Santorini.

At the time, we dated the eruption to sometime between 1480 and 1450 B.C.E. Modern radiocarbon evidence suggests it happened more than a century earlier, likely around 1600 B.C.E. Either way, the blast caused a large part of the island to sink, leaving only three smaller islands above water (including the largest, now called Thera or Santorini).

“During the 1960s excavations of Thera revealed that it had once been the home of the Minoans,” we wrote, “These were a highly civilized, seafaring people whose center was on the island of Crete about 70 miles from Santorini. The Minoans on Thera had been wiped out by the eruption. The well-preserved ruins now being uncovered are one of the major archaeological finds of this century.”

Here in the 21st century, Santorini is actually still making waves, literally. We reported last year that magma from the island’s crust caused a remarkable 25,000 tremors in just a 30-day period. And while advancements in tech like sonar have yet to turn up any evidence of Atlantis, intrepid adventurers have uncovered several other sunken cities, from the relics of Canopus and the Sanctuary of Poseidon at Samikon to the medieval city of Shipden and the “Atlantis of the Sands,” Ubar.

Next up on the list was Noah’s Ark. That readers in 1976 were dying to know where Noah’s Ark was is actually no surprise; it would be the same as folks in 2026 wanting to find the Trojan Horse after seeing The Odyssey. That’s because in 1976, a documentary called In Search of Noah’s Ark proved a box-office sensation, becoming one of the top ten highest-grossing films of the year.

Part of the film’s appeal was the sentiment that the remnants of the Biblical vessel could well be hidden away on Turkey’s Mount Ararat, and only the political strife of our modern times was keeping us from finding the ancient treasure. After all, during this time, the United States had actually implemented an arms embargo on Turkey after its actions in Cyprus in 1974, so things were undoubtedly fraught geopolitically in the region.

“7 Great Quests of Man” suggests as much. “Currently the Turkish government is discouraging foreign expeditions to Mount Ararat,” it concludes, “it’s in a politically sensitive area.” Back then, we said that Ark hunters would no doubt return to the site “as soon as restrictions are lifted,” which is the kind of thing you casually say when you don’t realize there’s about to be a violent military coup in four years.

Now, in the 21st century, some progress has actually been made in the search for Noah’s Ark. In October 2026, we reported that soil samples were taken from Mount Ararat’s Durupinar formation, a peculiar geological feature in the area that’s long been considered a potential resting place for the Biblical vessel. The preliminary tests showed a high concentration of organic material, such as wood. Further lab work is being undertaken to try and determine “if man-made activity or decaying wood sit in the soil.”

“The hottest quest going in 1976 is the quest for the Loch Ness monster,” we wrote in “7 Great Quests of Man,” and that was no joke. 1976 really was Nessie’s year, with coverage of the alleged cryptid even appearing in the pages of the MIT Technology Review and the New York Times.

Why was the Loch Ness Monster having such a moment during the Bicentennial? Simple: In 1975, new photographs purportedly showing the creature had surfaced. While we’re all familiar with the famous 1930s photo of Nessie’s alleged neck rising above the water, the two new pictures came courtesy of an underwater camera, and seemed to show the creature close up and beneath the waves. “One shows a close-up of what may be the head of an unknown animal,” we wrote in 1976, “the other what may be its head, neck and body.”

Back then, we cited numerous notable biologists who felt the images were “sufficiently suggestive of a large aquatic animal” and concluded that “the long search may be nearing a conclusion.”

Back in 2013, Scientific American blamed the photos’ appeal on pareidolia, our brain’s habit of finding faces and figures where there are none. The photo that was thought to show Nessie’s head “is most likely a gnarly tree-stump on the loch floor.”

That being said, the last few years have still yielded some interesting Loch Ness Monster talk, from a 2025 study concluding that Nessie wouldn’t look like you think (if it exists at all) to the recent recovery of a 1970s Loch Ness Monster trap with its own underwater camera (which captured no Nessie pictures, unfortunately).

So, in a sense, the Loch Ness Monster mystery is kind of like the Starland Vocal Band’s “Afternoon Delight.” It’s still around on the periphery today, and we’re all a little confused as to why it was such a big thing back in ’76.

2) Could Bigfoot beat the Six Million Dollar Man in a fight?

And in 1976, one of those questions was finally answered. In a two-part episode of The Six Million Dollar Man called “The Secret of Bigfoot,” Steve Austin (the character played by Lee Majors, not the professional wrestler) faced off against Bigfoot (played by André the Giant, the actual professional wrestler). Believe it or not, this was just one small component of the Bigfoot craze that overtook America in the 1970s. There were Bigfoot movies, Bigfoot TV shows, a Bigfoot board game and, unbeknownst to the average American, the FBI was even actively investigating the legitimacy of hairs that reportedly came from Sasquatch himself.

For real, Bigfoot has an FBI file, and we read it.

As our article pointed out back then, while talk of Yetis and Sasquatches originated near the start of the 20th century, 1970s Bigfoot mania was ignited by the famed Patterson-Gimlin film. You know the one. You’ve undoubtedly seen it. Back in 1967, amateur monster hunters Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin went out into the woods with a camera and captured footage of a seven-foot-tall creature covered in hair strolling by. While some were skeptical of the footage, thinking it was just a guy in a suit, back in 1976 our writer spoke to a primate expert at the Smithsonian Institution who said, “I could not see the zipper and I still can’t.”

Now in 2026, though, you can see the zipper if you want—in a manner of speaking, anyway.

We don’t want to bum out the Bigfoot believers here. Look, maybe there is still a Sasquatch out there somewhere—and if you ask that one guy, there certainly was one, but it’s dead now). But as for the Patterson-Gimlin film? That received a thorough debunking in 2026 thanks to the revelatory documentary Capturing Bigfoot. The film, which debuted at SXSW in March 2026, confirms that the famous footage was a hoax, revealing never-before-seen “rehearsal footage” shot by the men in 1966, featuring a different design for the Sasquatch.

“Oak Island, a small island on Mahone Bay off the coast of Nova Scotia, is the site of what has to be the most frustrating quest of modern times,” we wrote back in 1976. “There may be a treasure on the island. People have known where the treasure is buried for nearly 200 years. But it is so cleverly protected that all attempts to recover it have been foiled.”

From the supposed “Money Pit” to the cipher stone to the Oak Island Curse, this north-of-the-border treasure hunt has built up its own glossary of lore and lingo over the last two centuries as eager treasure hunters braved booby traps in search of a historic payday. Popular Mechanics first covered the Oak Island treasure hunt 100 years ago, in the March 1926 story “Hunting Hidden Treasures,” and its allure attracted the attention of major names like John Wayne and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Here in 2026, we can say that the Oak Island mystery stands out from the other “Great Quests” outlined in our pages 50 years ago for one specific reason: the “7 Great Quests of Man” list itself had a direct influence on the current-day search for answers about Oak Island.

How do we know that? Well, the new faces of the Oak Island treasure hunt said so themselves.

“Growing up, I loved that magazine. Absolutely loved that magazine,” Marty Lagina told us. “There is one connection to Popular Mechanics too, aside from our interest in the magazine,” brother Rick Lagina chimed in. “There was an article in Popular Mechanics about Oak Island.” The two men are the stars of the long-running television series The Curse of Oak Island, currently airing its 14th season. While they’ve yet to uncover some massive trove at the bottom of the much-discussed Money Pit, the show’s efforts have helped uncover some of the island’s previously undocumented history, and the series’ popularity has kept the mysterious island in the cultural zeitgeist.

“Did visitors from other planets come to earth in ancient times?” we asked in 1976. Then we answered: “Recently, yes has become a very popular answer to that question.” And this was no exaggeration. People really were all in on this theory in the 1970s, and not just the fringe conspiracy crowd.

To give you an idea of just how pervasive alien fever was, we need to touch on a film called Chariots of the Gods. Based on the pseudoscientific work of Erich von Däniken, this 1970 documentary laid out the theory that the world’s religions and early human development were all influenced by ancient extraterrestrial visitors.

How did audiences in the Disco Decade receive this claim? Well, not only was the film a commercial success, it actually managed to get an Academy Award nomination for Best Documentary Feature that year, putting it up alongside the historic concert film Woodstock and the MLK documentary King: A Filmed Record... Montgomery to Memphis. That would be like if this year You Can See Everything had to compete against an episode of Ancient Aliens at the Oscars.

Supporters of the theory pointed to ancient constructions they felt couldn’t have been built with “primitive tools,” and massive monuments constructed that could only be seen properly from the skies. Skeptics claimed these “view-from-above” tributes were intended for gods in the heavens, but true believers said it was a message to aliens.

In our world today, the ancient alien theory still gets bandied about from time to time. Recently, we’ve covered phenomena like the “Black Knight” satellite and the Silurian hypothesis, both of which have attracted their fair share of fringe “it was aliens” theories. But arguably the greatest cultural cachet the conspiracy theory has today is the face we’re all picturing when we read the sentence “it was aliens.”

You know who we’re talking about. You’ve seen the memes.

Author Giorgio Tsoukalos got the meme treatment all the way back in 2010 for his credulous role on the immensely popular television show Ancient Aliens. That series, which still airs today, took the torch of Chariots of the Gods and ran with it, keeping the “ancient aliens” theory in the popular discourse through 22 television seasons, a video game, and even an adjacent series in which audiences watch very stoned people watch the show. As a Great Quest, we’ve come no closer to finding proof of ancient aliens, but as a pop culture concept? The brand has literally never been stronger.

“Ask most scientists what they think of the ancient-astronaut theories, and they will just snort at you,” we wrote in 1976. “But that doesn’t mean that they don’t take the subject of intelligent life in space seriously. They do. They are now trying to contact extraterrestrial civilizations. That is the last, and perhaps the most exciting, quest of all.”

It’s likely the oldest of the “7 Great Quests of Man,” as well. For as long as mankind has been aware that there was more beyond our world, we’ve wondered if there’s anybody out there. Unlike the other quests, your Bigfoots and Noah’s Arks—which call for some credulity, some willingness to believe the thing is possible—to many people, the idea that there must be some other intelligent life out in our vast universe feels so plausible that it’s hard not to resist. Yet, despite how improbable it seems that mankind is really alone in the universe, no credible evidence has ever materialized that there’s intelligent life out there.

A few years before our article was published, in 1972, Pioneer 10 took off from Cape Kennedy carrying a gold-covered plate with images of a man and a woman accompanied by diagrams that scientists hoped could be understood by any intelligent life it reached. It wasn’t the first attempt to contact alien life (Dr. Frank Drake launched Project Ozma back in 1960), but the legendary Carl Sagan thought this “message in a bottle” approach might be the key to communicating with intelligent life among the stars.

In the 21st century, the search for intelligent life continues unabated, be it attempts to identify aliens moving about in our universe today, or searching for remnants of those who may have died off far in the distant past. At Pop Mech, we’ve continued to keep our eyes to the skies, while trying to contend with the perplexing Fermi Paradox—the question of why, in a universe billions of years old, we appear to be the only intelligent life to ever exist in it.

Yet, with all our new technology developed in the last 50 years, we still find ourselves gazing up at the stars and wondering who might be out there, just as we did when “7 Great Quests of Man” was written.

Back then, we posited that our message would be heard by whatever life is out there. “It may happen a thousand years from now, or tomorrow.” We’ll check back in on that in another 50 years.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

#6233. Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

On Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. Here, we look back at its most important discoveries, seen through groundbreaking space photos.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

The growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

"What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong."

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

NASA's Voyager 2 probe launched before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.)

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about."

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month

The close-up view showed that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

While passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely new avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker said. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking."

By viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any big craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker said.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km)

Some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image

A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

Voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

"That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker said, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture."

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five new moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere

The mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This showed that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

By 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

In a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot."

"We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker said. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is."

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image

Voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

"We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker said. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating."

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. With more than 20 years of editorial experience, his writing has appeared in The Washington Post, Reader's Digest, CBS.com, the Richard Dawkins Foundation website and other outlets. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

#6232. Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV Review: One Small Step for OLED, One Big Step for Roku TVs

Roku’s first OLED TV lowers the bar for bringing a new, high-performance OLED screen home.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It seems that the rumors of the end of OLED supremacy in the TV marketplace were greatly exaggerated. At the start of 2026, flashy new display technologies like RGB LED emerged to challenge that status quo, theoretically offering a brighter alternative to OLED panels, with greater color coverage. But at the end of the year, OLED TVs, with their ability to control each of a TV’s millions of tiny pixels point-by-point, remain the best option for overall picture performance. In fact, despite the fact that only two companies, LG and Samsung, currently make OLED panels, the number of TV brands that actually use those panels is expanding: Roku, the latest brand to jump into the space, released its first two OLED TVs this fall.

As you’d expect from Roku, both the baseline Roku Pro Series and the brighter and slightly fancier Roku Pro Series LX are value-oriented models, with list prices that undercut brands like Samsung and LG. But like many of our favorite picks at Popular Mechanics, they are designed to balance premium performance and great usability, with a simple setup and handy quality-of-life features that competitors lack, like a built-in remote finder.

After spending several days with the flagship Pro LX, I’m happy to report that Roku’s first foray into OLED TVs is already a strong contender for anyone curious about the benefits of upgrading to an OLED screen. The Pro LX’s picture quality doesn’t quite reach the heights of legacy OLED sets like LG’s C6 let alone flagships like the Samsung’s S95H. But it holds its own, and arguably outdoes them both when it comes to actually living with your TV. If you’re after a best-of-both-worlds OLED approach, the Roku Pro LX is an enticing new option at a very nice price.

Everything about setting up the Pro LX is built around simplicity. Like last year’s LED-powered Roku Pro, the LX eschews multi-piece pedestal stands and tiny bags of screws for feet that attach with screw-on knobs—no tools required. Dual stand positions include higher clearance for a soundbar, though the feet’s width of just over 42 inches on the 65-inch model I tested doesn’t leave much space up front on most consoles. The design doesn’t look quite as stylish as its LG and Samsung rivals, but the build feels stout, and the ultra-thin panel of just over an eighth of an inch up top adds a premium vibe.

The TV turns on automatically when plugged in, and immediately walks you through pairing the voice remote, which charges via USB-C so you never have to worry about batteries. It’s not quite as handy as Samsung’s solar-powered remotes, but its design is intuitive, including options like backlit keys and hands-free “Hey, Roku” voice control. If you’re not into an always-ready mic, you can mute it with a hard switch on the remote’s left edge.

Even the LX’s packaging is designed with forethought, including a plastic screen cover that peels off with a feather-light tug. But before you remove it, you’ll see a yellow arrow that points to my favorite feature by far: A remote finder button. A quick press emits a pleasant chirp from the remote buried in your couch cushions or, if you’ve got a toddler like me, hidden in any number of places out of reach from grabby little hands. I have no idea why this isn’t a standard option across brands, but kudos to Roku. It’s the simple things.

At the TV’s left flank, you’ll find a reasonably well-stocked input hub, including dual HDMI 2.1 inputs for gaming in VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz, an HDMI 2.0 port, and a separate HDMI eARC port for connecting a soundbar or audio system. That’s important because the Pro LX’s sound is particularly thin and weak, all but requiring an audio upgrade. Other inputs in the stack include Ethernet to back up WiFi 6 support, USB-C and USB-A inputs, optical input, and a cable/antenna tuner. It would have been nice to get a full set of four HDMI 2.1 inputs, which you’ll find in similar LG and Samsung TVs, but I appreciate that Roku offers two ways for serious gamers to connect apart from the HDMI eARC port.

Notable features include ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) for fast-paced gaming and support for all major HDR formats, including the top two advanced options, Dolby Vision and HDR10+. In contrast, LG TVs stop at Dolby Vision, while Samsung only offers HDR10+. It’s always nice to have options, and the addition of Dolby Vision, the most common format for streaming, gives Roku a leg-up over Samsung OLEDs.

As you’d expect from an OLED, the Pro LX delivers fantastic contrast between the lightest and darkest images from the moment you turn it on, starting with perfect black levels from its obsidian screen. A polarizing layer does a fine job diffusing reflections for moderately bright rooms, about on par with LG’s C6. It doesn’t offer the powerful ambient light control of matte screens like Samsung’s S90H, but I generally prefer the richer perceived black levels of glossy screens, and the Pro LX is happy to indulge with impressive depth in darker moments.

Roku claims that the Pro LX is around twice as bright as the standard Roku Pro OLED, and after tinkering with the settings a bit, you’ll get plenty of pep to contrast those rich black levels. Using the TV’s most accurate HDR Dark picture mode, I measured around 1200 nits of peak brightness in a 10 percent window with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software.

That’s around 150 nits less than I got with the C6, but the difference is negligible in real-world watching: both TVs look similarly bright in moments like the sun glancing off a windshield or a glowing candle in a dark room. Roku’s model provides more than enough power for impactful HDR punch and vibrant colors, especially since most streaming content tops out at 1,000 nits. Interestingly, you’ll need to change the TV’s separate Picture Brightness setting to the highest “Brighter” mode to unlock that peak brightness. Unfortunately, the picture doesn’t do as good a job following the intent of directors and mastering engineers here as in the dimmer “normal” mode. That said, while slightly overbright, the TV still looks quite good overall in “brighter” mode. It’s just more of a tradeoff than you’ll see with the C6 at peak brightness.

Likewise, the colors aren’t quite as accurate as the C6. You can see the difference in certain specific shades, like the deep oranges in Mad Max: Fury Road, which sometimes looked a little too, well, orangey. I also noticed some color banding, or image artifacts, in especially challenging test scenes, but it rarely showed up in regular films and TV shows.

For most of my viewing, colors looked rich and natural. The vivid coral adventures in Netflix’s Our Planet provide a dazzling rainbow of shades that gave me chills, and watching Spider-Man: Brand New Day was a cinematic experience, with an almost marbled touch to details. There’s enough vibrancy to get you lost in little moments like the flashing gold of Ego’s palace in Guardians of the Galaxy Volume II, or the glowing beads of light reflecting off the Mandalorian’s helmet in his spaceship.

Speaking of space, the TV’s pinpoint light control makes deep-space scenes look incredibly realistic and engaging, especially compared with backlit models like last year’s mini-LED Roku Pro. Shadow details are also impressive, even in challenging scenes from murky shows like The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, pairing with the TV’s flashy highlights for a lush experience. And while viewing the screen off-angle adds a slight green tinge, as it does with a lot of LG OLEDs, it’s worlds better than the pale colors and accentuated blooming you’ll see in the vast majority of LED TVs. Such is the advantage of OLED.

Of course, the biggest advantage of a Roku-branded OLED is marrying OLED’s technical prowess with a more accessible smart TV operating system. While Sony’s Google TV OLEDs are a solid alternative, Roku OS is notably simpler, more reliable, and in some ways more joyful to use than Samsung’s Tizen, LG’s webOS, and (especially) Panasonic’s Fire TV.

The fact that Roku OS just works exactly the way it’s supposed to is frankly half the battle. I’ve had fewer glitches with Roku OS in several years of TV reviewing than any other system, going back to TCL’s early Roku TVs. On top of that, I like the little extras Roku still offers like space themes, Star Trek-branded wallpaper, and silly movie references in the ever-expanding Roku City screen saver, like Cameron’s dad’s ill-fated Ferrari from Ferris Bueller’s Day Off.

Like all smart TVs I test, Roku OS has gotten less intuitive and more insidious in recent years, from plays to sell your data like ACR (Automatic Content Recognition) to pushier ads, such as a Home Depot-sponsored holiday wallpaper that suddenly appeared as I was writing this review. Luckily, you can turn that and most other annoying features off (though Roku immediately put the ad elsewhere). I’m also not as pleased with the latest Home screen layout, which pushes features like Continue Watching and the full list of apps below (you guessed it) more ads.

The upshot is that it takes more work to reorganize the layout for the best experience, but the good news is you can customize most options, and Roku OS is still the best built-in streaming system I’ve tested.

Roku’s Pro Series LX isn’t the best-performing OLED in its class, with both the Samsung S90H and LG C6 providing a cleaner, more accurate picture, but it is comparable and cheaper than either one at full price. (And will likely remain so for the rest of the year as holiday sales kick in.) Moreover, its slick blend of usability and performance could make it the top choice for OLED-curious folks who value a TV’s livability as highly as its picture quality. If you want to make the jump to OLED, and your budget is already stretched, Roku’s your new go-to.

Ryan Waniata is a professional writer, editor, video host, and product reviewer. A musician since childhood, his audio hardware roots go back to his days as a studio engineer in Nashville, TN in 2009. In 2011 he left the studio world to became a full-time journalist, with an emphasis on A/V, including TVs, speakers, headphones, and audio gear of all kinds. The author of hundreds of articles, Ryan has a passion for finding readers the best value on the best gear out there.

#6231. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially launched his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.
