#6165. Review: Park Hyatt Vienna, My Favorite Hotel In The Austrian Capital

The Park Hyatt Vienna is not only my favorite hotels in Vienna, but one of my favorite Hyatt properties in the world. With excellent service, nice amenities, delicious breakfast, and central location, our latest stay was another great reminder of what a superb property this is.

Although we could have connected directly to Zürich after landing in Vienna, I was able to force a 23.5-hour layover into the itinerary, which gave us a chance to stay to the Park Hyatt Vienna, a hotel I’ve enjoyed many times over the years but it was the first time my children had come along.

I booked this for 35,000 World of Hyatt points (versus a cash rate of over €700) and applied a “Guest of Honor” to the reservation, which essentially marks me as “Globalist” in the system.

Our Austrian flight landed at 11:30 am into VIE and I had emailed the hotel requesting an early check-in, specifically noting that we would be happy to forgo an upgrade in order to access our room a few hours early. Our request was honored.

The Park Hyatt Vienna is ideally located on Am Hof in the heart of the old town, an easy walk from St. Stephen’s Cathedral and many of the places I most enjoy visiting in Vienna.

Checking in, I was welcomed back to the hotel and the amenities were explained, including breakfast and pool hours (most important to my kids!).

We were assigned room 331, a standard room with two twins beds. While not an upgrade, the room was spacious enough and quite comfortable with a desk, round table, chair, and the two beds.

My daughter jumped right into bed to go to sleep (it was, after all, about 3:15 am in Los Angeles), but I pulled her out: no napping today would hopefully mean no jet lag tomorrow.

The bathroom featured really beautiful stonework behind the bathtub and included two sinks, a separate water closet, and walk-in shower.

The room had a wardrobe that included a coffee machine, hot water kettle, and mini-bar including snacks and drinks.

A welcome amenity was also waiting for us including various chocolates and candies.

The room had plenty of 220-volt outlets and also a safe to lock valuables. Unfortunately, the room did not have any USB-C ports or wireless chargers.

A primary reason I booked this hotel was for the pool and wellness. My kids love to swim and I can’t think of a better hotel pool than this one: we spent a lot of time here in the afternoon and evening.

The entire pool and spa area is posh, with a full-range of treatments available but nice say chairs with fresh peaches and plums, a locker room, and a wellness area with a sauna and steam room available to all guests.

Side note: the hotel has a cryogenic machine in the spa that will let you stand in -110ºC temperatures for three minutes…I was tempted and probably would have tried it had I been alone.

Thankfully, there was no drama this time in the sauna!

> Read More: Accused Of Being A Child Predator at Park Hyatt Vienna!

The fitness center is located in the spa area on the lower level, but accessible 24/7 with your room card and includes TechnoGym equipment. I awoke an hour before the kids and went down to workout…a nice way to start the day and fight jet lag.

You mustn’t skip breakfast here, for it is truly a treat.

The Bank is the most beautiful part of the hotel: an ornate dining room that was once the grand lobby when this hotel was still a bank. Breakfast is served from 7:00 am each morning until 10:30 am (11:00 am on weekends) and includes a delicious buffet plus an additional a la carte menu. If breakfast isn’t clouded in your rate, it is €58 each, which while steep is really worthwhile considering all you get with it.

There’s a bar section in The Bank that includes alcohol, including a large cocktail menu, and lighter food. It’s open from 9:00 am to 1:00 am on Monday – Wednesday, till 2:00 am on Thursday – Saturday, and from 5:00 pm to 1:00 pm on Sunday (good luck finding anything open on Sunday in Vienna…).

The hotel’s Viennese café includes cakes, coffee and chocolates, as well as alcoholic drinks and snacks, with an outdoor terrace. Open each day from 9:00 am to 8:00 pm.

Open from 9:00 am to 6:00 pm daily, the Lounge offers a more informal dining experience where you can enjoy hot and cold drinks plus a variety of food. Menu here.

Finally, 24/7 room service is available. Menu here.

There used to be really posh cigar lounge in this hotel, but now it is a beauty salon (Vienna has banned indoor smoking after being a smoker’s haven for so many years).

Our entire say was marked by one pleasant service encounter after another. I had a nice extended conversation with teh doorman and another great conversation with the agent who checked me in. We had a nice chat with our waitress in The Bank and the spa staff was also very friendly. I do speak German, albeit with an American accent, and appreciated that the staff was willing to engage in my less-than-perfect German as opposed to switching to English.

This was another wonderful stay at the Park Hyatt Vienna and I’ll sum it up by saying simply that I cannot wait to return.

My original review is below, dating all the way back to August 2014. Heidi and I went for my birthday just weeks after we got married…the hotel had recently opened and we had a great stay. It’s nice to see this hotel age so gracefully and what a joy it is to share this property and the lovely city of Vienna with my children.

Vienna is a stately city rich with majestic architecture, an erudite culture, and a regal sense of style. In the center of the old city, replete with cobblestone walkways, horse drawn carriages, and glistening statues of historical luminaries, a new Park Hyatt hotel has opened on the site of a former monarchical bank. My wife and I celebrated my birthday in Vienna last weekend and stayed for two nights at Park Hyatt’s newest property.

A historic property located on Am Hof 2 in the heart of the First District of Vienna, a UNESCO World Heritage site, the hotel’s location cannot be beat. Within a few paces is the Goldenes Quartier shopping district, St. Stephan’s Cathedral, Hofburg Palace, Spanish Riding School, and many museums.

We began the day in Frankfurt with an early flight on Austrian Airlines to Vienna. I sent a note to the main hotel e-mail, park.vienna@hyatt.com, just before takeoff requesting an early check-in and had a response waiting when I landed in Vienna – the room was ready.

From Vienna Airport you have two public transportation options for getting into the city – the City Airport Train (CAT) which travels non-stop to the heart of Vienna or a suburban train (S-Bahn) which calls at several stations on the way into town, taking about 15 minutes longer than the direct service. The CAT is 14EUR one-way while the S-Bahn is 4.40EUR. We took the S-Bahn into town, then connected on the underground train (U-Bahn) to Herrengasse Station, which is just a short walk from the hotel.

A smiling porter greeted us outside the door and took our luggage. Inside, a friendly young man checked us in, speaking first in English when he noticed my American passport but then switching to German upon the request of my wife that I practice my Deutsch! He escorted us upstairs and demonstrated the hi-tech features of our room. Like many Park Hyatt properties, lighting and draperies are electronically controlled by a central push-button unit.

I loved the room – a spacious standard room with tremendous natural light, a great view, and functionality. The room featured copious electrical outlets – an essential amenity when taking my business on the road, as I did here even on my birthday weekend. The layout of the couch in front of the bed in front of the desk nicely utilized the space in the room and the separate entry hall insulated the room from outside noise.

Two doors decorated in geometric art-deco style, closed off the bathroom and entry hall from the bedroom. The bathroom was very large (and well-placed mirrors made it appear even larger) and featured a sizeable bathtub, walk-in rain shower, two sinks, and a separate water closet.

A minibar featured an Illy coffee machine with several packets of complimentary espresso and snack and drink for purchase. The refrigerator did make a rather loud humming sound that could be heard even when the bedroom door was closed. I am a heavy sleeper, but my wife woke me up one night to “turn the climate off” yet it was not the air conditioning, it was the refrigerator! It was not terrible, just noticeable.

It was warm outside and we had a problem getting the air conditioning to activate. Turns out one of the windows was open just ajar – just make sure all your windows are tightly shut and your room key is in the slot by the door or else your air conditioning will not function. Once on, the room cooled down rapidly. Vienna boasts exceptional weather so most of the year there is no need for a/c anyway.

The hotel offers three dining options in addition to 24-hour room service; The Bank, Pearl, and The Lobby Lounge. Pearl bar features an outdoor terrace in addition to a contemporary indoor seating area and specializes in cocktails. A tapas menu is available with food as substantial as Wiener Schnitzel also available.

The Lobby Lounge offers drinks and light meals and sits next to the Living Room, a cigar and whiskey lounge that is one of the hotel’s best features. Admittedly, I see little value in setting fire to and then inhaling a plant that is linked to lung cancer but many of my friends and my brother hold a different opinion, so I find myself in cigar bars quite often. If you are a conneousier of cigars or just enjoy an opulent room to enjoy a drink in with friends, this bar is not to be missed. With plush couches and rich wooden paneling on the walls, I felt like I was part of the gentry mulling over world affairs in the cigar and brandy room onboard the Titanic.

Finally, The Bank is the hotel’s most opulent restaurant and central to the character of the property. Here, on the site of the former cashier’s hall, we had breakfast each morning. Breakfast was 33EUR and the buffet was expansive with all that you would expect in a comprehensive breakfast—fresh squeezed juices, cereals, fruits, breads, cold-cuts, cheeses, breakfast meats, and eggs. Coffee (it was tremendous) as well as pancakes, waffles, French Toast, and eggs are included in the buffet and can be ordered from your server.

We spent hours in here each morning enjoying a leisurely breakfast (breakfast ends at 10:30a during the week and 11:00a on weekends) and found the service to be warm, personal, and punctual. I thought everything was great – my wife had a problem with her eggs on the first morning (soft boiled eggs came out hard-boiled, then an omelet ordered with no cheese was delivered with cheese) but the issues were quickly remedied and did not reoccur the next morning. The juices were remarkably tasty (apple, orange, and even grapefruit were exceptional) and my favorite part of the breakfast was the cheese-covered cooked tomatoes.

Lunch and dinner are also offered each night in The Bank and you will find no menu posted online because the menu, sourced with local ingredients, changes often. Prices were moderate and I was prepared to dine at the restaurant for my birthday, but when mentioning that I was especially looking for fish, the concierge directed me to a restaurant called Kornat about 15 minutes away by foot, which specializes in fish and seafood.

So I missed trying out The Bank for an evening meal, but I did appreciate the restaurant recommendation for the food was amazing and we enjoyed a prime outdoor table thanks to a call ahead from the concierge.

I do have one gripe and only one true gripe about the property: the in-room wireless internet speed was unreliable. The Park Hyatt Vienna offers complimentary wired and wi-fi internet, which is a nice feature, but I found myself on multiple occasions banging my hand on the desk with disgust as poor connectivity led to unacceptably long page load times and the inability to make internet-based telephone calls. Other times, though, the interent worked perfectly well with pages loading fast and no issue with Skype calls or viewing YouTube videos. Admittedly, I did not not bring my ethernet cable converter for my MacBook Air so I was unable to test the wired internet speed.

A large fitness studio with state-of-the-art, brand new equipment was much appreciated. Several bikes, treadmills, and ellipticals filled one side of the room while strength training equipment and free weights filled out the other. The room itself, with brass candelabras and wooden floors was an elegant place to work out and apples, bottled water, refrigerated towels, newspapers, and magazines were available.

The gym overlooks the swimming pool below, which sits on the site of the former bank vault. With an ornate frieze relief and elongated white leather couches, it offers a refreshing antidote to the hot afternoon sun (or cold). Adjacent to the pool is a lounge with chairs to relax and also steam room and sauna facilities. My one regret is that we did not spend an extra day in Vienna just to lounge around the spa. Certainly, seeing Vienna is the priority if your time is limited, but this is a great complimentary benefit of the hotel that seems to go unutilized, as I saw many hotel guests and no one using the pool or spa lounge. Full spa services are available here in the Arany Spa and you can even see the original 3-ton bank vault door.

This hotel is a category six property, meaning it is 25,000 Hyatt Gold Passport points per night or 12,500 points plus a $150 co-pay (my preferred method of payment to help stretch out my points). The daily rate during the summer is about 375EUR or $500. Gold Passport availblity is good.

I can’t tell you how much I enjoyed the city of Vienna and both my wife (who is not usually a city person) and I wish to return soon. When we do, we will definitely choose the Park Hyatt again, allowing an extra day for the spa and enjoying at a more leisurely pace one of Europe’s greatest capital cities.

#6164. Why This It-Girl Ski Brand Is My Go-To Every Single Winter

If there’s one thing I take almost as seriously as chasing some good snow, it’s having the right wardrobe to go with it. I’m a lifelong snowboarder, a fairly recent convert to skiing, and someone who has spent plenty of winters bouncing between mountains on the east coast and out west. I’ve learned that the best of the best ski gear needs to do a lot more than look good in a lodge photo. It has to hold up through long lift rides, changing conditions, unexpected snowfall, and the occasional unglamorous tumble.

But that doesn’t mean style needs to take a backseat. In fact, I’d argue that the two should go hand in hand. That's a big part of why the popular ski brand, Halfdays, first caught my attention three years ago—and why I keep coming back season after season. Founded in 2020 by former Olympic freestyle aerial skier Kiley McKinnon and Ariana Ferweda, Halfdays came onto the ski scene with a refreshing take: women's ski apparel that actually considers women. Not just smaller versions of men’s gear or the usual boxy, so-called unisex silhouettes, but (finally) thoughtfully designed outerwear that takes fit, function, and fashion all very seriously.

Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is wearing the Halfdays Ashton jacket and Alessandra pant in Stowe, Vermont

The outdoor apparel industry has come a long way, but finding technical pieces that feel just as considered aesthetically as they are functional on the mountain can still be a bit of a treasure hunt. So as someone who has accumulated her fair share of ski and snowboard gear over the years, I immediately fell in love with the brand’s mission, and eventually, the gear itself.

While I’ve come to adore its ski suits, bibs, and winter jackets, Halfdays' assortment has expanded beyond the big-ticket ski uniform. The brand offers sweat-wicking baselayers, cozy fleeces, everyday outdoor staples, and chic accessories that make sense well beyond your stay at a ski resort. My favorite pieces from Halfdays keep me feeling comfortable and put together on harsh winter days in New York City too, from knit headbands that cover my ears to winter leggings and warm socks that aren’t too thick.

Of course, Halfdays isn’t the same brand it was when I first discovered it. What began as a ski-focused label has evolved into an outdoor brand with spring and summer collections spanning hiking, running, and more warm-weather pursuits. Its arrival at major retailers like Nordstrom, REI, and Backcountry, the opening of its Denver flagship (along with plenty of other storefronts), and a string of collaborations have helped solidify it as a functional brand for every outdoor adventurer.

Chapel is wearing the Parks Projects x Halfdays set on the slopes in Park City, Utah

That said, the brand has been having some fun with its fashion credentials, most recently teaming up with Gigi Hadid’s Guest in Residence on an eight-piece winter capsule. The result is a nostalgic take on mountainwear, bringing Guest in Residence’s signature knitwear looks to Halfdays' mountain-ready vibes, with playful retro details that feel just as at home at après-ski as they do on the slopes.

On the performance side, though, I’m excited about the brand’s newest launch: Halfdays has officially joined forces with Gore-Tex for its most technical outerwear collection yet. From down jackets and shells to bibs and mittens, the colorful collection brings together trusted waterproof, windproof, and breathable technology with the fit and design that initially made me fall for Halfdays in the first place.

As another winter of snow chasing commences, I’m giving my cold-weather wardrobe yet another Halfdays refresh. Below, my tried-and-true ski season favorites from Halfdays, along with a few winter staples I’ve got my eye on.

The Lawrence jacket is designed with Primaloft insulation, keeping you warm on the coldest winter days. It features underarm vents and an exterior chest pocket with an attached phone leash. Plus, the hood is adjustable, so you’ll get a perfect fit over your helmet every time. The jacket is best for bluebird days given its cropped length, but it’s also available in a longer version too.

I like to pair the Lawrence jacket with these matching shell pants. With a slim fit, an adjustable waistband, a water-resistant exterior, and zippered hems for snow boots, this pair is just as practical as it is stylish. Pro tip: Try these bad boys on with a pair of your favorite winter leggings underneath before hitting the mountain, just so you know that you’ll be comfortable and warm all day long.

Don’t underestimate the importance of a solid baselayer. The Johnson top features mesh underarms and a sweat-wicking finish, so you don’t have to worry about overheating in your ski gear. The long-sleeve layer also has a silicon grip on the inside hem, preventing it from sliding up as you move.

Pair the Johnson top with these leggings for a stylish, mountain-ready set. They’re sweat-wicking and feature a layer of mesh on the calves for added breathability. Even better, they’re versatile enough to wear off the mountain too, whether you’re shopping at a holiday market or strolling through the park.

Made with 100% merino wool, this chic Jacquard headband will keep your head and ears warm on the slopes—and it tastefully reps the brand too. I have (and love) it in the color Blue Fog, but it’s also available in black and red.

I’m obsessed with these Gore-Tex x Halfdays mittens. Along with the insulated, breathable, and waterproof design, there’s also a leather palm construction for added grip and durability.

I can’t wait to put this three-layer shell jacket to the test on my trip to Stowe, Vermont, this December. It has all the classic Gore-Tex technologies that make the collaboration so enticing in the first place: engineered with durable water- and wind-proof material, and breathable protection without added insulation.

For a matching set, grab this three-layer shell bib constructed with the same Gore-Tex build. With adjustable shoulder straps, a drop-seat construction, thigh vents, and gusseted hems, you’ll be covered and ready for anything, from head to toe.

Ah, one of the early Halfday classics. The tried-and-true Ashton jacket does it all, from ski trips to cabin getaways. With an adjustable (and removable) belt buckle enclosure, a helmet hood, and its many pockets for your phone and ski pass, it offers every bit of function you need for a full day on the mountain.

For those who favor a puffy yet packable one-piece, the Murphy ski suit is another one of Halfdays' original bestsellers. I own this bad boy in red, and wear it when I need extra warmth on the mountain. One thing to note: I’m 5'3", and it’s just a bit long on my legs when I’m not in snow boots—but it’s not very often that I wear the suit without them.

While I haven’t shopped the new Guest in Residence collection yet, I’m eyeing this chic ski sweater that looks straight out of a ’70s après-ski scene. I can already picture myself wearing it post-slopes, sipping on a spiked cider at the ski lodge.

For another vintage-inspired piece from the Guest in Residence collection, this cable knit inspired down jacket is all about staying warm in style. (And I’ve already added it to my cart.)

Get your hands on one of the Parks Project x Halfdays ski jackets while you still can. This gorgeous print is inspired by the Rocky Mountains—and I always receive compliments from other shredders when I wear it out on the slopes. Not to mention, it keeps me warm and comfy while doing so!

#6163. The Best Resorts in Turks and Caicos: Readers’ Choice Awards 2026

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in New York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best hotels in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View all of the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here, and the best resorts in the Caribbean here.

Turks and Caicos’s bustling yet beautiful island of Providenciales (affectionately dubbed “Provo”) has had its moment in the proverbial sun. Consider venturing southeast to South Caicos for a more intimate and undeveloped look at what are arguably the Caribbean’s most jaw-dropping beaches. The first property to put down literal roots with nearly 800 acres of primarily local vegetation is Sailrock South Caicos: a stunning, 40-unit property on the southeastern island’s northern tip where the Atlantic Ocean and Caicos Bank converge to house the area’s latest and greatest escape. Travel to South Caicos is also more convenient than ever with two direct flights from Miami on Wednesdays and Sundays via American Airlines. This means guests can now bypass a layover in Providenciales and reach paradise in less than two hours.

At the Ritz-Carlton Turks and Caicos, guests can sandwich sun-soaked days of lounging in a private cabana or on Grace Bay’s idyllic slice of beach with plenty of on-site experiences. A favorite for its white-sand beachfront and unrivaled centrality on famed Grace Bay, there’s no shortage of pursuits here—it’s a choose-your-own-adventure property with great amenities for young kids. 147 luxury ocean-view rooms and suites—with the Ritz-Carlton standard—awe and delight. There’s also a collection of luxury residences and penthouses for longer stays, each, of course, with stunning floor-to-ceiling views of Grace Bay’s turquoise waters. Interiors are all creams and whites with gentle pops of beachy colors, large windows, and pristine linens. As the most central property in Grace Bay, everything is within walking distance: the best restaurants, shops, and even a grocery store. For families with little ones, the Ritz Kids club is the place to be for guests ages 4–12. Drop the kids off and embark on the resort’s luxury sailing catamaran, the Lady Grace.

Basking on a coveted stretch of Grace Bay, this well-appointed resort is as lax as it is luxe. While there’s plenty of opportunities for R&R at the blissful on-site spa and for romance to blossom over candlelit dinners, the Sands at Grace Bay also know a thing or two about picking up speed. It wouldn’t be a proper Turks and Caicos vacation without hitting the water, and the resort provides complimentary access to a variety of water sport equipment ranging from sea kayaks to snorkeling gear to explore the mirror-clear seas. If you’re traveling with little ones who aren’t quite ready for the open ocean yet, there’s also kid-friendly pools and sprawling perfect for their next adventure. If you’re looking for a resort that grows up alongside your family, look no further.

Wymara Resort + Villas sits on the western curve of Grace Bay in Providenciales, just a 10-minute drive from the airport. It’s a place for travelers who like their luxury understated and favor the clean lines of minimalist design. Rooms and suites open to sea views and sun-washed balconies, while the villas—set apart from the main resort on a 15-acre peninsula—offer private pools, over-water decks, and personal hosts. The food is sustainably sourced: Indigo serves refined Caribbean dishes, and the Pink Bar is a magnet for sunset watchers. The spa, using island-grown botanicals and 111SKIN products, is intimate and calm. Service is polished yet relaxed, with staff who are friendly and will remember your preferences. Eco credentials are strong, from solar-powered electricity to refillable amenities. Complimentary wellness activities include yoga, pilates, HIIT, and sound baths, while evening entertainment leans local and cultural.

This mega-resort sets itself apart from other all-inclusive properties throughout the region with its family-friendly activities. There is a 45,000-square-foot waterpark and kids clubs for different ages, including one with Caribbean-ified Sesame Street characters, the Xbox Play Lounge, and a teen disco. For the rest of the family, there are 10 swimming pools, 21 restaurants, 15 bars (some of them swim-up), and access to the 12-mile Grace Bay Beach. The 758 rooms and suites are spread across five themed villages, with architecture that represents different regions: France, Italy, the Caribbean, and Key West. With 43 room categories, the resort truly offers something for everyone.

Grace Bay Club offers not one, but three distinct accommodations to its discerning guests: the adults-only Hotel building, the family-friendly Villas Suites, and the Estate, a resort within a resort, with exclusive access to dedicated amenities, such as a separate pool, cabanas, and more. Despite catering to different crowds, they do have a few common features, including spectacular oceanfront views and personal concierge service. Head to the oceanfront Infiniti Restaurant & Bar for bites of such fresh local fare as a warm South Caicos lobster salad, garnished with shaved carrots and crispy basil, or the Mahi Mahi carpaccio, with a kick of jalapeño, served to the sound of breaking waves. Looking to stake your umbrella in the sand a little while longer? Rent one of the homes in the Private Villa Collection, a cluster of five freestanding private beachfront residences that come with all the amenities and services of a superior hotel stay, including roundtrip airport transfers, daily housekeeping, and complimentary breakfast.

A fan-shaped trio of seven-story buildings curve around a beachfront pool and patio at this Grace Bay resort, close to Providenciales's shopping district. Enormous rooms in soft colors have marble baths and soaking tubs, proving that bigger can mean better. Staff members always serve with a smile and make a point of remembering names. The restaurant Seven dishes up Caribbean-inspired cuisine, with entrees like house-made stone crab ravioli, or you can opt for private beachfront dining, complete with a personal butler and a playlist of your choosing. If you're traveling with the family, the kids camp provides diversions such as lizard hunting and sand-castle building—or you can all go for a dip in the island's only heated saltwater pool.

#6162. Delta Air Lines Cuts JFK–Dulles Route After More Than 30 Years

Delta Air Lines will end nonstop service between Washington Dulles and New York JFK in February, leaving the two airports without a direct link. The cut removes another connection to Delta’s JFK hub and follows similar exits by United and JetBlue.

Delta will operate its final flight between Washington Dulles (IAD) and New York Kennedy (JFK) on February 10, 2027. The move eliminates the only nonstop link between the two airports (JetBlue cut the route in 2019 and United in 2014). Delta is not leaving Dulles, nor will this route cut eliminate flights between Dulles and the New York metropolitan area. United serves Newark and LaGuardia from its Washington hub.

But passengers who specifically want to connect at JFK on Delta or its partners will lose an option.

This route has run for over 30 years, so the route cut is certainly newsworthy. Without seeing Delta’s route economics, I’m not going to speculate how much money this service made or lost. But I struggle to see a large number of passengers who need this particular connection and cannot reasonably be accommodated elsewhere. I’m frankly surprised Delta operated a route like this for so long, which sounds like the sort of slot-squatting United does by scheulding so many flights between Washington National and Newark.

The case for this route has always been onward connections at JFK, particularly to international flights. But even there, Delta has alternatives. Washington-area passengers can begin at Reagan National (DCA), while travelers who prefer Dulles can connect through another Delta hub, such as Atlanta or Detroit, depending on their destination. I cannot imagine that there is so connecting traffic from Northern Virginia and the broader Washington area that Delta cannot handle it through DCA or another hub.

While I’m sure there will be “regulars” who are greatly inconvenienced by this route cut, that’s no justification to keep any route going and we do know the load factor was lower on this route than its network average.

This brought back memories of my coverage of United ending JFK–Dulles service in October 2014.

“Two-thirds of traffic on the route is connecting traffic that does not generate sufficient yields.”

United’s circumstances were somewhat similar. Dulles was its hub, while JFK had become a small station focused on flights to Los Angeles and San Francisco. Today, Delta operates a substantial hub at JFK, but it only flies to its hubs, now less JFK, from IAD.

In both cases the underlying question is similar: does the connecting revenue justify using an aircraft and scarce airport access on a short route when passengers have other ways to reach the network?

United decided it did not. Delta is now removing the same airport pair from its schedule.

More than 12 years later, I still find United’s explanation brutally honest as to why it cut that route (and eventually pulled out of JFK altogether).

I have written about Delta becoming more selective at JFK, including cuts to domestic feeder routes and international destinations. With air traffic control congestion and slot restrictions still in place, it makes sense to me that Delta would want to funnel less travel through JFK and more throughout other hubs: the focus must be on local traffic or at least costal traffic that can command a higher premium.

Meanwhile, United is preparing to return to JFK through its partnership with JetBlue. Does this create an opening for United to restore Dulles service? Perhaps, but I would think it would be difficult to work now just like it was then and has been for Delta. United already has extensive Washington–New York connectivity through Newark, and its initial JFK access will be limited. Each available slot will have more compelling uses via transcon traffic.

I do not think the disappearance of Delta from this route will make starting that route attractive to United, especially since United previously abandoned it.

Delta will end JFK–Dulles flights after February 10, 2027, removing a useful option for some Washington-area passengers connecting through Kennedy. Even so, the decision makes sense to me. Delta can accommodate much of that traffic through Reagan National or other hubs, and local Washington–New York travelers have several alternatives…so no, this isn’t a sign that Delta is continuing to lose ground in New York.

United cut this route in 2014 because connecting traffic did not produce sufficient revenue. Delta has not publicly supplied the same explanation, but the commercial question remains much the same. A “useful connection” for many passengers does not necessarily mean a profitable or smart one for the airline.

Back when I worked in Washington and flew to and from DCA weekly, I used to take advantage of Delta’s duplicative flights at IAD. That was also when a Sky Club membership granted you access to the Air France/KLM lounge at IAD even when flying Delta on a domestic trip.

For starters, IAD and DCA (along with BWI) were considered the same airport (coterminous) for purposes of same-day change.

Second, in the event of an IROP at DCA, you could easily switch over to IAD.

Third, upgrades in or out of IAD were marginally easier to obtain than upgrades in or out of DCA.

With all of that said, I do wonder about the impact on connections at Dulles since there are several SkyTeam carriers or Delta partners who fly into Dulles. Presumably, some of those passengers have onward connections within the US.

There’s very little if any “sky team” connectivity behind Dulles. Dulles and the region can support AF/KL/KE nonstops to their markets because the DC region is a huge wealthy region that generates lots of traffic. It doesnt rely on “sky team” connectivity to make those work.

The DL lounge at DCA and faster drop off-to-gate time probably attract many people who could fly DL out of IAD. But also, I suspect there are far more people flying out of the national capitol area to JFK to make Skyteam connections in JFK than there are people flying DL to IAD to make a Skyteam connection out of IAD.

#6161. Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from new software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin said “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work."

Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications."

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment."

Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a new one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and said their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

At issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

Yes, Serbia requires U.S. citizens to have a passport to enter.

Small tips are customary at restaurants and hotels.

Taxis are cheap and plentiful, but public transport within the city is free.

Yes, Serbia is generally considered safe for travelers. The U.S. State Department currently lists it as Level 2, so travelers should exercise increased caution, but no severe threats are present.

September-October offers long days with plentiful sunshine, while April-May is when the city starts to warm up before the full heat of summer.

You might have seen Serbia in the news lately. The country’s recent national elections enacted a political sea change spearheaded by student groups seeking greater freedoms and opportunities.

The jubilant energy unleashed, combined with the Serbian capital’s soon-to-shine spotlight as it prepares to host the 2027 World Expo make now the perfect time to plan your visit to Belgrade. That’s why the city made our list of top destinations for next year.

Sleepier than some other European capitals, yet vibrant and buzzing with a construction boom, Belgrade is coming into its own. It’s also easier than ever to get there, thanks to plentiful airline connections not only to other European hubs but also to the U.S. via the country’s national carrier, Air Serbia.

So start your points planning and make Belgrade a part of your next transatlantic trip.

The fastest way to get to Belgrade’s Nikola Tesla Airport (BEG) from the U.S. is aboard Air Serbia from Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport (ORD) or New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). The airline also recently announced that it will launch twice-weekly service to Miami International Airport (MIA) in May 2027.

Air Serbia’s main major airline partner is Etihad, so your best bet for booking award tickets is to use Etihad Guest miles. The program is a transfer partner of:

That said, award availability is hard to come by since these flights only operate a few times a week. Instead, you might want to consider redeeming Flying Blue miles for flights on Air France via Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) or via Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS) on KLM.

For Star Alliance flyers, award availability between the U.S. and Belgrade is plentiful on carriers like LOT via Warsaw Chopin Airport (WAW) and Lufthansa via Frankfurt Airport (FRA) or Munich International Airport (MUC) and Swiss via Zurich Airport (ZRH), starting at 42,500 Aeroplan points each way in economy and 75,000 Aeroplan points each way in business class. Taxes and fees range from about $100 to $150 in each direction.

Belgrade is expecting to see its first Intercontinental open in early 2027, just in time for the World Expo. Until then, there are plenty of other hotels where your points will come in handy.

Located in the new riverside Belgrade Waterfront District, which is home to a sprawling luxury mall, a promenade with tons of bars, cafes and restaurants, and more than a few high-rise apartment buildings, the St. Regis Belgrade opened in November 2024 in a striking glass-and-steel tower. The hotel has just 119 spacious rooms and suites with floor-to-ceiling windows, a beautiful spa with an indoor pool, a cafe-patisserie, a continental restaurant and an outpost of the brand’s signature St. Regis Bar. Rates start at $290 or 43,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

The Hyatt Regency Belgrade is a comfortable, modern hotel in Novi Beograd, the city’s main business district, across the Sava River from the historic core, so it’s not the best for leisure travelers. That said, you can’t beat nightly rates that start at $148 or 6,000 World of Hyatt points per night.

The Hilton Belgrade is centrally located near Slavija Square, within walking distance of attractions like the Nikola Tesla Museum and the Church of Saint Sava. It has 242 rooms and suites and a restaurant that serves contemporary Serbian cuisine. Rates start at $170 or 50,000 Hilton Honors points per night.

You won’t find Uber in Serbia, but taxis are plentiful and can be hailed via apps like Yandex, Pink Taxi Nova and Car:Go. The apps make it easy to pay with a credit card. Just be sure to use a credit card that earns bonus points on ride-hailing services or on travel charges in general.

Sometimes drivers will not accept rides unless you are paying cash, though, which you can also book through the app and then take a metered ride. So be sure to pull some cash out at the ATM at the airport before heading into the city.

Once in Belgrade, it’s easy to get around by public trams and buses, which are free to use within the city center.

Related: The best credit cards for commuting expenses

For a city of its size, Belgrade’s restaurant scene is surprisingly diverse. Of course, you should make it a priority to try typical Serbian dishes like grilled cevapi sausages with fluffy bread and ajvar red pepper sauce, and sarma, which is pickled cabbage stuffed with spiced meat and rice, not to mention the plethora of cured meats and mountain cheeses. Bela Reka is a great place to try a smattering of Serbian specialties, many of them sourced from the restaurant’s own farm in the Homolje Mountains.

Perched on the riverbank, Suvenir serves traditional dishes like roasted lamb and bacon-wrapped prunes in a beautiful setting.

For a contemporary take on Balkan cuisine, Iva is a sophisticated hideaway tucked into a courtyard near Saint Sava church where age-old dishes are reinterpreted through a modern lens. The piping-hot burek pastries stuffed with cheese, baked peach, hot pepper and honey are not to miss ($12), as is the confit river pike-perch with gnocchi and charred Swiss chard in a white wine sauce ($20). A glass of crisp Deuric Severna Morava white wine from the Fruska Gora region is the perfect accompaniment ($7).

Be sure to book ahead for a table at S5 by Angie, a fine-dining bolthole hidden in an otherwise unremarkable apartment building in the city’s quiet Zemun district. Spend a while enjoying a cocktail in the living-room-like parlor, complete with a vinyl record collection, then settle in for a multicourse feast prepared by chef "Angie" Risimic that might include dishes like creamy labneh with tart tomatoes, fluffy ravioli with mild ricotta-style cheese doused in a green herb and blackberry sauce with trout roe, and tender pork in a rosehip demi-glace with end-of-summer morels. Prix-fixe menu prices vary but range from $75-$150, though a la carte ordering is also possible.

For something more casual, spend an evening strolling cobblestones of Skadarska Street in the bohemian neighborhood of Skadarlija, just a short walk from Republic Square, where you will find over a dozen traditional kafane, or taverns, serving similar menus of hearty dishes along with plenty of plum-flavored rakija spirits.

Tri Sesira, or the Three Hats, was a favorite of the Serbian Romantic poet and painter Dura Jaksic, a statue of whom sits outside his humble former house nearby.

Belgrade has a handful of worthwhile museums, but not so many as to commandeer your entire timeline.

The National Museum has exhibits ranging from prehistoric artifacts to medieval Balkan icons, Italian Renaissance and Flemish masters, French Impressionists and modern artists, including pieces by well-known Yugoslav painters like Sava Sumanovic. Entrance is $3 for adults.

It’s free to stroll the grounds of Belgrade Fortress and Kalemegdan Park, which overlook the confluence of the Danube and Sava Rivers and are popular places for sunset meetups.

Some of the museums at the fortress have their own entrance fees and operating hours. The citadel dates to the third century B.C.E., though it has seen hundreds of battles and been destroyed, rebuilt and expanded dozens of times in the ensuing millennia.

Even if churches aren’t your thing, no visit to Belgrade would be complete without a stop at the brilliant white, copper-domed Church of Saint Sava, which is one of the largest Eastern Orthodox churches in the world.

The interior mosaics gleam with gold and are utterly breathtaking. Entrance is free.

Nearby the Nikola Tesla Museum is a fun, interactive affair. It offers guided tours every 45 minutes, but they fill up fast, so get there at least half an hour before the next one to line up. Entrance costs $7.50 and includes a short film, then demonstrations using Tesla coils before a small exhibit spanning the inventor’s life and some of his personal effects.

Sitting in a small park of its own, the Museum of Yugoslavia is a memorial to the former country’s late strongman, Josip Broz Tito, who rose to prominence in the resistance to the Nazi occupation of World War II and eventually oversaw every aspect of life in Yugoslavia until his death in 1980.

The complex includes his mausoleum — the so-called “House of Flowers” — an older building with some of his personal belongings and displays about daily life in Yugoslavia and a larger wing with temporary exhibits including a recent one on themes of propaganda in wartime. Admission is $7.50 for adults.

The pedestrian shopping street of Knez Mihailova is also well worth a wander, if only for unique souvenirs produced by Serbian craftspeople at the Belgrade Window boutique.

It might not have been on your radar before, but Belgrade is well worth a visit, especially with all the events on the calendar for 2027, including hosting the World Expo. Along with some luxurious new hotels and a growing crop of exciting new restaurants, plus a small but impressive cadre of museums and galleries, it might just become one of your favorite European capitals.

#6159. At Our Annual Points of View Summit, Experts Make Their 2027 Travel Predictions

When planning our 2026 Points of View Summit, we wanted to be sure to set time aside to hear directly from our travel specialists—the behind-the-scenes experts who work tirelessly work to curate ambitious and deeply personal itineraries around the world. Spliced between compelling panels on Lowcountry heritage, summer travel trends, and the evolving appeal of all-inclusive stays, the breakouts allowed for extended discussions with Traveler editors on a range of themes. From culinary experiences inspired by Hilton Head Island's Gullah cuisine, to the evolving dynamics of multigenerational travel and a new guard of ultra-luxe globetrotters, we got the inside scoop on where travelers are going and how they're getting there.

Jim Berkeley, founder and CEO of Destinations and Adventures International, speaks on culinary moments.

Inspired by Hilton Head Island's rich tapestry of culinary traditions, senior features editor Megan Spurrell and editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez led a discussion on traveling for taste—from the rising interest in foraging over traditional cooking classes to the draw of big-name chefs contrasted with harder-to-find local gems, and the hotspots that deserve to be on our food maps.

Our specialists all agreed that travelers yearn for “authentic” food moments, though defining authenticity—and actually finding it—often becomes tricky. To Omolola Campbell, sixth-gen Gullah descendant and executive producer of Gullah short documentary The Spirit We Move With, it's about who provides the experience. “Taking a cooking class is much different than getting it from a local chef who can tell stories about why a dish means so much to this locality,” she said, explaining how so many of South Carolina's Gullah dishes contain okra because its seeds were sown into the hair of West Africans who were brought to the South for slavery. The plant has come to represent resilience, and it's that integral context, according to her, that gives a meal its soul. “That's how you differentiate the person who really knows why they're cooking what they're cooking,” Campbell concluded.

Dana Kravis, Madison Flager, and our travel specialists explore multigenerational travel trends.

When it comes to multigenerational trips, the grandchildren are choosing the destinations and the grandparents are paying—it's their way of leaving a legacy amongst those dearest to them. During a discussion led by global executive director of video Dana Kravis and commerce director Madison Flager, our travel specialists observed that, because people today tend to wait longer to have children, grandparents are older than they used to be. Travelers in their 80s and 90s are increasingly joining trips, shifting the multigenerational travel dynamic away from the traditional picture of grandparents in their 70s. To trip designers, this means there must be layers of options catering to different activity and exertion levels.

Many in this session agreed the most successful family trips provide opportunities for separating and coming back together. Three itinerary choices in one day are ideal, so younger folks can be out and about, with the whole family reuniting for mealtimes and perhaps an afternoon activity. Boat and yacht experiences were especially recommended as spaces where the family is forced to be together—grandkids cannot simply run off and do their own thing.

What's luxury to one traveler might seem the furthest from it to another; some long for jam-packed, once-in-a-lifetime itineraries, while others want total disconnection and the privilege to do absolutely nothing for a week. Features director Rebecca Misner and commerce writer Jessica Sulima led this breakout, as specialists debated the definition of luxury itself. “Luxury is being able to pass on meaning to kids [and] exposing families to the broader world and its cultures,” Virgi Schiffino Kennedy, managing partner at Lux Voyage, said of its intangible appeal. To Ruchi Harnal, founder of Harnal Travel, true luxury “is not about the resort or the villa but the personalization of the trip.” As for who’s spending money on trips? Thomas Robinson, MR at Dehouche, has observed that Gen Z and Millennials are more inclined to spend but want to know where that money goes. Additionally, the specialists largely agreed they’re seeing a shift away from parents taking their children on trips, and towards 30- and 40-somethings treating their parents to a vacation. In Harnal's experience, milestone birthdays and anniversaries are driving clients to book a trip.

Between rising temperatures and overtourism, our specialists discuss the factors impacting European summer destinations.

What is the impact of overtourism, price inflation, and rising temperatures on our Euro summers? Director of special projects Lale Arikoglu and commerce editor Meaghan Kenny opened the floor for our specialists. “If you’re thinking of traveling to the Dolomites, consider Switzerland instead. There’s history and beautiful scenery with fewer crowds,” Brian Dore, owner of CIU Travel, said. For the hiking curious, some added that Switzerland offers plenty of one-day hiking trails or “soft adventure” travel—three-to-four days combined with a lake or city destination. Others agreed that traveling to the Alps offers a significant advantage—higher elevations means cooler temperatures—and that Slovenia is a great alternative to Italy. To dodge the crowds, travelers might also consider Belgium, Denmark, or Norway (where ocean ships and river cruises are opening earlier in March). For families, consider Umbria (hot tip: plenty of festival and craft opportunities for kids), Austria, Ireland, or Croatia.

For those who want to stick with more tried-and-tested European itineraries next summer, consider going as early as possible, for instance, in May instead of August. When it comes to traveling to France specifically, folks advised flying into Paris or Nice, then venturing out to the countryside or oft-overlooked Atlantic Coast. And our specialists could not stress it enough: Always, always check the temperatures in advance of your trip.

As discussed by Mei Zhang, chairman and founder at WildChina, during the panel on summer travel, the demand for travel to Asia is only increasing. Global features director Erin Florio and editorial assistant Kat Chen continued the conversation with travel specialists on the destinations and experiences driving this growth. For Silk Road Treasure Tours president Zulya Rajabova and her clients, it's the destinations with indispensable craft identities, such as Samarkand in Uzbekistan with its millennia-old design traditions, that make the continent so varied yet distinct. Meanwhile, Marigold Wood, travel designer at Blonde Atlas, explained that she's been recommending routes going through China, such as Yunnan's tea trails, which offer trekking and hiking opportunities. For Ethan Crowley, lead trip designer at Asia Desk Ltd, educating his travelers on navigating countries like Cambodia, beyond their most-visited landmarks, is key.

If 2026 was the year of the fan, 2027 is ushering in even more reasons to travel for entertainment. Associate editor Charlie Hobbs and commerce writer Jessica Chapel helmed this breakout on the sporting events, music festivals, and art fairs that specialists are seeing people travel for (and the subsequent hurdles they must overcome to). From Pink at the Sphere, where access requires a Venetian hotel package to the Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, where full-house and package buyouts, high-demand events are increasingly forcing bundled purchases.

The specialists also highlighted how limited legal protections in the States enables extreme ticket scalping for stadium concerts and makes domestic events increasingly unaffordable. Stephanie Malakie, founder of Empress Travel Club pointed to a related challenge: With so many events and providers, travel advisors find it hard to filter the options and identify the right fit for clients. Rather than just acquiring a ticket, specialists agreed the focus should be on curating the surrounding experience or tapping into evergreen and niche experiential travel, with events like the Jets playing in London or F1 in Shanghai. Cultural milestones like Vatican City trips featuring Papal Blessings or European Christmas markets pair well with entertainment, too. To Zhang, set-jetting to filming locations also offers value, minus the headache of peak-event ticketing.

Hannah Towey co-leads the breakout session on outdoor travel.

Everyone is hiking, or so it seems. Helmed by Jamie Spain, travel bookings commerce editor, and Hannah Towey, news editor, this breakout explored nature as wellness and why it is we're increasingly longing for all things outdoorsy. However, our specialists offered a frank reality check on our dumbphone fantasies. “Guests all want to have access [to Wi-Fi] for emergency reasons at a minimum… I don’t have a single guest who wants to [fully] digital detox," Kate Doty, trip designer at Geographic Expeditions, said. It seems that many travelers want to be disconnected until the time comes for true disconnection, and Lou Lagrange, trip consultant at Luxury Travel Advisor, added, “Even planning for national park trips, [you have to] warn them there won’t be Wi-Fi.” However, the group observed that services such as having photographers on small ships, helps reduce a traveler's dependency on their phones.

There's still a real demand for glamping, as guests want access to nature but with a side of luxury. And when it comes to extreme weather events, instead of having travelers write off entire regions or countries, Doty has figured out collaborative ways to shelve them for potential future trips. In Travel Studio founder Kerri Lisa's case, it's a matter of reframing the perks of a destination and its seasons; the rainy season, for example, might be exceptionally lush and green. There's always something to be learned in welcoming a bit of playful unpredictability into our itineraries.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6158. Aer Lingus Unveils Business Class Suites With Doors And Its First Premium Economy Cabin On A330s

Aer Lingus has announced a cabin overhaul for 10 Airbus A330 aircraft, with the first refurbished jet scheduled to enter service on October 1, 2027. The initial route will be Dublin–New York JFK, on select EI104/EI105 services. Additional North American routes will follow as more aircraft are refurbished.

This is an A330-only project for now: there will be no corresponding cabin overhaul for the Airbus A321LR or A321XLR.

The refurbished aircraft will feature 28 Collins Elevation business class suites in a 1-2-1 layout. Every passenger will have direct aisle access and a closing door, with each seat converting into a 78-inch flat bed. Improved bedding and amenity kits are also planned.

The renderings look attractive to me. Green upholstery and lighter finishes give the cabin an Irish identity and a premium feel (hello Singapore Airlines). More importantly, the layout addresses a weakness I encountered on my Aer Lingus A330-200 flight from Dublin to Los Angeles. I had a window seat with a passenger beside me and no direct aisle access. Storage was limited too.

I slept well, but the seat was behind what many competitors offered. The lovely crew helped redeem that flight, though warm service should complement a competitive seat rather than compensate for one. Doors are fine, but giving every passenger access to the aisle is the more consequential improvement.

Aer Lingus also plans refreshed dining and a self-service business class snack and refreshment bar, much like SAS offers its on its A330 aircraft:

The new premium economy cabin will have four rows of Recaro R4 seats:

Passengers will receive an upgraded three-course meal, complimentary drinks, bedding, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing headphones. It’s a hardly a unique or transformative hard product compared to its peers, but it’s an increasingly important middle way providing a noticeably more comfortable seat at a price that makes sense relative to economy and business class.

This fills an obvious gap for Aer Lingus. Someone who wants more room than economy offers but cannot justify a business class fare currently has limited options within the airline’s own cabin lineup. A genuine premium economy product gives that passenger another reason to stay with Aer Lingus.

Economy will retain the A330’s appealing 2-4-2 layout, with new seats and adjustable headrests. A self-service snack station is coming to this cabin too.

If I fly economy class, I prefer the A330 or 767. Two seats together by the window remain a compelling reason to choose an A330 when traveling as a couple, especially compared with being part of a block of three on most other widebody aircraft.

Aer Lingus promises more personal space, but we will wait for the final seat pitch and total economy seat count before drawing conclusions about legroom. A redesigned seatback can improve knee clearance without increasing the distance between rows, but padding is also essential.

The refurbished A330s will receive Panasonic Astrova entertainment systems, with 4K screens, Bluetooth headphone pairing, and USB-C charging.

Free Starlink Wi-Fi will also be available, though Aer Lingus says that service is already offered across its transatlantic routes. Passengers do not need to wait for the new cabins to benefit from it. My previous A330 flight featured an entertainment system with missing graphics and internet that was slow but stable. Working screens and fast connectivity would improve the experience considerably.

For a daytime transatlantic flight, I place enormous value on reliable internet. A better seat may help me sleep on the overnight journey to Dublin, but Starlink makes the flight home a far more useful part of my day.

The first aircraft is still almost a year away, and the announcement does not provide a completion date for all 10 retrofits.

An October 1 launch on select JFK flights should not be confused with every Aer Lingus A330 having the new cabins from that date, even to JFK. During the transition, you’ll be able to tell which aircraft have the new business class because that aircraft will also be selling premium economy seats.

I hope Aer Lingus makes the differences clear during booking and handles aircraft substitutions sensibly…

Aer Lingus is giving 10 A330s new business class suites, adding premium economy, and refreshing economy class, with the first aircraft scheduled to debut between Dublin and New York JFK in October 2027.

My last longhaul flight on Aer Lingus left me impressed by the crew but disappointed by parts of the onboard product. This overhaul addresses the seat and technology shortcomings that made me reluctant to seek out the airline. I look forward to trying it. Aer Lingus already showed me how pleasant its service can be. Pair that with a competitive seat and better catering, and I might go out of my way to book it again.

JSX is launching a new nonstop route between the New York metro area and North Texas.

Starting Feb. 17, the public charter service will connect Teterboro Airport in New Jersey with Dallas Love Field. Flights will operate daily.

The service will be available only to members of the carrier’s free loyalty program, Club JSX.

#6156. How I Travel: Audra McDonald Needs a Humidifier in Her Hotel Room

Theater legend Audra McDonald possesses one of the most powerful, lauded voices of her generation, a soprano so stunning that she’s been nominated for more Tony Awards than any other performer in history. So what elixirs, potions, and special teas does she keep with her to ensure the quality of her voice as she travels the world to sing? “I mask up on planes. I’m traveling all over the country to do concerts; I can’t land and be sick,” she says. “And I try to make sure there's a humidifier in the hotel room. Those are the two main things.”

While her role in the period drama The Gilded Age doesn’t require singing—yet!—McDonald and the many Broadway legends in the cast released a holiday album this month, ‘Voices of the Gilded Age: The Christmas Album,’ and the fourth season is currently airing on HBO. She spoke with Condé Nast Traveler from Australia, where her husband Will Swenson is currently starring in the Oz production of A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical, about traveling with their 10-year-old daughter, the unspeakable glories of New Zealand, and why you simply can’t top New York City in the final months of the year.

I don't think you can beat New York City. I've lived there for 36 years and it's always such a beautiful time. We have dear friends with a kid around my youngest child's age, and we've been going to the holiday spectacular at Radio City. My sister makes sure that she takes my daughters to The Nutcracker every year at City Ballet. We always try to go see the tree at Rockefeller Center. The one day I don't like in New York City during the holidays is Santa Con, but other than that, I'm down.

Her favorite venue on Earth in which to perform:

There's something about Carnegie Hall [in Manhattan] that is magic. I last sang at Carnegie Hall about six, seven months ago—I'm on the board there now, as well—and the nerves I normally get [before a performance] are always tenfold when I'm getting ready there.

Then the minute I step out on that stage, the hall just gives you a hug that says, You're here to do what you're supposed to do. You're supposed to make music, you're supposed to celebrate music, you're supposed to commune with your audience, and glorious sounds are supposed to be heard. Carnegie Hall is built for all the sound to be glorious. That [venue] takes care of me.

Don't worry about how they act up on a plane. Do what you can, but it's not the flight attendants’ first time at the rodeo. You're never going to see any of these other people again. When we flew out to Australia, my daughter got some weird stomach bug that started the minute they shut the door, and she vomited for the first eight hours of that 15-hour flight. The flight attendants just kept bringing bags and stuff and were like… [mimes a blasé hand gesture]. There was nothing we could do! We were over the ocean. I was giving myself grace. I was giving my poor daughter grace. I just wanted her to feel better, and I was doing the best I could. That’s what I would say to other parents. They’ve seen it all, so don’t worry about what other people are thinking. Everybody has headphones now! We’re fine!

I am not preparing for work! That's the ADHD in me. I am also not sleeping because I cannot sleep on planes very well, unless I'm really knocked out with the help of sleeping pills or something, and I don't like to do that. I try to watch movies, but I'm not good at it, either. My dad was killed in a plane crash about 20 years ago, so normally what I'm doing on a plane—when I'm not taking care of my daughter vomiting—is watching the flight path and seeing where we are in the sky. Then, if there's Wi-Fi, I check to see the weather ahead. Like I'm helping! I don't know what I'm doing, but it calms me down to be like, “Okay, I see that there is weather up ahead, so I should expect that it's probably going to be bumpy.” I don't know if in my mind, I'm thinking [as if] I can warn the pilot. I’ve got to go to therapy, but that's what I do on a plane.

New Zealand, holy wow. My husband and I were asked to sing on a Playbill cruise in Tahiti. We flew to Tahiti with our two daughters, and then I had three and a half weeks off before I started my Australian tour, so we went to New Zealand. I'm going to get emotional talking about it. Every place we visited—the North Island, the South Island, Queenstown, Rotorua, Hahei Beach, the Southern Alps, Christchurch, Wellington—all of it was just one wow after another. The people were lovely. We went to Hobbiton. We drove everywhere, and every second of it was mind-blowing. We even did the mailboat, where you go with this guy on a boat to deliver the mail in an area you can only access by water. I want to go back!

The destination she swears she loved before everyone else:

When we first start going, I wasn’t hearing about a lot of people there, but now everybody goes to Portugal. We have friends who live there, so we started visiting a lot, and not just Lisbon or the Algarve or Porto, though we love Porto. It was also the beautiful countryside and hills and tiny little villages. The topography there is stunning. It’s getting more expensive now, but we used to get incredible bottles of wine for €3! In fact, we have a farm there now, we love it so much.

Toothbrush and toothpaste. Not every hotel provides that, and I just love it when they do. If they've got a toothbrush and toothpaste in there, they've probably gotten a lot of the other amenities right too.

The farthest flung place she’s ever been recognized:

Here in Australia. I was in the South Melbourne neighborhood we've been living in, and I went into a little bookstore near my daughter's school, and someone recognized me. They said, “Were you the one who recorded Emily Wilson's translation of The Iliad book on tape? I loved your work in that.” And I was like, “Whoa, what? Yes I did, wow, thank you.” Doing The Iliad on tape almost killed me. It was the hardest thing I've ever done, so the fact that she wanted to thank me for it? I don’t think my mom knows I did that!

I really want to take a trip to Africa. Obviously, I want to go to Ghana and see where our journey started. I want to go to Kenya and do a safari. I want to go on a trek to see the gorillas. I've been to Egypt, to Cairo, but that's the only time I've been to Africa. I want to wait a couple more years, until my daughter's about 13, and then I will take her. That's going to be our trip.

You'll need a valid passport to enter the Cayman Islands. U.S. citizens do not need a visa for stays of up to 30 days, though you'll receive a tourist entry stamp on arrival. Make sure your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond your travel dates to be safe.

Yes, many restaurants automatically add a 15% gratuity to your bill, so check before tipping on top of that for exceptional service. Cash tips are fine, but many places also take cards.

English is the official language and is widely spoken everywhere you'll go as a visitor. You won't need a translation app.

Grand Cayman is compact and manageable by taxi, rental car, or ride-sharing services. Taxis are metered and reliable; rides typically start at  $8–15, depending on distance. If you rent a car, remember to drive on the left side of the road. Uber does not operate here, but other services are available.

The Cayman Islands are generally safe for tourists, with a strong police presence and low rates of violent crime. Standard travel precautions apply: don't leave valuables unattended, be aware of your surroundings at night, and keep a copy of your important documents separate from the originals.

November through April offers the best weather, warm and comfortable. In peak season, expect higher prices and more crowds. May through October is hurricane season, so be aware that even though direct hits are rare. If you're flexible, September and October can offer lower rates and fewer tourists, with the tradeoff of higher humidity and occasional afternoon storms.
