#6136. To Write ‘The Brightness,’ Chad Harbach Planned a Friends Trip to Block Island

This is Write Here, a column where authors and literary luminaries tell us about the travels they took to find inspiration and create their latest books.

In this installment, author and n+1 editor Chad Harbach describes his love for Block Island, Rhode Island, and a 2016 trip that informed a keystone part of his latest novel The Brightness. In the book, a bildungsroman that tackles topics like campus politics, the discourse around sexual assault, and the anxiety of being in one’s twenties, Block Island serves as the dramatic setting for a long, eventful wedding night that alters the lives of Harbach’s characters—particularly that of Pella Affenlicht, who originally appeared in Harbach’s 2011 debut The Art of Fielding. Below, Harbach recalls gathering his own friends for a summer holiday on Block Island as an excuse to refamiliarize himself with the destination as he began to write it in fiction—and the local peafowl that nearly made it into the book.

“In the early stages of writing The Brightness, one of the first things I decided was that the book’s centerpiece, the big wedding of the character Owen, would be located on Block Island, Rhode Island. I wanted the scene—which is now this 150-page stretch of the story, when all sorts of crazy things happen over a single, almost Shakespearean night—to be on the island’s eastern shore where houses are positioned at the top of these stone cliffs. I pictured an outdoor dance floor overlooking the beach and the ocean with the moon in the distance. Essentially I wanted to write the destination wedding I desperately wanted to attend. But as I was working on it, I realized I needed to go back there to check if my memories of the place were accurate, to have it fresh in my mind.

My then-partner and I organized a trip to Block Island with a large group of friends in the summer of 2016. We rented a big house and folks came from places like New York, Philadelphia, California, and Amsterdam. It felt like a wedding in that sense—everyone gathered for this joyous celebration in a beautiful place. We didn’t do all the terrible stuff to one another that’s maybe required for the juicy plot of a novel, but we did spend eight days cooking together, playing the piano, singing songs, drinking a lot, and staying up very late.

But we couldn’t sleep in very late because, well, there were these peahens. There was a sort of farm with animals, maybe a petting zoo, near our house, and their peahens liked to come and roost in the trees on our property. Every morning at 5 a.m., after we had been up until 2 or 3 a.m., the peahens would just start. I don’t know if you’ve ever heard the squawking of peahens, but suffice to say it was awful. It’s funny: When I started doing publicity for The Brightness, an announcement mentioned that part of it is set on Block Island. I got texts from friends who were on that trip, saying, congrats, we’re so excited, the fucking peahens better be in there. I initially did have this whole bit about the peahens, but there was so much going on in the plot that I cut them—not without really trying to make it work first.

Other than the loud birds, it was a great trip. The place struck me as just as magical as it had when I first went at 19 years old, when I was in college. I had a friend whose grandparents had a house there. I’ve visited several times since, and always loved it. But this was the only time I’ve ever gone somewhere for book research, and I was able to lock in some granular details like what the downtown looks like, the shape of the buildings, the sight of the marshlands, and what it’s like to bike out to the airport.

I was also excited to find that the feel of it was exactly as I remembered. Block Island has this rugged, natural beauty—it’s a rocky, tree-filled place surrounded by ocean, where everyone just rides bikes around, and part of it is a protected nature preserve. It’s sort of the forgotten sibling of Nantucket or Martha’s Vineyard. Some people don’t even know that Block Island exists, which keeps it from changing too much, even though it was settled by Europeans in the mid-1600s. The cemetery there has the tombstones of families that date back centuries, long before the United States became a country. I think some of those same families still live on the island now. So there’s this sense of continuity and timelessness.

Even before you reach Block Island, there’s just something about climbing on to the ferry and heading out into the open water, this freedom and openness that’s very inspiring to me. I grew up in Wisconsin, on Lake Michigan, which isn’t an ocean but looks like one, and I’ve always loved that feeling of vastness and mystery that comes with a massive body of water—that literal depth. It reminds me that we as humans actually haven’t mastered everything, and there are many things in this world that are not easy for us to touch.

All of this made Block Island a helpful setting in The Brightness. What happens on this wedding night propels the characters toward life paths that are very different from what they thought they were going to have, and having the story be imbued with the island’s sense of openness, possibility, and what might be feels fitting. As a writer, that can be part of the work: tapping into that feeling or gestalt of a place. It can be very easy to do at times, and difficult at others. And, you know, sometimes it’s just hard to write. So it was a great help writing about somewhere I love visiting literally and creatively. Instead of resisting sitting down at my desk, I’d be like, I’m ready to go to Block Island. It’s this setting I could picture well, enjoy being in, and keep traveling to—even if it was just in my imagination.” —As told to Matt Ortile

We’ve just witnessed one of the most significant air travel disruptions in recent memory.

The recent Federal Aviation Administration outage led to more than 18,000 flight cancellations over three days and left millions of passengers scrambling to deal with the fallout.

And that's just the latest air travel meltdown to hit the U.S.

In recent years, we’ve seen major travel woes triggered by bad weather, government shutdowns and tech glitches.

Our TPG reporters have covered all of these issues, and occasionally even gotten stranded at airports themselves.

In the wake of this latest major disruption, we’ve put our heads together to share some of our best tips for dealing with airport chaos.

When I fly, I am constantly checking my airline’s app for any sign of trouble. I monitor my incoming flight, and often spot delays or cancellations as soon as they pop up.

This allows me to immediately rebook myself on another flight.

When flight woes are brewing, it can sometimes make sense to book yourself a backup flight with miles, says Becky Blaine, TPG’s managing editor of newsletters.

“Don’t wait for the airline to rebook you,” she says.

Just remember to cancel it if you end up not needing it.

Most U.S. carriers will return your miles if you decide to cancel — just be sure you avoid booking basic economy on these three airlines.

Also, be careful about booking a backup ticket on your original airline. Some carriers will cancel one of your reservations if the system detects possible duplicate bookings.

Whatever direction you take, be decisive, TPG’s senior director of content Summer Hull suggests.

“Either be proactive, or be willing to accept that you might be stuck for a while,” she says.

If you’re going to book a backup flight with points, lock it in. If the airline offers you a flight option you like, take it.

During travel chaos, seats will disappear rapidly as other flyers pivot. And the longer you wait, the fewer options you’ll have.

“That will sometimes mean you might have wasted some money or points being proactive,” Hull adds. “But if you wait until you know for sure ... your options will decrease.”

Sometimes, it also pays to know when to call it quits and get a room for the night.

If the flight board is a mess, planes aren't taking off, and your chances of getting out are slim, throwing in the towel and getting a hotel room can be the smarter move.

This is another case where being decisive matters.

“Book your hotel as soon as possible if you think you’ll get stuck overnight,” TPG’s Eric Rosen says.

When there’s mass flight trouble, empty rooms near the airport can disappear fast.

These days, your airline’s app is often your best bet for rebooking yourself.

But if that’s not cutting it, you could be looking at a long customer service line or an even longer wait by phone.

TPG lead writer Katie Genter recommends a different option: Try contacting the airline via social media.

Some carriers will assist customers with reservations via direct messages.

Just be sure to have your confirmation number handy, because that’s the first thing the airline agent will ask for.

Most airline lounges have customer assistance desks, too.

If you have access to your airline's lounge, the wait may be far shorter there than down on the airport concourse.

Keep in mind, representatives in credit card-affiliated lounges are typically not able to help you with your reservation, since they don’t actually work for the airline.

When dealing with airline customer service, you can help your cause by doing your own homework, says Ben Mutzabaugh, managing editor of aviation.

He recommends looking up available flights and presenting the agent with options.

When on the phone with an airline agent, a flyer who has done their homework is able to come up with quicker solutions by saying things like: “What about the 7:30 flight instead of the 5:30?" or "I can fly into Newark instead of JFK" or, "I see this other airline has a flight to my city that’s not canceled. Any chance I can get on that?"

If all else fails, go back to the basics, recommends Carly Helfand, TPG director of content.

Her strategy if she’s not getting the answer she needs: "Be very nice, ask for exactly what you want, and hang up and call again. Eventually, you’ll find an agent who will give it to you."

Be just as persistent when searching for a replacement flight.

Often, the airline will offer you rebooking options when your flight is delayed or canceled. Sometimes, the ideal flight isn’t available, but that doesn’t mean it’s a lost cause.

“Keep checking,” TPG’s Clint Henderson says. “Often during irregular options, seats open up as people abandon flights.”

What is your top strategy for navigating flight trouble? Let us know in the comments below!

#6134. 11 Best Airbnbs in Stockholm for Historic Architecture, Saunas, and Beach Access

For a break that balances the buzz of discovering a new city with a good dose of fresh air, Stockholm’s mix of lush parks and eclectic architecture is an enduring choice. The city is formed of 14 islands, meaning you’re never too far from a waterfront to amble along. It's packed with historical charm (head to Gamla Stan to see one of Europe’s oldest medieval cobbled streets), as well as stylish boutiques and museums championing everything from Abba to the world’s best-preserved 17th-century warship. While the city is home to a slew of excellent hotels, from elegant converted townhouses to the former home of Astrid Lindgren (author of the beloved Pippi Longstocking book series), you’ll want to look to Airbnb for a real home-from-home vibe.

These 11 excellent rentals throughout the city and its outskirts balance top-notch amenities with the freedom that only comes with a private booking. True to Nordic form, there’s a clutch of homes with their own sauna and steam rooms, and all have either sea or skyline views. Below, the best Airbnbs in Stockholm to book for a weekend of weaving through medieval streets, gallery hopping, and lots of cinnamon buns.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic architecture, prime location, dedicated workspace

Subverting traditional Scandi minimalist sensibilities, this cool retreat in the hip heart of Södermalm channels a moody, more underground kind of charm. On the top floor, light-flooded, open-plan living areas are packed with rich, creamy furnishings and crisp architectural lines—multiple previous guests say that this is one of the most stylish homes they’ve ever stayed in. Downstairs, two tranquil bedrooms are carved directly into the exposed natural rock, so you can sleep beneath historic vaulted ceilings after a long day skipping from sight to sight. On that note: Södermalm is an eclectic area of town, with plenty of vintage shops and wine bars, after which you can hole up in this cocooning, cave-like retreat, as though you’re stepping into your own secret—and very stylish—bunker.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Riddarholm Church, Stockholm City Museum

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Forest access, indoor fireplace, outdoor gas grill

Blink, and you might miss this off-grid, A-frame cabin, hidden among a thick swathe of pine trees. It’s worth searching for: Once you make your way through the foliage, you’ll find a truly wonderful Swedish escape for two. The glass-fronted structure invites in all of the elements, while inside, it’s time to switch off—there’s a crackling open hearth where you can grill all of your meals, and precious little noise other than the rustle of wind through the canopy. Fair warning: There’s a very rustic toilet and seasonal shower about a 30-second walk down the forest path, so if you’re not a DIY fan, perhaps look elsewhere. Nonetheless, for more adventurous sorts, the trade-off means absolute tranquility surrounded by happily grazing sheep and twinkly starry night skies—all within a hop and a skip of the capital.

Neighborhood: VärmdöThings to do nearby: Lillsved Beach, Buddharama Temple, Stora Sandön

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic warehouse, steps from the lake, wood-burning fireplace

Wood-beamed ceilings, clattering floors, a muted color scheme, and a signature bright exterior welcome you in from the cold—this former warehouse just oozes 19th-century charm the moment you round the corner. Better yet, it’s totally massive, sprawling across three roomy floors, with a prime spot perched right on the peaceful banks of Åkers canal. A snazzy and social kitchen space opens onto a central island and a fireplace, where all the family will want to gather. When it’s time to bed down, there are cozy curtained sleeping nooks and an additional attic dormitory, adding a playful, rustic vibe. You can rent canoes from host Cecile to paddle down the canal, or jump on an e-bike to explore the surrounding nature reserves. When you return, fire up the outdoor grill and gather around the dining table for a long dinner with more endless views.

Neighborhood: Norrö-StavaThings to do nearby: Prästfjärden lake, Näsudden nature reserve, Åkersbro walking trails

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Sea views, sauna, hot tub

This joyfully bobbing houseboat turns the gray blue waters of the Baltic into something akin to your own front lawn—and it does so just 15 minutes from the heady sights of central Stockholm. Panoramic floor-to-ceiling glass means you feel that you’re virtually out on the water—and, of course, you can dive straight into the lake from your bedroom deck. Dry off and hop into the private wood-fired sauna to warm up. Hop off the boat, and you can sunbathe on the jetty, cook up some local catches on the barbecue, or jump into the complimentary canoe. All in all, this is an idyllic waterside playground that active types will love.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Kringelgården bakery, Saltsjöbadens golf course, Artipelag

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sauna, beach access, pet-friendly

Expect some truly good seascape ASMR when you stay here—you’re so close to the water you can hear the waves rolling onto the shore right from the porch. Grab the kayak from the cupboard and head down to the beach to make the most of this beautiful location. It’s a short drive from the home to Stockholm’s city center, but you’re rewarded with much serenity and glorious views instead. For those seeking a secluded family stay, this is the place.

Neighborhood: TyresöThings to do nearby: Sandholmarna nature preserve, Tyresta nature reserve, Lilla beach

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wood stove, sauna, beach access

This spacious waterside cottage is not in Stockholm’s city center, but by compromising on a 30-minute commute into town, you gain something really special. The owners took the original 130-year-old structure down piece by piece, rebuilding it on their own property. It was worth the effort. Now, it lies surrounded by pine trees in a nature reserve beside a sparkling, clear lake, with the sea just a few steps further in the other direction. A large porch provides the spot for barbecue dinners and sunbathing sessions in the summer, and there are two spas within walking distance for those looking for their Scandi sweat fix—the sea-facing Skepparholmen Spa, and Japanese onsen-style Yasuragi. But you don't have to head that far, as the property has its own sauna. Stay in as long as you can muster, then cool off by jumping in the lake—something all the more satisfactory in the winter months.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Boobadet Beach, Nyckelvikens wildlife refuge, Sushi Bar Namiyama

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Rooftop views, beach access, pet-friendly

A previous guest says this flat has a New York City vibe, and we can see why—the interior space is small but stylish, with an industrial bent and views all over the coolest part of Stockholm from the balcony. It’s on the top floor of this apartment block, so the vistas can’t be beat. It’s been a winner for those on work trips, thanks to superfast WiFi and a dedicated workspace, and, unusually for Airbnb stays, you can bring your dog too.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Liljeholmsviken waterfront, Högalid Church, Skinnarviksberget

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroomWhy we love it: Steam room, in-unit washer/dryer, fully equipped kitchen

For an Airbnb stay that’s as close to checking into a luxury hotel as possible, look to this plush apartment right in the city center. The whole place is brand new, and no expense has been spared on the fittings—there are genuine oak floorboards, Italian travertine surfaces, underfloor heating, and a slew of top-notch furniture, plus little touches such as a shower seat and a gloriously powerful rainfall shower. The best bit is the steam room; there’s no better way to decompress after a long flight or a blustery autumnal walk by the river.

Neighborhood: VasastanThings to do nearby: Vanadislunden park, Odenplan plaza, Swedish Museum of Natural History

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Proximity to metro, private patio, in-unit washer/dryer

If dopamine itself could be characterized as a building, it’d be this one. The place (all 300 square feet of it) is pure joy from top to bottom—with a pink-tiled kitchen, mint-green bathroom, and cozy bedroom nook with yellow walls and blue candy-striped bedding. Cheery artworks add a final flourish. Despite its bijou size, there’s room for two more guests on the pullout bed, and there’s a patio with twinkly fairy lights to sit out on sunny afternoons with a book, a glass of wine, or both.

Neighborhood: ÄlvsjöThings to do nearby: Älvsjö Forest Nature Preserve, Herrängens Gård, Långbro park

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Beach access, sauna, kayak

Forget your average homely fisherman’s cottage—this home here, on the cusp of the lake in the city’s swish Stocksund neighborhood, marks a newer, more modern breed of lake house. It’s chic as anything you’ll find in the city, with smooth, polished concrete floors and knotty pine walls finished with a moody, cocooning interior palette. Sweeping glass windows make the most of the beautiful views that stretch over the water and right to the city as it twinkles on the other side. Grab the kayak and spend an afternoon bobbing on the lake, then stop in for a well-deserved sweat session in the private sauna.

Neighborhood: StocksundThings to do nearby: Restaurang Hemma, Svanholmsparken park, Swedish Museum of Natural History

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Wood-burning fireplace, Aesop toiletries, garden view

This traditional Swedish apartment has had a modern facelift recently. Now it pairs gorgeous original features, including imposing 10-foot-high ceilings and whitewashed floorboards, with a sleek new kitchen and selection of cool designer furniture pieces. There's also a truly cloudlike sofa just made for cozy nights in. The surrounding streets are just as cool as the interiors; this home is smack dab in SoFo—by far Stockholm’s trendiest district—so you're just one street over from a clutch of the best of the city’s bar, restaurant, and café scene.

#6132. Alaska Airlines Eyes New Long-Haul Boeing 787 Route: But There's A Major Twist

Alaska Airlines is keen to fly to Lisbon, which is the capital of Portugal and an important destination for tourism. The oneworld member has previously expressed interest in flying there. A major ongoing stumbling block is the lack of slots, at least until, and if, Lisbon's new airport opens in many years.

As Ishrion Aviation has pointed out, Alaska Airlines applied for slots for a daily service to Lisbon. Unsurprisingly, it was not granted any of them. Slots do exist, but only in limited numbers and at particular times. It is likely that the growing US operator would either have to reduce its request substantially (say, to a logical three weekly flights) or accept inferior times, as WestJet did. Given Alaska Airlines' hub structure, a poor schedule would not be sensible.

The carrier has big plans for its long-haul network, although it is finding the going tough for now. Recently, it called its long-haul routes 'a drag', but they'd always take time to develop, even before the rise in the price of fuel. Against this backdrop, it'd be reasonable to question the appeal of potential future flights between Seattle, obviously Alaska Airlines' primary hub, and the Portuguese capital.

In the 12 months to September 2026, booking data via OAG shows that 22,700 round-trip passengers flew indirectly between the two cities. Obviously, that volume is small, although nonstop flights, along with hopefully strong promotions, would easily grow that by 40% to 50% in the first season.

Nonetheless, the supposed daily frequency would be highly excessive (three weekly flights would make much more sense). As such, it would therefore rely even more than usual on lower-yielding transfer traffic via Seattle.

Despite the low existing traffic, Lisbon is Seattle's third-largest unserved European market, excluding places like Athens, which Alaska Airlines has already announced. Zurich was the top unserved market (36,100 passengers), which stopped having nonstop flights with the Swiss leisure operator Edelweiss in 2025, followed by the oneworld hub of Madrid (25,500).

Of course, traffic (both existing and likely stimulated) is just one part of it. Across all airlines, cabins, and passengers, the average fare to Lisbon was $641 one-way (excluding a fuel surcharge, taxes, and add-ons). That was similar to Barcelona, to which Delta Air Lines began flying this year, almost certainly to get in before Alaska Airlines announced the route. However, Lisbon flights would cover less distance and be less expensive to serve.

The airline's international expansion continues.

More notably, and perhaps worryingly, Seattle-Athens had an average one-way fare of $646, which was less than 1% higher than Lisbon's. However, flights to the capital of Greece, which Alaska Airlines will begin on May 12, 2027, will cover 19% more distance and be much more expensive to operate. Of course, in these instances, and elsewhere where it is the only operator, it should get a reasonable price premium for the convenience of flying nonstop.

The carrier's debut to Europe took place in April 2026, when the first flight from Seattle to Rome took off. The launch came after Alaska Airlines began its first-ever long-haul service, which was to Asia. The first route was from Washington State to Tokyo Narita in May 2025, followed by Seoul Incheon four months later.

Alaska Airlines' Planned Operations To Europe: July 2027

Faces British Airways, Delta, and Virgin Atlantic

After Rome came London Heathrow (May 2026), followed by Reykjavík (May 2026). Next year, Alaska Airlines will begin flying to Athens (May 2027) and Paris CDG (May 2027). When writing, the carrier currently plans five transatlantic routes, with a big emphasis on leisure markets, just like WestJet from Canada to Europe. This is perhaps why Alaska Airlines has not announced flights to Madrid, in what would be a logical tie-up with fellow oneworld member Iberia.

Let's narrow the focus to mid-July 2027. In that week, Alaska Airlines will be one of 12 airlines flying from Seattle to Europe, which will collectively have 147 weekly departures (21 daily). Discover Airlines will be there, as the Lufthansa Group's leisure unit is replacing Lufthansa itself. Alaska Airlines will have 28 weekly departures (four daily) and rank second behind Delta (35 weekly; five daily).

Could they fly to South America? Like São Paulo

The Chase Ultimate Rewards program just added Cathay Pacific Asia Miles and Qantas Frequent Flyer as transfer partners. Eligible Chase cardmembers can now transfer Ultimate Rewards points to both of these programs at a 1:1 ratio.

TPG's Nov. 2026 valuations peg Chase Ultimate Rewards points at 2.05 cents each, compared with 1.3 cents each for Asia Miles and Qantas Frequent Flyer points. However, that doesn't mean you can't get excellent value by transferring Chase points to either program for an award flight; transferable rewards are generally worth more because of their flexibility.

Cathay Pacific and Qantas are part of the Oneworld alliance. This means that, in addition to Cathay Pacific and Qantas flights, you may also find award availability through these airlines on flights operated by other Oneworld alliance airlines, including American Airlines and Alaska Airlines.

Chase already partners with several Avios programs, which provide access to many Oneworld award flights. However, the addition of Asia Miles and Qantas Frequent Flyer gives cardmembers more ways to compare award pricing and availability across the alliance. Of course, not all award flights are bookable through every partner program, so you'll want to check award pricing and availability with each program before transferring Chase Ultimate Rewards points.

These two new transfer partners also provide additional ways to book award flights across the Pacific. While Cathay Pacific premium-cabin award space can be extremely limited through other Oneworld programs, Asia Miles may offer access to additional award availability.

Business and first availability between North America and Hong Kong is currently sparse even through Asia Miles, but you can fly in premium economy on some dates for as little as 52,000 Asia Miles one-way.

And if you have your eye on an around-the-world award, Qantas has a special Oneworld Classic Flight Reward that can cover up to 35,000 miles of travel on a single itinerary for 152,200 points in economy or 365,800 points in business. You'll need to fly at least two Oneworld airlines other than Qantas to qualify for this award.

You can also transfer points from several other transferable rewards programs to Qantas Frequent Flyer and Cathay Pacific Asia Miles. Now, Chase Ultimate Rewards points provide another way to top off your account when you're short of the miles needed for an award.

#6129. Mullin: Wave of Tech Failures May Be Linked to AI

Artificial intelligence could be playing a role in the cascade of high-profile technology failures seen over the last week, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Monday.

Mullin told FOX News’ Sean Hannity that he spoke with someone in the tech industry, “one guy who is very smart with tech,” who identified AI as a possible culprit.

“He said, ‘I believe that it’s the SI, because the programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is,'” he said.

The individual suggested that the technology’s ability to move fast and fix itself created “ripple effects” that overwhelmed older conventional systems. The secretary said that theory “kind of makes sense to me.”

The Trump administration uses the term “super intelligence,” or SI, in place of AI.

Mullin said his source did not want to be identified but ruled out at least one famous personality from the tech sector.

Multiple large, U.S.-based networks have crashed over the past week, including the FAA’s air traffic control communications system, United’s internal applications, Microsoft’s business services, and software used by banks such as JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo.

Mullin said there is no indication from the intelligence and cybersecurity communities that the outages are part of a cyberattack.

The FAA has blamed Friday’s nationwide ground stop on a faulty or improperly installed router, which flooded other routers with data and ultimately crashed the system.

#6128. 12 Times The Speed Of Sound? A Look At The World’s 1st Hypersonic Jet Powered By Hydrogen Fuel

Imagine an aircraft streaking across the sky at over Mach 12, which is twelve times the speed of sound! Moreover, it is powered not by conventional jet fuel but by hydrogen fuel, meaning that it produces 0% CO₂ emissions. Sounds like science fiction, but it may become a reality soon. That’s precisely the bold ambition of Hypersonix Launch Systems (HLS), the Brisbane-based company charting a new frontier in high-speed flight. In our article, we pull back the curtain on that vision: the promise of hydrogen-fueled hypersonic vehicles, the engineering hurdles, the history behind them, and where things stand today.

Pure research, defense projects, and a limited number of experimental flights have long dominated the race for hypersonic flight. However, we now see a company targeting hydrogen-powered scramjets for operational platforms. Why hydrogen? Why hypersonic? And what happens when you combine the two? We’ll explore how Hypersonix is attempting to create the world’s first hydrogen-powered hypersonic jet, what we know so far, and how these fit into the broader sweep of aviation and aerospace history.

Hypersonic flight, typically defined as speeds exceeding Mach 5, is one of the most significant challenges in aerospace: it involves extreme temperatures, air-breathing propulsion, advanced materials, and high energy requirements. For decades, most hypersonic vehicles have been either rocket-boosted (non-air-breathing) or scramjets powered by kerosene or other hydrocarbon fuels.

But the new trend is experimenting with hydrogen. On its website, Hypersonix states that its engines are “hydrogen-fueled for higher Mach” and produce only H₂O exhaust when using green hydrogen. Their proprietary scramjet engine, known as the “SPARTAN”, is described as “3D-printed, reusable, capable of reaching Mach 12 with no moving parts” in public materials.

The idea is that hydrogen’s high energy density per unit mass and its clean exhaust (water rather than CO₂) make it ideal for high-speed flight in the atmosphere. Combine that with a scramjet (supersonic combustion ramjet), and you get a propulsion system that ingests air at hypersonic speed, mixes it with hydrogen, and burns.

Of course, “twelve times the speed of sound” remains a very ambitious goal. Hypersonix is developing “the world’s first hydrogen-powered hypersonic jet” and mentions Mach 12 as a target, according to Interesting Engineering.

In short, the vision is to create a reusable, hydrogen-fueled hypersonic aircraft, or arguably the first hypersonic jet of its kind, with major implications for defense, space launch, rapid transport and sustainability.

In many ways, the heart of the story is the engine: the SPARTAN scramjet. Developed by Hypersonix, this engine is reportedly 3D-printed, air-breathing, hydrogen-fueled, and aims to reach speeds up to Mach 12 without moving parts.

3.5 meters long, hydrogen-fueled SPARTAN, hypersonic testbed.

8 meters in length, hydrogen-fueled, four SPARTAN engines, Mach 5-10 range indicated.

3D-printed, hydrogen-fueled scramjet, up to Mach 12, no moving parts.

Aerospace Testing International, Hypersonix, The Government of Australia

The technical implications are substantial: installing a scramjet, feeding hydrogen fuel at high Mach speeds, managing extreme heat loads, and manufacturing via additive methods (3D printing) all point to a transformative engineering effort.

There are some incredible hypersonic aircraft in the works.

Although Hypersonix is breaking new ground, the roots of hydrogen-fueled flight and hypersonic air-breathing engines go back decades.

Hydrogen-fueled aviation: Hydrogen has been considered a potential aviation fuel since at least the 1950s, with successful test flights in recent years on regional and general aviation aircraft using experimental hydrogen-powered engines. Hydrogen benefits include high specific energy and clean combustion (producing water vapor rather than CO₂). The challenge lies in producing and storing hydrogen (either in cryogenic or high-pressure form), considering the volume and insulation required, and integrating it within aircraft design constraints, ultimately enabling supersonic speeds.

The concept of “zero-emission” aviation often refers to hydrogen as a potential solution. For example, the concept of Zero Emission Hyper Sonic Transport (ZEHST), proposed by EADS/JAXA in 2011, envisioned Mach 4.5 using hydrogen and a combination of engine types, as described in the ResearchGate paper. At the same time, Airbus is conducting its own research to develop conventional, subsonic, hydrogen-powered aircraft suitable for passenger and cargo transportation.

Hypersonic air-breathing engines (scramjets and beyond): Australia has already been researching this technology for over 20 years. The university project HyShot (University of Queensland Centre for Hypersonics in Australia) in the early 2000s demonstrated supersonic combustion under flight conditions, as reported in another ResearchGate analysis. The idea of scramjets, or supersonic combustion ramjets, has been explored in many national defense and space launch programs.

Hypersonix is combining these two threads: hydrogen fuel and scramjet hypersonic propulsion, and attempting to integrate them into operational platforms.

This combination is crucial: hydrogen fuel is lighter, allowing for higher exhaust velocities (in theory), and when applied in scramjet architectures, offers a path to pushing Mach 8+ and Mach 10-12 regimes, rather than the Mach 2–4 domain of most supersonic jets.

The headline figure of “Mach 12” (approximately 12 times the speed of sound) sounds impressive, serving both as a technical target and a signaling device. But what does it mean, and what is the science behind these numbers?

Let's break it down. Mach 1 is roughly 1,235 km/h (at sea level). Mach 12 is therefore approximately 14,820 km/h (at sea level; 12,000 km/h at an altitude of 30,000 meters). At these speeds, the aircraft traverses about 245 km per minute. For reference, the International Space Station (ISS) orbits Earth at approximately Mach 22 (27,600 km/h). Imagine spanning continents in under an hour, with impressive cosmic speeds!

At the same time, technical hurdles encompass everything related to physics and its limitations. At Mach 12, you are in what atmospheric engineers call the “hypersonic regime”: flying in the Earth's atmosphere and not in space means that the heat loads on the airframe are extreme, the air begins to dissociate, shockwaves dominate the flow field, and engine integration (intake, combustor, exhaust) becomes extremely challenging.

That’s why it's easier to reach hypersonic speed in space than in the dense atmosphere. Materials must survive severe thermal stress, and aerodynamic design must maintain stability at high speeds and altitudes. Hydrogen fuel introduces additional complexity: cryogenic or high-pressure storage, fuel handling at high speeds, and mixing/igniting hydrogen in supersonic airflow.

But why does hydrogen help? According to Hypersonix, hydrogen enables higher Mach numbers due to its higher specific energy and cleaner exhaust. Their website states, “Air-breathing scramjet propulsion with no moving parts. Hydrogen-fueled for higher Mach.”

Why it matters: The practical implications of reaching Mach 10–12 are multifold.

Lockheed Martin’s SR-72 “Darkstar” could be real. From Top Gun fame to Mach 6 specs, here’s what we know about the hypersonic spy plane’s future.

What do we actually know about the current status of Hypersonix’s program, and how does it compare with other initiatives?

Hypersonix’s current status: Hypersonix recently raised US$46 million (Series A) to accelerate its hydrogen-powered hypersonic aircraft and engine development, according to Aerospace Testing International. This funding will support the NASA-backed launch of DART AE under the US HyCAT program, advanced manufacturing capabilities in Queensland, and the development of VISR.

Hypersonix is not the only company researching hypersonic flight. Other hypersonic propulsion efforts exist globally; for example, the Franco-Swiss company Destinus Aerospace (Destinus) is developing a hypersonic hydrogen-fueled UAV and passenger aircraft concept.

Currently, the vast majority of traditional hypersonic programs (especially for the military) use kerosene-fueled scramjets or rocket boosters + glide vehicles. Hypersonix’s unique angle is combining hydrogen and scramjets for operational platforms.

The broader aerospace and defense context sees many nations investing heavily in hypersonics (US, China, Russia, Australia), both for strategic reasons and for commercial purposes.

However, there are numerous challenges to making this sci-fi technology a reality. First, demonstration flights are still pending; claims of Mach 12 targets remain unproven in sustained atmospheric flight. Secondly, hydrogen storage on aircraft remains non-trivial, as volume, insulation, cryogenics, and high-pressure systems all add weight and complexity. Additionally, reusable hypersonic air-breathing vehicles are, by definition, more complex than one-off testbeds; therefore, transitioning to a fully operational “jet” is a steep climb. Lastly, thermal management, engine life, material fatigue, and aerodynamic control at hypersonic speeds remain active areas of research.

Thus, while the ambition is real, operationalization is still in progress. But Hypersonix's securing major funding and being under contract via the US DIU/HyCAT program is a strong signal of industry confidence.

The potential of hydrogen-powered hypersonic flight reaches far beyond breaking speed records. If Hypersonix succeeds, the implications for global transport, defense, and space access could be transformative. A hydrogen-fueled jet capable of Mach 12 could cut intercontinental travel from hours to minutes, letting passengers or cargo move between continents in the time it takes to watch a short film. In logistics, that same speed could deliver critical supplies and equipment across the globe almost instantly. Meanwhile, in the space sector, reusable hypersonic craft could serve as the first stage of orbital launch systems, cutting costs and emissions at the same time.

For aviation, hydrogen is not merely a cleaner alternative but a catalyst for higher performance. Its high energy density allows sustained propulsion at hypersonic speeds while emitting only water vapor when burned with oxygen. Hypersonix’s SPARTAN engine embodies this balance between speed and sustainability, meaning that “green flight” and record-breaking velocity can coexist. The company’s focus on reusability is equally important: if hypersonic vehicles can fly repeatedly rather than serve as expendable testbeds, the economics of high-speed flight could change overnight, paving the way for commercial viability.

As Hypersonix co-founder Dr. Michael Smart explains, the SPARTAN is “more than a propulsion system - it’s a breakthrough in reusable hypersonic flight.” His words highlight a broader vision: one where clean hydrogen power, efficient manufacturing, and revolutionary speed come together into a practical aviation platform. With the DART AE and VISR programs progressing and hydrogen scramjets moving from laboratory tests to the runway, the line between today’s aerospace science and future air travel is starting to blur. The era of sustainable hypersonic flight might arrive sooner than anyone expected.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

There is no material that would allow those speeds inside the atmosphere. Why would someone write such unscientific junk?

#6127. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

Some pretty significant changes are coming for Hyatt loyalists in 2027.

After introducing a five-tier award chart and annual category changes this May, we weren't sure what to expect with this announcement — but the good news is that the updates are largely positive, save for a few changes that might frustrate higher-tier members.

"We’re shaping the future of World of Hyatt around what our members value most. After a year of listening, one thing is clear: members want more distinctive benefits, more freedom to use their awards, and the opportunity to choose awards that matter most to them,” said Laurie Blair, senior vice president, global marketing and loyalty, Hyatt. “We’re continuing to deliver more of what members want, with the ability to combine valuable awards, earn Tier Qualifying Nights faster, and choose more of the experiences they love. Together, these new options make every milestone a chance to personalize the journey ahead."

From a newly minted Delta partnership (with exciting double-dipping benefits) and more flexibility with awards and earnings, here is what we know about the changes, which will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Related: Complete guide to the World of Hyatt loyalty program

For years, Hyatt has allowed members to redeem one award per stay. If you wanted to use a Category 1-7 certificate, you couldn't also use a Suite Upgrade Award. If you gifted Category 1-4 certificates to friends or family members, they couldn't also use Guest of Honor awards to receive your Globalist benefits.

Starting Jan. 1, members will be able to stack Free Night Awards, Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards and Free Parking Awards (more on this in a bit) on the same reservation. This is a fantastic improvement that addresses a key frustration for many loyal members, who currently must carefully pick which award makes the most sense on a given stay.

In addition, all awards will now be available for 365 days from the date of issuance.

This is great news for the free-night certificates you earn through Hyatt's Milestone Rewards, which were previously valid for only six months. Next year, you'll have twice as much time to use them.

However, this will negatively impact Suite Upgrade Awards.

Today, you can select these upgrades starting at 40 nights, and when you do, they're valid through the end of the year plus an additional 14 months. Now, they'll have a shorter window of validity — potentially much shorter.

For example, if you reached 40 nights on Aug. 1, 2026, and immediately picked a Suite Upgrade Award, it'll expire Feb. 28, 2028 — giving you 19 months to use it. If you hit that same threshold on July 15, 2027, and again picked an upgrade immediately, it'll only be valid through July 14, 2028.

You'll still have up to 90 days to select each milestone reward, so come 2027, you may want to wait until the end of that window to commit to an upgrade award if you don't have an immediate use for it.

Related: How to redeem Hyatt points for free nights and more

One of the biggest changes within this update to the World of Hyatt program is the flexibility of Milestone Rewards — and the rewards themselves. Starting in January, Milestone Rewards will now begin at 10 qualifying nights or 20,000 Base Points, with additional milestones every 10 qualifying nights, up to 150 nights per calendar year.

Additionally, the company has added a handful of new awards, including the following:

Here is a full breakdown of your choices starting Jan. 1, 2027:

In addition to the new options, you'll have additional flexibility at certain milestones.

For example, the 30-night milestone is currently a Category 1-4 certificate plus a choice of other options. Now, you can choose between that award or 10,000 bonus points, plus a second choice among five options. And at 60 nights, rather than the one-size-fits-all approach, with the same four rewards for every member, you now get to pick three of the four.

Unfortunately, there are three (potentially) negative changes to flag here:

Losing free parking on award stays is a notable loss, as is the reduction in Suite Upgrade Awards. That said, just how impactful these are will depend on your individual stay habits.

In September, Delta and Hyatt announced an upcoming partnership, and we've finally learned about the details — and yes, elite SkyMiles and World of Hyatt members will be able to "double-dip" with their hotel stay and flight earnings.

As noted by TPG writer Sean Cudahy, there are two primary things to keep in mind about the Delta-Hyatt partnership:

When Delta SkyMiles and World of Hyatt members link their accounts, they'll be able to access the new Delta Milestone Rewards detailed above starting in 2027. These rewards start at 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 Base Points and include eCertificates, Delta Sky Club passes and even opportunities to earn Medallion Status.

Finally, World of Hyatt will also debut an updated booking flow through its app and website that will make it easier to tailor your trip to your needs and rewards. Right now, the "Pay My Way" options are fairly limited — essentially just cash or points. The new flow will give much more flexibility.

"Members can select, gift and redeem eligible awards online or in the World of Hyatt app, while an enhanced Pay My Way experience will let members tailor payment for each night using awards, points, cash or Points + Cash," the company shared in the press release.

Overall, we're calling these changes a net positive. The ability to combine awards on a single stay is the standout here, and it's great to have the extra time to use many awards that currently have a very limited window. The new Delta-Hyatt tie-up is also exciting, with reciprocal earning opportunities for elite members of each program. Finally, it's great to see an expanded list of Milestone Rewards and additional flexibility in customizing them.

That said, there are some notable drawbacks here, especially the loss of free parking on award stays for Globalists — though it's nice to have a transition period through February 2028 before that takes effect for existing Globalists.

As a reminder, these new perks won't launch until Jan. 1, 2027, so it's status quo until then.

The World of Hyatt program is making several changes that'll impact its most frequent guests starting in 2027. Between the long-awaited benefit of being able to combine awards, a slew of new Milestone Rewards and some shiny new partner perks with Delta, Hyatt is adding a lot of new potential value for members. Of course, it's not all positive — but many of us here at TPG are excited about what's to come.

What do you think about these program updates? Feel free to sound off in the comments section below!

JSX, the boutique semi-private flight operator, is launching a new daily route between New York City and Dallas, the company announced this week.

The new service will fly to Dallas Love Field (DAL) starting on Feb. 17, with one daily flight in each direction.

JSX did not immediately disclose which airport in New York it plans to fly from. JSX typically flies to New York’s Teterboro Airport (TEB) and Westchester County Airport (HPN), although various restrictions set by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey mean that JSX cannot publicly promote TEB as a destination.

Those restrictions limit JSX to only selling those New York flights to members of its free Club JSX program, which offers rewards and has no minimum spending or flying requirements. When logged into that platform, the new route is currently bookable from TEB.

Club JSX: Earn rewards and fly in comfort with JSX’s new loyalty program

The carrier will use its Embraer E145 aircraft on the route, which can seat up to 30 passengers in a 1-1 configuration. Introductory fares start at $799 one-way.

"New York City and Dallas are two of America's most influential business and cultural centers, and we believe traveling between them should be as seamless as the opportunities that connect them,” Alex Wilcox, CEO of JSX, said in a statement. "With this new daily service, we're bringing the simplicity, comfort, and convenience of JSX to one of the country's most important travel corridors."

The new flight to Dallas is JSX second New York City expansion in as many weeks; the carrier announced new flights between New York and Boston earlier this month. The Dallas route is the company's fifth route from New York — aside from Boston, JSX flies from New York to Fort Lauderdale Executive Airport (FXE); Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport (OPF); Naples Airport (APF); and President Donald J. Trump International Airport (DJT), formerly known as Palm Beach International, all in Florida.

JSX operates out of 30 airports across the U.S. and Mexico and functions as a public charter service, rather than a formal "airline." This lets the carrier's flights work more like private ones — although anyone can buy a ticket, the flights use posh private Fixed-Base Operators (FBOs) instead of public airport terminals. That allows passengers to venture from curb to seat in just 20 minutes.

More: JSX eyes more turboprops and new mountain routes after strong passenger response

The flight experience itself is equally luxurious with no middle seats, lots of legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, complimentary snacks and drinks and checked luggage that’s returned right at the side of the plane. The carrier has a fleet of 56 ERJ-family jets and 4 ATR 42-600 turboprop aircraft. Overall, the service pitches the idea of private jet convenience for a fraction of the cost.

JSX passengers used to bypass security screening, like passengers on most private flights. In 2025, the carrier implemented its own in-house screening process to address security concerns.

#6124. Barry Goldwater Saw a Way Out of the Wilderness

No matter how federal elections turn out, there’s always work to be done at the state and local levels.

Senator Barry Goldwater addresses supporters in Arizona during his 1964 presidential campaign.

Hulton-Deutsch Collection/Corbis via Getty Images

Barry Goldwater was acquainted with political setbacks. The morning after the 1964 presidential election, he could count the states he had won on two hands. Harder to number were the Americans who had spent that fall knocking on doors for the first time because a senator from Arizona had given voice to something they believed. Goldwater had asked them to help Americans reclaim power from Washington.

After the loss, Goldwater urged his supporters not to give up the fight for free markets, smaller government, and the American family. It was the collective conviction that Americans could build better lives for their families if they could keep more of what they earned and decide for themselves how to raise their children that kept these people invested in American politics.

Victor Riches is the President and CEO of the Goldwater Institute, leading the Institute’s efforts to help people in all 50 states live freer, happier lives.

#6123. Aer Lingus to Introduce First Premium Economy Cabin

Aer Lingus is moving to upgrade the widebody aircraft operating its transatlantic network.

The carrier said Wednesday that it will introduce its first-ever Premium Economy cabin on 10 refurbished Airbus A330s. The aircraft will also get upgraded Business Class seats – now enclosed as suites – and an improved Economy section.

“[This] is a transformation of the entire experience across our A330 fleet, elevating Business Class, Economy, and, for the first time in Aer Lingus history, introducing Premium Economy,” CEO Lynne Embleton said in a news release. “We want to give our customers greater choice, comfort, and connectivity while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus.”

The upgraded Business Class will have 28 Collins Elevation suites in a 1-2-1 configuration, giving each passenger direct aisle access. Each seat will have a fully flat bed, a closing door, enhanced bedding, and “well-being amenities.” A self-service snack and refreshment bar will also be available.

The carrier will also roll out new Economy seats with more personal space and six-way adjustable leather headrests.

New interior elements will tie the three cabins together, officials said. Plans call for mood lighting, artwork reflecting Irish landscapes, and custom fabrics in colors inspired by the sea.

All seats will have larger 4K high-definition entertainment screens, Bluetooth headphone connectivity, USB-C charging ports, and access to Starlink wireless internet. Starlink is already available across all of Aer Lingus’ transatlantic routes.

The first of the overhauled A330s will reenter service in October 2027, flying between Dublin and New York-JFK. The new cabin experience will become available on additional North American routes as work on the remaining A330s is completed.

Aer Lingus serves a total of 20 destinations across the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, including Boston, Newark, New Jersey, Miami, Los Angeles, Toronto, and Cancún.

#6122. Delta Air Lines' Basic Business Fare Keeps The Lie-Flat Seat, But Lounge Access Ends In 2027

Delta Air Lines has introduced a cheaper way for passengers to experience its Delta One business class cabin, but the lower price comes with some significant compromises. Its new Basic Business fare retains the features that matter most to many premium travelers, such as the lie-flat seat, alongside premium dining and priority boarding. However, passengers choosing this entry-level ticket will receive fewer benefits before and after their flight, with restrictions covering seat selection, flight changes, frequent flyer earnings, and eventually lounge access.

The most important change is scheduled for January 19, 2027, when Basic Business passengers will lose access to Delta One Lounges and dedicated Delta One check-in facilities. Until then, travelers can still enjoy these ground services, creating a temporary period in which the product offers more than its long-term structure promises. The development highlights how airlines are increasingly dividing business class into different price levels without necessarily changing the onboard experience.

Delta Air Lines introduced Basic Business in July 2026, with the fare becoming available for flights from September. The new option is designed to attract passengers who want a premium long-haul experience but are unwilling to pay the higher prices associated with traditional business class tickets. Rather than removing the lie-flat seat, Delta Air Lines has chosen to unbundle several benefits traditionally associated with its Delta One cabin.

This means passengers still receive the central feature of business class, allowing them to recline into a fully flat sleeping position on applicable aircraft. Premium dining also remains included, meaning travelers do not have to sacrifice the main onboard comforts that distinguish Delta One from economy and premium economy. Zone 1 boarding is another benefit that remains available, giving Basic Business passengers priority when boarding begins. However, the lower fare is not simply a discounted version of the existing Delta One ticket. It introduces restrictions that affect the journey at several stages, particularly when passengers want greater control over their seats or need to change their travel arrangements. These differences matter because business class travelers often value flexibility just as much as comfort, especially when flying internationally for work.

The distinction also gives Delta Air Lines another way to manage demand across its premium cabins. Some passengers may accept fewer benefits in exchange for a lower ticket price, while others will prefer paying extra for a more comprehensive experience. By introducing multiple fare levels within the same cabin, the SkyTeam carrier can appeal to both groups without redesigning its existing business class product.

The decision to retain the lie-flat seat is arguably the most important part of the Basic Business offering. For passengers traveling overnight or on long international routes, the ability to sleep horizontally can make a considerable difference to the journey. Removing this feature would have made the cheaper fare considerably less attractive, particularly when competing airlines continue to promote their premium cabins as places where passengers can rest comfortably.

Basic Business travelers also retain access to Delta One's premium dining experience. This means the cheaper ticket does not automatically translate into a reduced meal service, with passengers continuing to receive the elevated onboard food and beverage experience associated with the cabin. For travelers who primarily judge business class by the quality of the seat, food, and sleeping arrangements, this could make the entry-level fare appealing.

Zone 1 boarding is another important inclusion because it allows passengers to board ahead of most other travelers. This can be particularly useful on busy international departures, when finding overhead storage space and settling into a seat without unnecessary delays can improve the experience. Retaining this priority also means Basic Business passengers will not feel entirely separated from other Delta One travelers when entering the aircraft.

The latest data from ch-aviation shows that Delta Air Lines currently operates a fleet of 1,005 aircraft, with a further 319 on order, including 20 Airbus A350-1000 and 30 Boeing 787-10 aircraft, as shown in the table below:

*Not all aircraft of this type feature Delta One

Nevertheless, the similarities largely end with the onboard experience. Passengers choosing Classic or Extra fares retain additional benefits that are no longer included with Basic Business, making the differences between ticket categories more noticeable outside the aircraft. The product is therefore designed for travelers who prioritize the physical business class experience but are comfortable giving up some traditional premium conveniences.

The US legacy carrier is slashing business class prices.

One of the clearest restrictions concerns seat assignments, which are only provided after check-in for Basic Business passengers. This is a meaningful difference from more expensive Delta One fares, where travelers generally have greater control over selecting their preferred seats before departure. Passengers who want a particular position in the cabin may find the arrangement inconvenient.

Some markets may offer the opportunity to purchase advance seat selection separately, but this does not change the underlying structure of the fare. Travelers will need to consider whether paying extra for a specific seat makes the cheaper ticket worthwhile, particularly when comparing the final cost against the Classic option. For couples and colleagues, the uncertainty could be an important disadvantage.

Basic Business also excludes same-day confirmed flight changes and standby options. These benefits can be valuable when business meetings finish earlier than expected, connecting arrangements change, or passengers want to take an earlier departure. Without these options, travelers have less flexibility to adjust their plans on the day of travel, even when alternative flights have available seats.

Importantly, Delta Air Lines has confirmed that Medallion status does not restore these excluded same-day benefits. This is a significant departure from the expectations of frequent flyers accustomed to receiving additional flexibility through their loyalty status. Even passengers with an established relationship with the airline must accept the Basic Business restrictions, making the choice of fare particularly important for those whose schedules frequently change.

The most significant upcoming change involves access to Delta One Lounges and dedicated Delta One check-in facilities. Basic Business passengers currently retain these privileges, meaning travelers purchasing the entry-level fare can still enjoy the premium airport experience during the initial introduction period. However, this benefit will not continue indefinitely, with January 19, 2027, established as the cutoff date. From that date, passengers traveling on Basic Business tickets will no longer qualify for Delta One Lounge access through their fare. The dedicated Delta One check-in experience will also disappear from the package, creating a more noticeable difference between the entry-level ticket and higher-priced alternatives. The change effectively moves Basic Business further away from the traditional all-inclusive business class experience. The importance of this restriction becomes clearer when considering the role airport facilities play in premium travel. Delta One Lounges provide an environment where eligible passengers can relax, eat, and prepare for long-haul journeys away from busier public terminal areas. Dedicated check-in facilities also make the airport experience more convenient, particularly during busy departure periods.

For passengers booking flights before the deadline, the timing of travel will matter considerably. A ticket purchased months in advance will not necessarily guarantee lounge access if the journey takes place after January 19, 2027. Travelers comparing Basic Business with Classic should pay particular attention to the departure date rather than assuming that the benefits currently available will remain attached to the fare.

Delta Main Basic is one of the most restrictive fares in the US.

The financial differences between Delta Air Lines' business class fare categories extend to its SkyMiles loyalty program. Basic Business passengers earn just two SkyMiles per dollar spent, compared with five miles per dollar for Classic and seven miles per dollar for Extra. This creates a substantial difference in the rewards accumulated from otherwise similar journeys in the same premium cabin.

For occasional travelers, the reduced earning rate may not be especially important, particularly if Basic Business delivers meaningful savings. However, frequent international travelers who regularly purchase business class tickets could accumulate considerably fewer miles over time. Those miles contribute toward future flights and other redemption opportunities, making the difference relevant to passengers who actively participate in the loyalty program.

The reduced earning rate reinforces the idea that Basic Business is aimed at customers who primarily want the seat rather than the broader collection of premium benefits. Delta Air Lines is effectively placing a lower value on the loyalty contribution of passengers purchasing its cheapest business class product. This reflects the wider industry trend toward offering different rewards depending on how much customers spend.

Passengers will therefore need to compare immediate ticket savings against the longer-term value of the miles they would otherwise earn. Someone booking an occasional holiday might find the difference relatively insignificant, while a regular corporate traveler could lose a meaningful amount of potential rewards. The more expensive fare categories may consequently offer better overall value for passengers who prioritize loyalty benefits.

Delta Air Lines is not alone in experimenting with cheaper, unbundled business class products. United Airlines has introduced Polaris Base, while JetBlue has launched Mint Base, both offering lower-priced entry points into their respective premium cabins. These products reflect a broader industry shift toward separating the physical comfort of business class from additional services traditionally included in one comprehensive fare.

However, the different airlines do not necessarily apply identical restrictions. United Airlines' Polaris Base, for example, continues to permit access to standard United Clubs, demonstrating that lounge eligibility can vary depending on the product and the airline's wider premium travel strategy. Passengers should therefore examine the precise conditions rather than assuming every basic business class ticket follows the same rules.

For Delta Air Lines, the January 2027 lounge cutoff is particularly significant because lounge access remains available during the initial introduction period. This temporary arrangement could make Basic Business more attractive to travelers booking journeys before the deadline, although passengers should avoid treating the current benefits as permanent features of the fare. The eventual restrictions are an important part of understanding what the product actually offers.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Ultimately, Basic Business gives Delta Air Lines another way to compete for customers who want a lie-flat seat without paying for every traditional business class benefit. Premium dining and Zone 1 boarding help preserve the appeal of the onboard experience, but reduced mileage earnings, restricted flexibility, and the removal of lounge access create clear differences. From January 19, 2027, the fare will become a considerably more stripped-back proposition, leaving passengers to decide whether the seat alone justifies the price.

#6121. White House budget aide Ueland slated to head GAO

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters said.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

"I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

"To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad."

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

Before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

#6120. American to Renovate, Expand Phoenix Lounges

American Airlines plans to refresh and expand its three Admirals Club lounges at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.

The carrier said Tuesday that it will add seating, upgrade amenities, and improve food and beverage service across all three spaces in Terminal 4.

In the near term, the Admirals Club lounge in Concourse A between gates A19 and A21 will get a new servery area, infrastructure enhancements to support expanded food and beverage offerings, and facility updates to improve the overall customer experience.

Longer-term plans call for nearly tripling the combined footprint of the Concourse A lounges, the other being above gates A7-A9. New furniture and finishings will be brought in, and seating capacity will expand by 150%.

The lounge in Concourse B, between gates B5 and B7, will get a new self-service food and beverage area and have its seating capacity increased by 20%.

“Phoenix continues to be an important hub in our network, and these investments reflect our commitment to giving customers more space, comfort, and convenience when they travel through PHX,” American Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden said in a news release. “While we look forward to the development of the new West Terminal, these enhancements will help create an even more seamless travel experience for the millions of customers who pass through Phoenix each year.”

The planned West Terminal will be built on the west side of the airport between Terminal 3 and Taxiway U. American is expected to serve as the terminal’s primary carrier.

According to the airport’s timeline, the project should be finished by 2033.
