#6119. Democrats Have the Electoral College in Their Sights

Will the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact soon cross the 270-vote threshold?

Delegates point to an electoral map at the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia, Pa., in 2016.

The blue wave washed over a slew of state legislative chambers and six new governorships. Next year, a majority of Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governing trifecta. One of the biggest dangers of Democrats’ new political clout is that they will now push to override the Electoral College and effectively force the country into a nationwide presidential popular voting system as early as 2028.

Their vehicle is called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote, no matter which candidate carries each state. The compact was born after former President George W. Bush’s narrow Electoral College victory in 2000, and it was turbocharged following Donald Trump’s 2016 win despite his losing the popular vote. The District of Columbia and 18 states have joined, accounting for 222 electoral votes.

#6118. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

As airline executives say, every route has to earn its place financially in a carrier’s network.

As for the four new destinations, Alaska will serve each of those with one daily flight from its Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) base. The additions are:

The carrier will also add a new nonstop from SEA to Guadalajara International Airport (GDL) in Mexico. Alaska will offer three weekly flights on Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays with a 737-800 from March 18, 2027 through Aug. 9, 2027.

As part of its PDX growth, Alaska Airlines opened a new, $18 million lounge at the airport in June.

#6116. The New Changes That Could Make The US Air Force's C-17 Globemasters Become Fighters Instead Of Transport Aircraft

Bluebearwing | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

The United States Air Force is exploring a concept that could fundamentally change how it generates long-range strike capabilities by turning conventional cargo aircraft into formidable missile-launching platforms. Known initially as Rapid Dragon and now progressing under the Dragon Cart initiative, the program uses specially configured pallets to deploy multiple air-launched cruise missiles from aircraft such as the Lockheed Martin C-130J Super Hercules and Boeing C-17 Globemaster III.

Rather than developing entirely new combat aircraft, the concept leverages the existing air mobility fleet to provide commanders with additional precision-strike capacity. With growing demand for affordable, mass-produced munitions and the need to expand the US military's weapons stockpile, this approach could give the Air Force a significant advantage in future high-intensity conflicts.

In 2019, the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) initiated experiments that could, if successful, transform conventional transport aircraft such as the C-17 and C-130 into dual-use aircraft with immense firepower. Once deployed, these cargo haulers will be able to carry significant numbers of rapidly producible cruise missiles and saturate a battlespace, augmenting strike aircraft and heavy bombers.

The AFRL noted that the program has brought together more than "30 stakeholders, including Air Force Major Commands, the Test and Evaluation Enterprise, Program Offices, Mission Planners, other Services, Foreign Partners & Allies, and Industry to develop and demonstrate the capability through modeling, simulation, analysis, demonstration, and flight tests."

The project began as Rapid Dragon and is now known as Dragon Cart. The project tested the possibility of loading palletized munitions, such as JASSM-ER cruise missiles, into C-130s and C-17s. Air & Space Forces Magazine states that the "Rapid Dragon program performed several tests on the C-130 and C-17, including a live-fire test at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, in December 2021." AFRL has also stated that Rapid Dragon has employed the palletized munitions concept on three separate continents, including the EUCOM and INDOPACOM theaters.

According to CENTCOM Citadel, a C-130J Super Hercules can carry two pallets, each containing six missile tubes, enabling the aircraft to deploy up to 12 air-launched cruise missiles. Meanwhile, the C-17 Globemaster III, with a maximum payload capacity of 170,900 lb (77,519 kg), could theoretically accommodate five nine-missile pallets carrying up to 45 JASSMs. This substantial weapons payload could temporarily transform the cargo aircraft into a formidable standoff strike platform.

The US Air Force Research Laboratory is at the cutting edge of weapons and general technology development for the US military and partner states.

As demonstrated by Operation Epic Fury, during which US strike aircraft deployed approximately 1,100 JASSMs, from an estimated inventory of 4,400, the need for affordable mass in this category of munitions has become increasingly apparent. Further, the ability to deploy these weapons flexibly would allow US commanders to strike targets without placing additional demands on bomber, fighter, and strike aircraft crews.

Due to the need for an expanded stockpile of missiles, particularly more affordable varieties, Dragon Cart dovetails with the Air Force's investment in its Family of Affordable Mass Missiles (FAMM) program. This initiative is designed to expand the service's munitions stockpile with comparatively inexpensive, less exquisite air-to-ground missiles. To this point, Air&Space Forces Magazine reports that just last July, the "Pentagon announced framework agreements for multiyear deals with three companies to produce and develop two versions of FAMM weapons—FAMM-Lugged, for fighter aircraft, and FAMM-Palletized, for airlifters."

As part of this plan, the Air Force has requested $355 million in its FY2027 budget to procure 1,000 weapons under the broader FAMM program. Its five-year budget projections call for the purchase of 28,000 missiles for $12.6 billion, as detailed by Defence Industry Europe.

The massive buildup of precision missiles will be supported by companies such as Anduril, whose Barracuda cruise missile recently received certification as the Air Force's first large-scale production munition compliant with open systems architecture. This certification provides a clear path forward for the new weapon, which offers commanders greater flexibility, as technicians can swap out payloads and reconfigure other features depending on mission requirements.

Under the FAMM program, Air&Space Forces Magazine states that "Anduril, CoAspire, and Zone 5 Technologies were selected. The agreements call for the three companies to produce 8,000 missiles annually once production ramps up. That timeline targets 5,300 missiles in 2028, rising to 8,000 by 2031." Anduril is slated to deliver its first Barracuda missiles to the Pentagon in early 2027.

Comparing France's exquisite omnirole jet to the leading fighters.

With the missiles getting ever closer to delivery and the capability already within the Air Force's grasp, the service is planning to field this new weapon system in 2027, according to Defence Blog. Regarding the impending deployment of the missile delivery system, General Kenneth S. Wilsbach, US Air Force Chief of Staff, stated: “As you might gather, capabilities like FAMM-P blur the distinction between our combat air forces and mobility air force mission sets. That’s a cultural shift we need to be prepared for, and I need every mobility Airman in the room to embrace that change.”

Regarding this blurring of the line between combat and air mobility, this new weapons capability could potentially turn suitably equipped C-130s and C-17s into platforms capable of striking targets across a given theater. Between its active-duty, Air National Guard, and Reserve units, the Air Force operates 428 C-130s and 222 C-17s. That's a substantial number of potential missile-launching platforms. Another consideration is that any adversary will now have to devote resources and plan for the possibility that cargo aircraft operating in the area could be carrying a devastating payload of cruise missiles, placing high-value targets under potential threat.

Manufactured with a longer fuselage, C-130J-30 for combat delivery

Special Operations; aerial and ground refueling (US Air Force-only variant)

Search and rescue support missions; aerial and ground refueling (US Air Force-only variant)

Search and rescue/maritime support missions (US Coast Guard–only variant)

Civil-certified multipurpose air freighter

If the aircraft are called upon to strike hostile military sites, the missile pallets are loaded like standard cargo through the aircraft's Cargo Handling System and secured in place using pallet locks and a restraint system. Once over the designated launch area, the crew pushes the pallet or pallets out through the rear cargo door, much like any other airdropped load. Once clear of the aircraft, the pallet deploys a parachute, allowing the missiles to be released into the air. Their engines then activate, and the missiles maneuver toward their designated targets.

One of the program's greatest advantages is that, during contingency operations or high-intensity conflicts, the Air Force could support ground operations and provide substantial follow-on strikes without placing additional demands on its dedicated strike aircraft and heavy bomber crews. Further, using cargo aircraft as precision-strike platforms could provide commanders with highly accurate firepower against multiple targets, offering considerable value in support of ground operations.

Over 2,700 C-130-family aircraft have been produced so far, with production expected to run into the 2030s.

Despite the advantages of converting transport aircraft into missile-launching platforms, the concept is not without operational challenges. The C-130J Super Hercules and C-17 Globemaster III were designed primarily for air mobility, not penetrating heavily defended airspace. Consequently, these aircraft would need to operate at considerable standoff distances from hostile air defense systems, relying on the extended range of their cruise missiles to engage targets without entering contested airspace. This places greater importance on missile range, accuracy, and mission planning.

Further, deploying palletized munitions requires coordination between aircraft crews, mission planners, intelligence personnel, and weapons operators. Although the Cargo Handling System allows missile pallets to be loaded using conventional cargo procedures, aircraft must accommodate specialized release equipment, parachute deployment, and systems to coordinate missile launches. Additionally, cargo aircraft assigned to strike missions would temporarily be unavailable for traditional responsibilities, potentially placing additional demands on an already heavily tasked air mobility fleet.

Another consideration is the availability of suitable weapons and the ability to integrate different missile systems across multiple aircraft platforms. Rapid Dragon and the broader Dragon Cart initiative aim to make this process more flexible through palletized configurations and modular weapons architectures. However, individual aircraft and missile combinations still require testing, integration, and operational certification. The Air Force also has to ensure sufficient missile inventories are available to support conventional strike operations and expanded palletized weapons deployment. These considerations will determine how effectively the concept transitions from experimental demonstrations into a dependable component of US long-range strike capabilities.

The Rapid Dragon concept represents a significant shift in how the US Air Force could generate and deploy long-range strike capabilities. By adapting existing cargo aircraft to launch palletized cruise missiles, the service could substantially expand its available weapons-delivery platforms without relying exclusively on traditional bombers and fighter aircraft. The transition toward Dragon Cart, alongside the development of affordable, mass-produced munitions such as Anduril's Barracuda, further demonstrates the growing importance of flexible weapons deployment.

Although operational challenges involving aircraft availability, weapons integration, and survivability remain, the potential benefits are considerable. With hundreds of C-130s and C-17s across its active-duty, Air National Guard, and Reserve fleets, the Air Force has a substantial transportation infrastructure that could serve an additional combat role. Ultimately, Dragon Cart could reshape how the US generates strike capacity in future conflicts.

#6115. A Trump–Xi–Putin Summit Could Remake the World Order

Can a triangle of the U.S., China, and Russia create a sustainable equilibrium of power, rules, and values?

From left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping

NR illustration; Alexander Kazakov, Kevin Lamarque, Tingshu Wang/Reuters

The proposed Trump–Xi–Putin meeting in Shenzhen this month could become one of the most consequential diplomatic encounters since the Cold War. Whatever the three leaders might negotiate concerning Ukraine, Taiwan, trade, nuclear weapons, or artificial intelligence, its larger significance would be unmistakable: The three powers most capable of shaping the international order would be gathering not primarily to defend it but to renegotiate their positions within, or against, it.

The irony is extraordinary. Russia seeks to overturn an order from which it believes itself excluded. China seeks to reshape an order from which it has benefited enormously. The United States, which created and sustained that order, increasingly regards its maintenance as an excessive burden. The revolutionary, the reformer, and the reluctant guardian have become, in different ways, revisionists.

From left: Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping

NR illustration; Alexander Kazakov, Kevin Lamarque, Tingshu Wang/Reuters

The  is getting a significant overhaul, pairing a higher annual fee with new Atmos Rewards earning rates and a collection of perks for businesses that regularly fly on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

Starting Nov. 18, new applicants can earn 10 points per dollar on qualifying flights booked through Atmos™ for Business, receive four Alaska Lounge passes annually and work toward flight discounts and bonus status points through spending.

The biggest winners may be companies with multiple employee cardholders that regularly book Alaska or Hawaiian flights. They'll pay a flat $195 annual fee regardless of how many employee cards they issue, while benefiting from new travel perks.

However, the refresh also eliminates some valuable benefits, including the annual $99 Companion Fare and the $100 discount on an Alaska Lounge+ membership. Existing cardholders won't automatically transition to the new version and can keep their current benefits.

New applicants can earn a limited-time offer of 90,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases within the first 90 days of account opening, worth about $1,440 based on TPG's November 2026 valuations. By point total, that's the largest offer in TPG's recorded history for the card, but it's not the richest because the new offer doesn't include Alaska's famous $99 Companion Fare.

Starting Nov. 18, the Atmos Rewards Business card will feature a new flat annual fee regardless of the number of cards, stronger rewards on flights booked through Atmos for Business and several new travel-day perks.

Annual fee: $195 for the company, with no additional fee for employee cards (was previously $70 + $25 per card, including for the primary cardholder)

The refresh also takes a few things away.

New cardholders will no longer earn 2 points per dollar spent on gas, electric vehicle charging, shipping and local transit/ride-hailing. New cardholders will also lose the ability to earn the annual Companion Fare through card spending and the $100 discount on an annual Alaska Lounge+ membership.

Overall, the theme is clear: The refreshed card concentrates its value around Alaska and Hawaiian travel, especially for companies willing to book through Atmos for Business and issue cards to multiple employees.

If you opened your before Nov. 18, 2026, you won't automatically receive the refreshed benefits or move to the new annual-fee structure.

Instead, Bank of America says existing cardholders will keep their current benefits, including the opportunity to earn the annual $99 Companion Fare under the previous card's terms.

If you're interested in switching to the refreshed card, you can call Bank of America at 1-800-892-3219 to explore your options.

Applications submitted before Nov. 18 will also remain under the previous card offering, even if they're still pending.

One of the biggest changes is the new annual-fee structure.

The previously charged $70 per company plus $25 per card, including the owner’s card. Now, it’s a flat $195 regardless of how many cards you have. A solo business owner will now pay more than double what they paid before, a company with five cards pays the same as before, and one with six or more pays less. This is arguably the most significant part of the refresh.

Each cardholder will continue to receive a free checked bag for themselves and up to six guests on the same reservation when the flight is paid for with the card. They also receive preferred boarding on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian flights.

That could make the card particularly appealing to small businesses with several West Coast or Hawaii-based road warriors. The more employees who consistently use the travel benefits, the easier it becomes to justify the companywide fee.

Solo owners who do not need employee cards may find one of the personal Atmos cards better suited to their needs.

In that case, you won't earn points from business spending, but you can enjoy similar perks with the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card for a lower annual fee or take advantage of more generous benefits (albeit with a higher fee) on the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card.

However, neither is a direct replacement for a business card, particularly for owners who want to separate business expenses or issue employee cards.

Related: Atmos Ascent vs. Atmos Summit: The Summit is better—but not for everyone

In addition to checked-bag and preferred-boarding perks, the refreshed card will include one Alaska Lounge pass per calendar quarter, for a total of four per account anniversary year. That cadence is best suited to a consultant or salesperson who flies throughout the year, rather than a company whose only major trip is an annual conference.

Meanwhile, the waived fee for same-day confirmed changes ($50 on most Alaska flights) could be particularly useful for employees whose meetings finish early, run late or move unexpectedly. That practical flexibility may save some employees frustration — and save the business itself money on fees.

The card also adds a $50 Instant Travel Delay Credit voucher, which can be used toward a meal or drink at the airport when an eligible flight is canceled or delayed by at least two hours on the day of travel.

Despite the new higher fee, even a solo business owner could potentially offset much of the $195 annual fee through these travel benefits. Someone who checks a bag on two round-trips would save $180; visit a lounge on each of those trips and you'll save another $130 compared to buying day passes.

Related: Alaska Airlines airport lounges: How to get access to this VIP space

Earning 10 points per dollar sounds exceptional, but it only applies to flights booked through the Atmos for Business website, the airlines’ self-managed booking platform. That means companies that don't qualify for Atmos for Business — it requires a minimum of $5,000 in annual travel spend — or businesses that book through a corporate travel agency or another platform won't earn this higher return.

Other eligible Alaska and Hawaiian purchases earn 3 points per dollar spent, dining earns 2 points per dollar spent and everything else earns 1 point per dollar. Companies with an eligible Bank of America business account also receive a 10% bonus on points earned from card purchases, effectively turning the 10-point rate into 11 points per dollar.

Lastly, travelers who select the Price Paid earning option and hold Atmos Platinum or Titanium status can earn 20 points or more per dollar on qualifying flights booked through Atmos for Business.

The card's weak general spending rate makes it better suited as a secondary card specifically for Alaska and Hawaiian spending than as a business’s only credit card.

The refreshed no longer includes its annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23), which cardholders prior to Nov. 18 earned after spending $6,000 during an account anniversary year.

That is a significant loss for owners who could redeem it for two travelers flying together. Four lounge passes and same-day change flexibility may be more useful for employees traveling alone, but they aren't an automatic replacement for a Companion Fare.

While the new discounts could be valuable for businesses with substantial spending, the $100,000 threshold is significantly higher than the previous $6,000 requirement for earning a Companion Fare.

The welcome offer drops the Companion Fare too, but it includes more points than past offers. Its 90,000 points are enough for three round-trip economy tickets between the West Coast and Hawaii on Alaska or Hawaiian, a one-way ticket on American Airlines in transatlantic business class or a round-trip premium economy ticket from Seattle to Tokyo on an Atmos partner airline.

The refreshed Atmos Rewards Business Card has a higher starting price, but it also has a clearer identity: It's built for companies with multiple cardholders and for recurring Alaska or Hawaiian travel.

Businesses that need employee cards, book substantial airfare through Atmos for Business and have employees who can use the lounge passes and same-day change waiver may come out well ahead.

However, the loss of the Companion Fare and several business spending bonus categories makes the card less appealing for some existing cardholders.

Sole proprietors or companies that don't book through Atmos for Business may still have a case for the card, but they'll need to run the numbers more carefully. And companies that rarely fly either airline or primarily need rewards on everyday operating expenses will likely find the card too specialized.

#6113. No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A big takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

If you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

#6112. Here's How Much Larger The Boeing 737 MAX 7 Is Over The Jet It Directly Replaces

Wirestock Creators | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

The Boeing 737 MAX 7 finally received airworthiness certification from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on August 3, allowing it to enter production and succeed the legacy 737-700 Next Generation. Aside from being a modernized replacement with better fuel efficiency and superior technology throughout the airframe, the MAX 7 is quite a bit larger than its predecessor. It is essentially the direct result of specific requests from the type's best customer, Southwest Airlines.

Although the MAX 7 first flew in March 2018, its rollout stalled following the 737 MAX groundings. Southwest Airlines holds roughly 237 to 264 firm orders for the Boeing 737 MAX 7, accounting for nearly 90% of the model's entire order book. Since Southwest operates an all-737 fleet and is the world's largest 737 customer, Boeing essentially custom-built the MAX 7's stretched dimensions to keep Southwest from defecting to Airbus.

Adding two rows of seats lowers the cost per seat-mile, making the jet far more profitable on high-frequency domestic routes than a direct size-for-size replacement would have been. Those make the plane six feet longer than the 737-700 NG, while its wingspan is nearly identical, but it weighs over 20,000 lb (10,000 kg) more. It boasts the longest range in the entire 737 MAX lineup as a result of its shorter, lighter airframe using the wing, fuselage center, and gear of the larger 737 MAX 8.

Boeing initially marketed the 737 MAX 7 as a direct, one-for-one replacement for the 737-700, keeping nearly identical length, seat capacity, and layout. However, the heavier CFM LEAP-1B engines added dead-weight drag without increasing passenger capacity. As the launch customer whose massive, single-fleet 737 commitment gave it overwhelming leverage, Southwest was not impressed and threatened defection to the clean-sheet Bombardier CSeries, now the Airbus A220-300. SWA has even joined WestJet in demanding lower seat-mile costs from the smallest member of the 737 MAX line.

In response, Boeing scrapped the original blueprint it debuted at the 2016 Farnborough International Airshow and stretched the fuselage by 76 inches (1.93 meters), adding 30 inches (0.76 meters) forward of the wing box and 46 inches (1.17 meters) aft. That increased the MAX 7's two-class capacity to 153 passengers. Paired with twin LEAP-1B turbofans and larger fuel tanks, the heavier airframe stretched its unrefueled range out to 3,850 nautical miles (7,130 kilometers).

The new cabin gave Southwest a dozen additional revenue-generating seats on every flight without adding cockpit crew. Stretching the fuselage brought the jet's seat-mile costs down to competitive levels. While the 175-seat MAX 8 is Southwest's workhorse on major trunk routes, it is too large to fly profitably multiple times a day on thinner point-to-point routes or off-peak business schedules. Getting Boeing to stretch the MAX 7 gave Southwest A220-level capacity while keeping a 100% 737 fleet.

Certification delays for the 737 MAX 7 left launch customer Southwest Airlines unable to build reliable schedules around its order book of roughly 300 jets meant to replace aging 737-700s. To keep new aircraft arriving, Southwest converted large blocks of slots into 175-seat 737 MAX 8s, creating network imbalances as the larger jets flew half-empty on thinner routes while 25-year-old 737-700s required costly structural overhauls.

During these delays, Airbus saw an opportunity and made a strong pitch for the clean-sheet A220-300. The A220-300 is built with carbon-fiber composite wings, aluminum-lithium fuselage panels, and Pratt & Whitney geared turbofans. Its operating empty weight is about 81,790 pounds (37,100 kilograms), about 17,600 pounds (7,983 kilograms) lighter than Boeing's all-metal MAX 7. This results in a significantly lower trip fuel burn on 130-seat missions.

Despite the A220-300's clean-sheet fuel efficiency, Southwest and Boeing resolved to preserve the carrier's 50-year single-fleet business model. Breaking its all-737 discipline to introduce an Airbus jet would have forced Southwest to build separate pilot training pipelines, split spare-parts inventories, and sacrifice the operational flexibility to swap aircraft seamlessly during weather disruptions.

Boeing optimized the extended MAX 7 to use raw gross weight, range, and seating density to offset the structural advantage of the A220. The MAX 7 provided equivalent seat-mile economics while maintaining uniformity for all pilots, mechanics, and gate crew on a single aircraft family by carrying up to 12 more passengers in high-density single-class layouts and traveling 400 nautical miles (741 kilometers) farther than the A220-300.

What's behind the hold-up, and how does it impact the airline’s future?

Following its August FAA certification and planned March 2027 passenger debut, the MAX 7 takes over missions from Southwest's nearly 290 retiring 737-700s. Its smaller size relative to the MAX 8 means Southwest can offer multiple daily flights between mid-sized cities without having to cut ticket prices just to fill the plane. The 150-seat-count cabin also lets the airline fly with three flight attendants instead of four, saving on crew costs while still carrying more passengers than its predecessor.

Already numbering over 340 jets in Southwest's active fleet, the MAX 8 is found flying high-demand routes between major focus cities such as Dallas, Denver, Las Vegas, Chicago Midway, and Baltimore. With 175 seats, it delivers the lowest cost per seat-mile in the fleet and maximizes revenue at slot-controlled or congested airports where adding extra daily flights is not possible. Notably, the MAX 7 also handles tough flying conditions better than its bigger sibling.

Pairing the lighter body of the MAX 7 with the MAX 8's wings, engines, and fuel tanks gives it extra climbing power and range. That makes it a great plane for serving fields with short runways or high-altitude airports, or for long trips to Hawaii and the Caribbean, where a heavier MAX 8 might have to leave passengers or bags behind to take off with enough fuel.

Southwest's latest interline deal opens connections to Paris, Tahiti and the Indian Ocean while strengthening French bee's US reach.

Southwest’s recent transition from a traditional low-cost carrier into a more conventional, legacy-style airline was distinctly marked by ending its 54-year open-seating policy in January. SWA has since added extra-legroom sections, introduced checked bag fees, and is now planning airport lounges. This paradigm shift in the identity of the airline directly shapes how the MAX 7 fits into its network.

Flying a heavier jet changes the economics of Southwest's schedule. Because airports base landing fees on aircraft weight, the 22,500-pound (10,206-kilogram) jump over the 737-700 makes short, cheap regional hops less profitable. To offset those higher airport charges, Southwest has to put the MAX 7 on longer routes where its fuel-saving engines and higher-priced extra-legroom seats earn enough to cover the extra weight.

The trade-off of the MAX 7's design gives Southwest the cabin space, amenities, and long-haul capability to compete with Delta, United, and American Airlines of the 'Big Three.' The stretched cabin allows the airline to carve out a dedicated extra-legroom section without sacrificing total seat count or adding a fourth flight attendant.

The MAX 7 gives Southwest the right-sized tool to attract higher-spending business and leisure flyers. Still, even after Boeing hands over the first jets in late 2026, Southwest needs roughly three months of ferry flights, maintenance checks, and FAA-monitored proving runs before carrying paying passengers in March 2027.

They'll all take off in time for Thanksgiving. Find out more here!

Following extensive test flights across the western United States, the Federal Aviation Administration granted final certification for Boeing to begin full production of the MAX 7 in August. Roughly 30 completed MAX 7 jets are finally preparing to depart long-term storage to enter service since earning FAA approval. Technicians are now unwrapping those stored jets and installing the anti-ice upgrades ahead of deliveries to Southwest, setting the stage for passenger flights in early 2027.

The Max 7s have been waiting at the main plant as Boeing spent years clearing out the massive 'shadow factory' of hundreds of grounded MAX 8s and MAX 9s in Moses Lake, Washington. At the same time, mechanics are reworking the parked inventory; Boeing has been overhauling its manufacturing footprint to build new MAX 7s alongside the rest of the MAX family. Newly built MAX 7s are scheduled to start rolling off the Renton line for Southwest in February 2027.

To break years-long supply-chain bottlenecks as it ramps up toward a target of 47 MAX jets per month, Boeing activated a fourth 737 assembly line dubbed the North Line. Yet, getting the MAX 7 has also turned the spotlight in Renton directly toward the largest member of the family, the 737 MAX 10. Southwest anchors the MAX 7 order book with more than 300 orders through 2031, but major carriers like United, Delta, and WestJet are counting on the 230-seat MAX 10 to rival the Airbus A321neo on high-capacity routes around the globe.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Yet the stretched flagship remains stuck in regulatory limbo over flight management software flaws, unique telescoping landing gear, and strict cockpit alerting rules. Until the FAA signs off on those final design changes, airlines across North America are left waiting to see if Boeing can break the last remaining logjam in the MAX lineup and finally close out its troubled narrowbody certification saga.

#6111. James Talarico’s ‘Incarnational Politics’

The new senator from Texas has bad ideas about Christianity and democracy, but the press seems okay with that.

The day after the Democrats trounced the Republicans in the midterm elections, Ezra Klein of the New York Times tweeted, “One of the more exciting parts of this election — among many — is the return of a religious left.” Accompanying the enthusiastic remark was a clip from his interview earlier this year with James Talarico, the Democrat who won the Texas senatorial race. In the clip, Talarico — a Presbyterian seminarian — advocates a political attitude in which Americans recognize each other as being made in God’s image and treat each other accordingly. He calls this “an incarnational politics.”

Incarnational politics — hoo boy. The term, a nearly paradoxical union of the sacred and the profane, sounds just enough like intersectional politics to catch the attention of progressives. It also sounds like an edgy indie band that never quite made it. (“I saw Incarnational Politics open for Bad Religion in ’91.”)

#6110. Transfer Amex Points To Avianca Lifemiles With 10% Bonus: Worth It?

The Amex Membership Rewards program has just introduced a new bonus for points transfers to Avianca Lifemiles. While this is hardly the biggest bonus, something is better than nothing, and the program is useful for Star Alliance redemptions.

Between November 16 and December 16, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 10% bonus when moving points from Amex Membership Rewards to Avianca Lifemiles. This is being offered on Amex’s end, so when you go the points transfer page, make sure that you see this offer available.

Ordinarily points transfer between programs at a 1:1 ratio (in increments of 1,000 points), while through this promotion you’d get 1,100 Lifemiles for every 1,000 Amex Membership Rewards points transferred. Points transfers from Amex to Avianca are typically instant, and the bonus miles will post the same time as the standard miles.

We see transferable points currencies frequently offer bonuses on transfers to Lifemiles, and we’ve seen such promotions from most major transferable points currencies in the past year.

Avianca is in the Star Alliance, which means you can redeem Lifemiles on all Star Alliance airlines without any fuel surcharges. Really this is the core value proposition of the program, since this is a great way to book Star Alliance premium cabin seats at a huge discount. Check out my guide on how to redeem Lifemiles for ideas on how to use these miles.

With a specific use in mind, this could represent a great value, whether you’re looking at traveling first class on All Nippon Airways, or are looking at traveling in business class on a countless number of airlines. Everyone has to crunch the numbers for themselves and decide whether this makes sense or not.

Let me emphasize that in some cases, Lifemiles doesn’t have access to the same award availability as Star Alliance partners, for better or worse. Sometimes Lifemiles doesn’t have access to partner awards that other programs do have access to, and other times the inverse is true.

That’s why I always recommend doing some “dummy” award searches before buying miles, so you can get a sense of how award availability lines up with your needs.

Through December 16, 2026, the Amex Membership Rewards program is offering a 10% bonus on points transfers to Avianca Lifemiles. If you’re looking to redeem on Star Alliance partners, there’s definitely some value to be had here.

With the 10% bonus, you can potentially get a very reasonably priced award on Avianca or one of its Star Alliance partners. As always, the challenge is actually finding award availability. Admittedly I wouldn’t make a speculative points transfer, though, as we have seen some bigger transfer bonuses in the past.

#6109. Transfer Capital One Miles To Qatar Airways Privilege Club With 15% Bonus: Worth It?

The Capital One mileage program has just introduced a new bonus for points transfers to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. While the percentage bonus amount isn’t huge, there’s potentially value to be had, especially given the flexibility these rewards offer.

Between November 15 and December 14, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 15% bonus when moving points from Capital One to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. This is being offered on Capital One’s end, so when you go the mileage transfer page, make sure that you see this offer available.

Ordinarily rewards transfer between programs at a 1:1 ratio (in increments of 1,000 miles), while through this promotion you’d get 1,150 Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios for every 1,000 Capital One miles transferred. Points transfers from Capital One to Qatar Airways are typically instant, and the bonus rewards will post the same time as the standard rewards.

We see transferable points currencies frequently offer bonuses on transfers to a variety of Avios currencies, and you can of course move rewards between those various currencies. We’ve definitely seen bigger than 15% bonuses in the past, but there’s no guarantee we’ll see a higher offer return anytime soon.

I’d argue that the Qatar Airways Privilege Club program is pretty lucrative nowadays. For one, keep in mind that Qatar Airways uses Avios as its rewards currency, so it’s possible to transfer Avios at a 1:1 ratio between the various programs that earn Avios. That includes Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Finnair Plus, and Iberia Plus.

This means that you could use this offer to indirectly convert Citi ThankYou points into British Airways Avios with a 15% bonus as well. That’s something that will no doubt interest some.

However, there’s also huge value directly with the Qatar Airways Privilege Club program. Privilege Club has decent award pricing on Qatar Airways flights, and also has access to more business class award availability than partner programs (though availability still isn’t great). Privilege Club also has several unique airline partners, ranging from JetBlue, to RwandAir, to Virgin Australia, opening up valuable redemption opportunities.

Through December 14, 2026, the Capital One program is offering a 15% bonus on points transfers to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. If you’re looking to acquire any “flavor” of Avios, this could be a great value, as this is also a way to get rewards with British Airways, Iberia, etc.

However, if you’re thinking of making a speculative transfer to earn Avios, I might wait for a bigger offer, as we do sometimes see 30%+ bonuses on transfers to some Avios currencies.

#6108. Why The World's Debut Boeing 747 Was Built In Half The Time Of Other Aircraft Of Its Size In 1968

The Boeing 747 has earned its title as one of the most iconic airliners ever built for several reasons. It was the first widebody aircraft, easily distinguishable by a humped second deck, a key enabler in opening up aviation to the masses, and it enjoyed roughly fifty years of production. But equally as impressive as the Queen of the Skies itself is how it came about.

Boeing took the 747 from the drawing board to rollout remarkably quickly. That is, notably faster than the Airbus A380 program took to churn out its first model after officially launching, and quicker than both Boeing and Airbus took with their latest widebodies. What is more, Boeing pulled it off decades ago in the late 1960s.

Just 29 months separated the 747 project’s official launch and the rollout of the first model. Boeing announced on April 13, 1966, that it would build the 490-seat passenger transport that would come to be known as the 747. Exactly two years, five months, and 17 days later, on September 30, 1968, the first 747-100 ceremoniously rolled off the production line at a new purpose-built assembly plant in Everett, Washington.

Less than five months later, on February 9, 1969, the aircraft took off for its maiden flight. Test pilots Jack Waddell and Brien Wygle, accompanied by flight engineer Jess Wallick, took the controls, and the jumbo jet passed the major test with flying colors, paving the way for its introduction into service just under a year later in January 1970.

All told, that saw the Queen of the Skies go from a mere concept to carrying passengers in under four years. While that is no doubt a rapid turnaround by today’s standards, the reasons behind the pace are plentiful and clear-cut.

Behind it all was keen interest from Pan American World Airways, which had set out to source a jet two and a half times larger than the existing Boeing 707 against the backdrop of an increasingly busy market. Though the industry was mulling whether supersonic flight would come to dominate in the years ahead, there remained appeal for a huge, versatile airliner that could handle cargo operations rather than passenger services in the future, if needed.

As it turned out, Boeing had already looked into something similar, having lost out in a 1965 military transport design competition to the Lockheed C-5 Galaxy. Although the 747 was ultimately largely built from scratch, research into high-bypass engine technology and the thinking behind the 747’s distinctive hump can be traced back to the military project bid. As such, when Pan Am head Juan Trippe and then-Boeing president William Allen met that same year for initial discussions about the 747, something of a basis was already there.

It was Trippe himself who is said to have pushed so heavily for the 747. He had spent years beforehand attempting to open up aviation to the masses, overseeing the introduction of the world’s first economy fare in 1958, for instance. Given that an ambitious project like the 747 would only aid in reaching that goal, Trippe reportedly told Allen in 1965: “If you’ll build it, I’ll buy it.” By April 1966, the commitment was solidified through a $525 million deal — worth almost $5.5 billion today — for 25 of the new jumbo jets. This set an ambitious deadline of 1969 for the first delivery, though.

The 747 transcended aviation and became an iconic silhouette.

Nonetheless, Boeing did not waste any time in dwelling on the task at hand. After signing the contract with Pan Am, the design team of just a few hundred workers conceptualizing and writing up requirements for the 747 ballooned to 4,500 almost instantaneously. These workers, who would later become part of a group known as The Incredibles, were led by Joe Sutter, who would similarly earn the title of the Father of the 747 over time.

Sutter himself enjoyed a 40-year-long career at Boeing, although he recalled in a 2013 interview fearing for his job as he and his team rushed to get the 747 ready. Without public backing, Boeing found itself racking up debt on the back of the project, leaving Sutter under pressure to cut jobs. Instead, he requested hundreds more engineers. “I figured that was the day I lost my job at Boeing,” he said, “but I went to work the next day, and nobody said anything, so I kept working."

According to Boeing, some 50,000 employees ultimately ended up working on the jumbo jet over the course of its development cycle. Armed with an eye-watering 75,000 drawings, physical assembly of the first model got underway in September 1967, a year prior to its initial presentation to the world and only 16 months before the first flight. All of this, of course, required a specialized facility for production to actually be carried out.

Such a factory did not exist when Boeing first unveiled plans for the 747, so it had to be built almost in conjunction with the first model. Among the battles Sutter fought in his bid to steer the project to a timely conclusion was one over where his team would be based. Faced with the proposal of being sent to California, Sutter argued against it and insisted his engineers stay close to where those who would eventually build the aircraft would work.

This turned out to be Everett, which was far from Boeing’s first choice to house the 747 program initially, but prevailed on similar fears that key personnel would not relocate in great numbers to a new facility elsewhere. Regardless of where the 747 would be built, a new building would have to be constructed to accommodate such a vast aircraft and all the equipment needed to build it.

Under the tight deadline set by the deal with Pan Am, Boeing set about clearing forest and then building the facility in 1967. Work began just before assembly of the first 747 started, but the two efforts overlapped, meaning the prototype was under construction in an incomplete factory for a period. When the former was eventually completed, it took the crown as the largest building in the world by volume — a title it retains to this day and a reflection of the mammoth undertaking by Boeing to get the project off the ground.

The original designs for the Boeing 747 were made with a different purpose in mind. Find out how the 747 came to be as we know it today.

Naturally, such an effort required vast financial backing, and it took a monumental amount of risk on Boeing’s part to get the first 747 successfully turned around at such a pace. Boeing had secured $525 million — or $21 million per aircraft — under its deal with Pan Am. This covered barely half of the program's total $1 billion costas it transpired; however, adjusted for inflation, it would exceed $10 billion today.

As a result, Boeing faced financial pressure and was forced to turn to the banks, which explains Sutter being asked to cut engineers midway through the program. He said in 2013 that “it was a big gamble,” adding, “I think the only reason that it happened is that Bill Allen was a forward-seeking guy, and Juan Trippe from Pan Am also had that characteristic.”

Despite racking up debt, the gamble paid off, and the 747 was a resounding success. Not only did the first model get built and delivered on time, but the factory Boeing built for the jumbo jet has enjoyed decades of service since. Some 1,574 747s rolled out of the site over the life of the program, culminating in the delivery of a final 747-8 Freighter variant to Atlas Air in 2023. Notably, this saw production of the 747 end just a year before that of its primary challenger, the A380, despite its initial introduction decades earlier.

The A380 is an impressive feat of engineering in its own right. The industry moved in a different direction, and while Boeing hit a sweet spot with the 747, the appetite for huge quad jets was by no means as strong as it was at the A380’s commercial entry in 2007. All told, this saw the 254th and final A380 completed in 2021.

Airbus grappled with a string of delays between officially launching the A380 in December 2000, unveiling a prototype in January 2005, and then making the initial delivery to Singapore Airlines in 2007. How severely these impacted the A380’s long-term success is up for debate. Either way, the A380’s stretched timeline offers some context for how impressive Boeing’s effort was in getting the 747 up and running so quickly.

And it is not just the A380. Boeing itself took three years and six months to show off its first 777 after launching the program in October 1990. Its 787, despite going from concept to prototype in three years and three months, then took an additional two years and five months to first take off in December 2009. As for Airbus, the A350 and its answer to the clean-sheet 787 went from launch to initial rollout in six years and five months. Similarly, the 777X project took more than five years after launching in 2013 to produce a prototype, with certification still not secured today.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Boeing of today must be very envious of Boeing of 1960's

#6107. Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her new colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”

Not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” said Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

Rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

As returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

Not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” said Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number said otherwise.

“If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat currently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

“If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira said. “This is low on my priority list.”

Some members announced their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

“First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” said Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

“We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” said Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he said of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

“These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

#6106. Hello, OMAAT Readers! How I Got Here And What’s Next

Isn’t this a little surreal? After years of reading OMAAT, here I am writing my very first post.

First of all, a huge thank you to Ben for such a lovely introduction, and for everyone who gave me such a warm welcome in the comments already. I’m really looking forward to getting to know the OMAAT community Ben has built over the years.

In the first of what will undoubtedly be a lot of posts for One Mile at a Time, I thought I’d share a bit about who I am and what you can expect from me going forward.

I’m literally asking myself that as I write this.

Funnily enough, it was never my dream to be a writer, journalist, blogger, or anything similar. The only thing I can ever remember wanting to be “when I grew up” was a pilot. Despite several applications and reaching the final stage of cadet schemes with Aer Lingus and British Airways, it didn’t work out for me.

Determined to work in the industry, I quit my soul-destroying city job in London to do a Master’s in Air Transport Management at the University of Loughborough in the U.K. I was then offered 2 very different jobs: a junior marketing role with Air Transat, or to be part of a small team starting up TPG’s U.K. office. As a natural risk-taker, I took the latter. After almost 8 years of writing for various publications and dabbling in some video content, I’ve realized that this is what I was meant to be doing all along — the job just didn’t exist when I wanted to be a pilot as a kid.

So why OMAAT? Why now? I spent the last 2 years traveling the world, working remotely, in search of somewhere I felt connected enough to call home. In my heart of hearts, I always knew that was going to be Rio, so I moved here in September this year. I’ve also been considering a more permanent home for my writing and my online presence, so when happenstance did its thing and Ben offered me a full-time online home at OMAAT, it was the perfect opportunity.

I’m honored to have been entrusted to write alongside Ben, whose expertise I’ve learned from over the years. While I don’t promise to be an expert on everything, my almost 8 years of experience in this industry should hopefully mean my expertise meets the standard expected here.

What started out as a passion for planes and aviation has turned into a love of all things travel, loyalty, and the miles and points that help make it happen. I’m really looking forward to sharing some of my learnings, experiences, and tips and tricks from the past couple of years that should complement Ben’s breadth of knowledge.

To start with, much of what you’ll see from me will be written. But as Ben said, the plan is to gradually bring in more video and social content, which I’m really looking forward to helping OMAAT with.

I’m also a self-proclaimed expert on Rio and Brazil (I’ve been coming here since 2009), so if there’s any specific Rio, Brazil, or wider South American travel advice, reviews, or insights you’d like, I’d be more than happy to help, even if it means I have to hop a plane for the research. 😝

I’ll leave it at that for now, as I need to get packing to fly across the Pond for an exciting aviation event this week. All will be revealed soon. 🤓✈️

I’m very excited and honored to be Ben’s first full-time writer in a very long time. Today is the first day of a new adventure for myself, Ben, and the OMAAT behind-the-scenes team, and I can’t wait to bring you, the readers, along for the ride.

If you spend on the Delta Reserve Card, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can efficiently use the card abroad.
