Therefore if you wanted to earn elite status exclusively through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following amounts:

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

Delta One (business class) awards can be a great option, especially on roundtrip awards rather than one way itineraries. Using SkyMiles for shorter hops on Delta can be great, too. I’ve seen award flights between New York (LGA) and Orlando (MCO) for less than 20,000 miles roundtrip.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles.

You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air. You can also redeem SkyMiles on some airlines that aren’t part of SkyTeam but still partner with Delta, like LATAM and WestJet.

One of the primary things that sets the Delta Reserve Credit Card apart from other Delta Amex cards is the lounge access perks that it offers. The card offers Delta Sky Club® access, Centurion Lounge access, and even several Sky Club passes. How does that work?

The Delta Reserve Card offers 15 Delta Sky Club visits each Medallion year for the primary cardmember. Each visit is defined as all entries within a 24-hour period, including at different airports. In other words, if you have a connecting itinerary, you can visit multiple Sky Clubs at different airports while using only one visit allotment.

It’s possible to unlock unlimited Sky Club visits after spending $75,000 in purchases on your card in a calendar year. Once all 15 visits have been used, eligible cardmembers may purchase additional Sky Club visits at a per visit rate of $50 per person using the card.

In addition to the primary cardmember getting Sky Club access when flying Delta the same day, they also receive four Sky Club guest passes annually.

These can be used by the primary cardmember to guest others into the lounge, allowing you to skip the $50 guesting fee four times annually.

The Delta Reserve Card also offers complimentary Centurion Lounge access when traveling on a same-day Delta flight booked with the card. The primary cardmember is entitled to access, and bringing additional guests costs $50 each.

Centurion Lounges, for the most part, offer a significantly improved food and beverage offering compared to most domestic airline lounges in the United States, so this is a nice option to have.

The Delta Reserve Credit Card has a good bonus, though if I were just looking for the best welcome bonus offer, I would go for the Gold or Platinum version of the card, since the cards have significantly lower annual fees.

The reason you want to get the Reserve version of the card is because of the valuable long term perks that it offers. Above I’ve talked about how the Reserve Card can help you earn status and can help you access lounges, though there are lots of perks beyond that. Let’s take a look at some of those benefits.

Every year upon renewal of the Delta Reserve Card, you receive a roundtrip companion certificate valid within the United States (including Alaska and Hawaii), and to Mexico, the Caribbean, and Central America. This can be used for fares ranging from first class to economy, so the flexibility offered by that is pretty awesome, and for many will more than justify the annual fee.

You just have to pay the government-imposed taxes and fees for the companion. There are some things to be aware of when redeeming the Delta companion certificate, including:

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive a $200 Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you receive up to $200 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $200, if you wanted to. If used right, the value here is considerable.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive up to $240 in Resy credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $20 in statement credits each month after using your card on eligible purchases at U.S. restaurants that offer reservations on Resy.com and the Resy app, purchases made directly on Resy.com or in the Resy app, and purchases made via Resy Pay.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive up to $120 in rideshare credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers, including Uber and Lyft.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you get a first checked bag free. With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up:

Depending on how many bags you’re checking, a few trips with a companion could pay for the card’s annual fee.

You can receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Reserve. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you must ensure the primary cardmember’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation.

If you have the Delta Reserve Amex then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food, alcoholic beverages, and audio headsets, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card you can redeem miles for one cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn MQDs for taking those flights.

With the TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta. Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

Having the Delta Reserve Card gets you priority for complimentary upgrades, assuming you have Medallion status. That’s because the card acts as a tiebreaker.

If you have the Reserve Card you get upgrade priority over other Medallion members within the same Medallion level and fare class. Given how competitive upgrades are, this can make a material difference in terms of whether you clear or not.

The Delta Reserve Card offers complimentary Delta First and Delta Comfort upgrades on eligible flights for non-elite members. You will be toward the bottom of the upgrade list, but there are lots of situations where this could help you score a good extra legroom seat, or in some cases even a first class seat.

Those with the Delta Reserve Card receive a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit. This benefit applies once every four years. This can save you big time both at security and immigration, and is something I highly recommend signing up for if eligible.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive Hertz President’s Circle elite status, which is Hertz’s top-tier status. Status is valid for as long as you’re a cardmember. This should take the pain out of renting cars, and offers the following perks:

The Delta Reserve Card comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

The maximum benefit amount for Trip Cancellation and Interruption Insurance is $10,000 per Covered Trip and $20,000 per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Up to $500 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 6 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in holding multiple Amex cards so that you can get these offers on multiple cards and enjoy a variety of offers across cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page.

The Delta Reserve Credit Card has a steep annual fee, but the card also offers great benefits. The card offers perks ranging from lounge access, to a companion certificate, to up to two free checked bags, to upgrade priority, to all kinds of credits, to the ability to spend your way to elite status.

This card isn’t for the casual Delta flyer, but for someone who flies Delta moderately or often, I’d say this card is well worth considering.

If the Delta Reserve Amex sounds interesting to you but you are instead looking for a card for your small business, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve Business American Express Card.

Most of the benefits of the card are the same. One significant difference is that the business card earns 1.5x miles on all purchases after spending $150,000 annually, which could be useful for big spenders. Furthermore, the business card offers a $250 annual Delta Stays credit, rather than a $200 annual credit.

Many people might be trying to decide between the American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) and the Delta Reserve Card. The cards have some overlapping benefits:

But that’s largely where the similarities end:

The Delta Reserve Credit Card is Delta’s most premium credit card, though is it worth it compared to the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (learn more), which has a $350 annual fee (Rates & Fees)?

The Delta Reserve Card is Delta’s most premium credit card. While the card isn’t for everyone, I do think it’s well worth considering if you’re a frequent Delta flyer, and could benefit from lounge access, the companion ticket, improved upgrade priority, all of the credits, and the ability to earn status through credit card spending.

If you want to learn more about the Delta Reserve Amex Card, follow this link.

The following links will direct you to the rates and fees for mentioned American Express Cards. These include: American Express Platinum Card® (Rates & Fees), Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (Rates & Fees), and Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (Rates & Fees).

#6103. We Need a Better GOP

President Donald Trump attends the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, September 9, 2026.

The old Republican establishment could be out of touch, unimaginative, and too comfortable with revolving-door practices that enriched former officeholders and staffers, among other failings.

Beginning in 2016, Donald Trump burned this establishment to the ground and created a new one that has its own myriad deficiencies, some of which echo the failings of yore; the extremely online elements of today’s establishment, for instance, have found a whole new way to be out of touch.

We say this not to pine for yesterday’s establishment — parties never go back, only forward — but to make the point that every party elite reaches its point of exhaustion, and that’s where the Trump establishment is now.

There is a robust intramural argument on the right over how to interpret the historic loss in the midterms. We have our own views, but the most elemental need is a better GOP — one that is not beholden to the will of one man, doesn’t tolerate corruption, insists on strict adherence to the rule of law, encourages Congress to take up its allotted role in our constitutional system, rewards policy entrepreneurship on the part of officeholders, and focuses on results rather than performative provocations.

It’s possible to imagine any number of people leading such a national party, and it could have different ideological colorations depending on that leader and underlying circumstances. All that is TBD and should be a matter of fierce debate and competition. But unless the party moves beyond today’s establishment and renews itself, it risks subsequent devastating votes of no confidence from the American public.

Consider the issue of corruption, which was one of the biggest concerns of voters in the midterms. It is one thing for a party to suffer politically in the course of making progress on an important priority — say, stepped-up immigration enforcement. It is another to suffer from the perception — and, sadly, the reality — that politically connected people are engaged in untoward schemes for their own enrichment. The former is an inevitable political trade-off; the latter is a party’s elite feasting on its power and connections with no heed to the consequences for the larger cause.

President Trump, who has an overawing dominance over the party, is the source of many of the GOP’s current discontents. His influence is not going to drastically diminish anytime soon, and we know that many good Republicans have considered him better than the alternative, or have thrilled to his no-holds-barred assaults on the left. However one evaluates the Trump phenomenon, though, attempts to rely on the tropes that fueled his rise beginning in 2016, or ape his political style, will almost certainly fail — for the simple reasons that times change and Trump’s persona is not replicable.

The GOP could do much worse than look to the states, where Republican governors and legislators have cut taxes, restrained spending, pared back regulations, protected unborn children, and pursued reforms of schooling and housing. One reason that Florida constituted high ground beyond the reach of the blue wave is that it has been so well governed for so long, and it has had a series of reformist Republican governors focused on results.

At the national level, the GOP obviously needs a cost-of-living agenda that addresses high costs in health care, medicine, and education, and there’s much work that’s been done on these issues at the state level and among conservative policy thinkers. But arriving at a coherent agenda will require a seriousness of purpose and substantive focus that have been lacking for years now. That doesn’t mean the party should be dull and conventional — much can be learned from Trump’s zest for combat and vivid political branding — but it needs to recover a sense of institutional self-respect.

The new establishment, via President Trump, has worked its way back around to what were widely considered weaknesses of the old one. Republicans were once determined to make another push for amnesty after every election loss, and now, the president has floated that idea in response to the Democratic midterm victory; Republicans were once too soft on China, and Trump has been notably conciliatory in his second term; the GOP once talked a good game on deficit spending but didn’t do nearly enough to curtail it, while we are now adding to the debt hand over fist during a time of economic expansion and relative peace; the Tom DeLay–led Republican House was much too cozy with lobbyists, but prior GOP ethical lapses have been eclipsed over the past two years.

The old establishment had reached its expiration date and, regardless, isn’t coming back, while the current establishment is harmful to the party’s image and interests and an obstacle to change.

As Lincoln said, it is a time to think anew and act anew. The GOP desperately needs something fresh and different, with ideas and policies designed to meet the challenges of the day.

The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

#6102. Buy Hilton Honors Points With 120% Bonus By November 21: Worth It?

Through November 21, 2026, Hilton Honors is offering a buy points promotion, which is the program’s best-ever bonus on purchasing points! While Hilton Honors ordinarily offers up to a 100% bonus on purchased points, this time around the program is offering up to a 120% bonus, which is a cost of 0.45 cents per point. This could represent a great value for hotel redemptions, especially with an immediate use in mind, as members can purchase up to 528,000 points in one transaction.

As always, I only recommend buying points with a short term use in mind, and if you understand the mechanics of how award redemptions with a program work, including what redemption costs are like.

Link: Buy Hilton Honors points with this promotion with a 120% bonus

Between 12AM ET on October 7 and 11:59PM ET on November 21, 2026, Hilton Honors is offering a bonus on purchased points. Different Hilton Honors members may be targeted for different bonuses, so you’ll want to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for. It would appear that the best offer is for up to a 120% bonus, and that’s structured as follows:

Hilton Honors ordinarily charges one cent per purchased point, including all taxes and fees. That’s before any discounts or bonuses. If you’re eligible for the 120% bonus and maxed out the offer, you’d receive a total of 528,000 points at a cost of $2,400, which is a rate of 0.45 cents per Hilton Honors point.

Ordinarily, Hilton Honors lets members buy up to 160,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased by 50%, to 240,000 points. With a 120% bonus, that means you could purchase up to 528,000 points.

The purchase of Hilton Honors points is non-refundable, and points purchased don’t count toward elite status. Purchased points will post within 48 hours of finalizing the purchase (though in my experience, much faster than that).

While Hilton Honors has a strict limit on how many points you can buy, note that there are ways to acquire more points than that limit without violating the rules.

Hilton lets members combine points across accounts at no cost, so in reality you could acquire substantially more points by simply buying them across accounts and then consolidating them. Hilton Honors lets members transfer up to 500,000 points, and receive up to two million points, per calendar year. Each member can make up to six transfers to other members per calendar year, and new Hilton Honors members can only transfer or receive points a minimum of 30 days after enrollment.

Hilton also allows points pooling, whereby Hilton Honors members can combine points with up to 10 other members, with the same limitations.

When Hilton Honors offer a promotion on purchased points, it’s most common to see a 100% bonus (the equivalent of a 50% discount). So this 120% bonus is the best-ever promotion we’ve seen from the program, so that’s awesome.

Below is a chart with some of the recent buy points promotions we saw from the Hilton Honors program, before this one.

Hilton Honors point purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with a Hilton credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s Hilton spending.

I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

There’s potentially huge value to be had buying Hilton Honors points. Hilton Honors sells points at a reasonable cost, has lots of aspirational properties, has good redemptions with a fifth night free opportunity, and elite status is also easy to earn with the program. Hilton’s partnership with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) is also awesome, and offers great redemption opportunities.

However, people shouldn’t blindly buy Hilton Honors points, as there are also lots of redemptions where you won’t come out ahead. As I see it, the biggest value with buying Hilton Honors is for aspirational redemptions at expensive properties. Let me give some examples, based on current redemption rates.

For example, take the Waldorf Astoria Maldives, which is bookable for 250,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $1,125. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be $3,400, so that’s like two-thirds off. That’s pretty amazing!

As another example, take the Waldorf Astoria Los Cabos, which is bookable for 250,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $1,125. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be close to $2,200, so that’s like half off.

Above I mentioned the Hilton Honors partnership with SLH, so let me give an example there. RiverView Ranch Retreat is located in Montana, and is bookable for 220,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $990. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be over $3,800 (the screenshot below is for two nights, since that’s the minimum stay), so that’s close to three-fourths off.

Now, while the above are all examples of what a good deal it can be to buy Hilton Honors points, let me of course acknowledge that these are all top-end properties. Unfortunately I find that for your run of the mill Hilton properties, including many limited service hotels, the value just isn’t there in the same way.

For example, take the Hilton Garden Inn Tampa, which is bookable for 45,000 points per night. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $203. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be under $180, so there’s absolutely no reason to buy points, only to redeem them for less value than what you paid. You’ll find that to be pretty common, which is why I always recommend crunching the numbers before making a purchase.

Hilton Honors doesn’t have a published award chart, but rather the program has dynamic award pricing. This means that the cost of a standard free night award can vary depending on the day of the week, time of year, etc.

As a general rule of thumb, Hilton Honors free night awards start at 10,000 points per night, and go up to 250,000 points per night (which is a shame, because up until last year, properties maxed out at 150,000 points per night).

Sometimes you’ll see award costs that are way higher than these amounts. In those situations it’s because there’s not a standard room available, so higher pricing kicks in for premium rooms. That’s generally not nearly as good of a use of Hilton Honors points, and you’ll find that some awards even cost one million or more points per night. Obviously that’s a lousy value.

If you have Hilton Honors elite status (which is easy to earn, as I’ll outline below), you receive a fifth night free on award redemptions. This is a way to stretch your points even further, and whenever possible, I’d recommend making your Hilton Honors award stays in increments of five nights.

To take advantage of this, just log into your Hilton Honors elite account, and go through the process of making an award booking for five nights. When you get to the booking page, you should notice that the cost of the fifth night is automatically deducted.

Let me give an example how much value this can add. Say you want to book five nights at the Waldorf Astoria Seychelles Platte Island. At a rate of 150,000 points per night, you’d pay a total of 600,000 points for five nights, which averages out to 120,000 points per night. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, that’s like the equivalent of paying $540 per night. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be over $1,800 per night, so that represents absolutely massive savings.

One thing I love about the program is how easy it is to earn elite status with credit cards, including both Hilton Honors™ Gold Status and Hilton Honors™ Diamond Status. These tiers offer perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, hotel credits, and more. For example:

Hilton Honors points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 24 months. Eligible account activity includes earning or redeeming points, so buying points would even reset the expiration of your points.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Hilton Honors points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. As you can see, the pricing here is potentially better than what I value these points, and there are lots of ways to get outsized value with this promotion.

Hilton Honors doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, and all standard rooms are available for award redemptions. So this is about as good of a policy as you’ll find with any hotel group when it comes to award room availability.

There are lots of ways to earn Hilton Honors points, beyond just staying at Hilton properties or buying the points directly. You can easily earn points by using Hilton Honors’ co-branded credit cards, which also offer great welcome bonuses. These cards include the following:

You can also transfer points from Amex Membership Rewards to Hilton Honors (at a 1:2 ratio), and from Bilt Rewards to Hilton Honors (at a 1:1 ratio). I wouldn’t consider either of those redemptions to represent a good deal. That’s simply because I value Hilton Honors points at 0.5 cents each, while I value those points currencies at 1.7 cents each, so the math just doesn’t work out.

Hilton Honors is currently offering a best-ever bonus on purchased points, whereby members can receive up to a 120% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire points for 0.45 cents each. In the past we’ve generally seen bonuses of up to 100%, so this is a better offer than ever before. In fairness, Hilton Honors points have also been devalued a bit over time. With a short term use in mind, there are plenty of situations where this could represent a good deal.

Do you plan on buying Hilton Honors points with a bonus?

#6101. Transfer Chase Points To Virgin Atlantic Flying Club With 40% Bonus: Worth It?

The Chase Ultimate Rewards program is currently offering a bonus for points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While I’d only transfer points with a specific use in mind, there’s huge value to be had here, as a 40% transfer bonus is massive.

Between November 16 and December 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when transferring Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

This promotion is being offered on Chase’s end (in the United States), and is hard coded into the transfer ratio, meaning you should see the bonus at the time that you make the transfer. You can take advantage of this offer an unlimited number of times. Transfers from Chase to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club are generally instant.

We see a bonus like this to Virgin Atlantic a few times per year. We last saw a transfer bonus over the summer, so it hasn’t been a long gap at all. Past transfer bonuses have been in the range of 25-40%, so this is at the very top end of that spectrum.

There are several great cards earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points, and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Virgin Atlantic is a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic (with steep carrier imposed surcharges), there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta, as well as more broadly on SkyTeam airlines.

Nowadays Flying Club has dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. What’s exciting is that on the low end, redemption rates are very attractive, and it’s possible to fly Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and United Kingdom for under 30,000 points, in some situations. And that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

#6100. American Airlines’ Airbus A321neo Fleet Grows To 90, Expects 2 More & 1 A321XLR By Year’s End

American Airlines has expanded its Airbus A321neo fleet to 90 aircraft, with two more standard A321neos and one A321XLR expected before the end of 2026. The latest arrival continues the carrier's fleet modernization program, in which Airbus narrowbodies play an increasingly important role in its domestic and international networks.

The latest delivery follows an unusually busy period at the end of last month, when American received four A321-family aircraft in just seven days. Those deliveries included three standard A321neos and one A321XLR, registered N311NY. With no further Boeing deliveries expected this year, Airbus remains central to American's near-term fleet renewal strategy.

American's standard A321neo fleet has reached 90 aircraft, with two more expected before the end of the year. The airline is also anticipating one additional A321XLR, extending its investment in long-range, single-aisle aircraft. If all three outstanding deliveries arrive as planned, American will finish 2026 with 92 standard A321neos, alongside its growing fleet of 12 A321XLRs.

American's third-quarter financial disclosures showed that it had 165 Airbus A320-family aircraft on order as of September 30, with seven scheduled for delivery during the final quarter. The subsequent acceleration in October, when four A321-family aircraft arrived within a week, highlighted the program's pace. American also expects another 27 A321-family deliveries in 2027, although the precise split between the standard A321neo and A321XLR has not been disclosed.

The A321XLR is particularly important to American's international expansion, allowing it to serve longer routes with fewer passengers than a widebody aircraft would typically accommodate.

Brian Znotins, American's former Senior Vice President of Network Planning, highlighted the aircraft's importance when announcing the carrier's 2027 international expansion.

"The A321XLR is transforming our international network, expanding it to offer destinations to satisfy every travel palate. Combined with our investments enhancing our onboard product and in-flight experience, travelers have more reasons to choose American when they fly around the world."

American received its first A321XLR in October 2025, becoming the first US operator of the type. Its original 50-aircraft commitment was subsequently reduced to 40, including five delivered by the end of 2025. Each aircraft features 20 Flagship Suite business class seats, 12 premium economy seats, and 123 economy seats, emphasizing premium revenue over maximum capacity.

The XLR restores some of the long-range narrowbody capability American lost when it retired its 757s in 2020. Its economics make thinner transatlantic routes viable without deploying a much larger 787 Dreamliner. The aircraft initially entered service on premium transcontinental flights, before expanding into international markets as more aircraft became available.

American's 2027 schedule demonstrates its ambitions, with four additional European routes assigned to the XLR. Philadelphia-Vienna, measuring approximately 4,321 miles (6,955 km), is particularly notable as it will become the world's longest narrowbody flight. The route will operate daily from May 6 through January 2028, while New York gains new services to Amsterdam and Nice.

13 new routes were planned but now only seven are scheduled.

The standard A321neo remains central to American's high-capacity narrowbody strategy. With its fleet now at 90 aircraft, it still has firm orders for 126 more airframes as the airline continues investing in the type to support busy domestic routes and replace older aircraft.

Configured with 196 seats, including 20 First Class and 47 Main Cabin Extra seats, American's legacy A321neos accommodate 41 more passengers than the XLR. It is particularly valuable on busy domestic routes connecting American's major hubs and supports the gradual replacement of older narrowbodies. Its versatility extends internationally, with Philadelphia-Reykjavík scheduled to launch in May 2027.

American's Boeing 737 MAX 8s complement the A321neos, offering 172 seats on routes requiring less capacity. The airline also has substantial outstanding Boeing narrowbody orders, including the larger 737 MAX 10, although deliveries of that variant are not expected until 2029 or later. With an eventual planned fleet size of more than 250 A321-family aircraft, Airbus narrowbodies will continue to play a leading role in American's domestic modernization and expanding transatlantic network.

#6099. Rep. James Comer launches 2027 bid for Kentucky governor

Kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook issues, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.)

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”

While Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”

#6098. She Lived to the Sound of God’s Music

Remembering God’s gift to New York City girls and beyond.

From left: Sr. Christine Cosgrove, O.P., the author, Sr. Martha Kunesh, O.P., and speaker Kristen Hanson, an advocate against assisted suicide, at a National Review Institute/Sheen Center event on the virtue of hope.

Could anything sound more exotic today? This opening line comes from a 16th-century prayer by the Carmelite reformer St. Teresa of Avila. She carried it in the breviary she used for daily prayer. It also captures the quiet steadiness of Sister Martha Kunesh, O.P. (the initials stand for “Order of Preachers”), who entered a Dominican convent just before the opening of the Second Vatican Council. She took the religious name Sister Teresa Avila (“the ‘of’ was silent,” it was said). She eventually returned to her birth name, but she never lost the contemplative spirit of her first patron.

#6097. Atmos Rewards Upgrade Certificates: How Do They Work, Are They Worth It?

Atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. The program has four elite tiers — Silver, Gold, Platinum, and Titanium — and somehow I’m actually going to end the year as a top tier member, it looks like, without having once stepped foot on an Alaska or Hawaiian flight.

As I’ve worked my way through the elite ranks, I’ve become eligible for the milestone perks program, whereby you can select perks when passing various elite thresholds. Along those lines, At the higher tiers, one of the choices becomes upgrade certificates, so I’d like to talk about those a bit, as I’m trying to decide whether or not I should select these.

I’m intrigued by Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, given the increasingly global route network of Alaska and Hawaiian. At the same time, the execution of this upgrade program definitely leaves a lot to be desired, including the lack of confirmable upgrade availability.

I have to make a selection soon, so I’d like to talk through the Alaska and Hawaiian upgrade certificate program, and then get some feedback from Atmos Rewards loyalists. The last time I was focused on upgrade certificates at the airline was when Alaska Mileage Plan had Gold Guest Upgrades as the upgrade currency, and MVP Gold was the top tier status… those were the days!

Atmos Rewards issues upgrade certificates as part of the Atmos Rewards milestone perks program. This can be unlocked based on how many status points you earn over the course of a calendar year. Let me emphasize that these upgrade certificates are intended for confirming upgrades in advance, and they’re separate from the complimentary space available upgrades offered.

Specifically, Atmos Rewards members could earn upgrade certificates at the following thresholds:

Titanium status requires 135,000 status points, and I expect to end the year with roughly that many status points. That means I could select up to eight upgrade certificates. However, that would come at the opportunity cost of 70,000 bonus points, for example. Of course I could also mix and match, like selecting four upgrade certificates and 50,000 bonus points.

Now let’s talk a bit about the rules for redeeming Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, at least on paper. Upgrades are valid across the Alaska and Hawaiian route networks, and fall into one of two categories:

Upgrade certificates can be shared with others, but of course can’t be bartered or sold. One other interesting quirk is that if you cancel or change an itinerary that was upgraded, the certificate will be forfeited. However, a replacement upgrade certificate code can be requested through customer care. Let’s cover the details of upgrades based on the region.

When it comes to upgrading within North America, an Atmos Rewards upgrade certificate can be confirmed at the time of booking, as long as the “U” fare class is available. If it’s not available, the upgrade will be waitlisted.

To cover the very basics, the upgrade certificate is valid for one-way travel (with no connections longer than four hours), for tickets issued by and flown on Alaska and Hawaiian. Tickets purchased in Y, B, H, K, M, L, V, S, or N fare classes, are eligible for upgrades using certificates, while tickets purchased in Q, O, G, or X fare classes, are not eligible.

To search if a flight is upgrade eligible, select “Upgrade Certificate” in the dropdown in the “Upgrade type” section, during the booking process.

Then on the search results page, you should be looking for two things:

When it comes to upgrading outside of North America, Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates have completely different rules, both for better and worse. First, it’s worth understanding that an upgrade requires either one or two upgrade certificates, depending on the route, per the below chart.

When it comes to using Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates on global (non-North America) flights, there are both pros and cons:

I have to say, the execution of this perk is odd. Keep in mind that Atmos Rewards has a one-of-a-kind upgrade perk for top tier Titanium members, whereby they receive space available upgrades globally on the day of departure. So what’s odd is that if you’re a Titanium member you’re eligible for a complimentary upgrade close to departure, but having applied an upgrade certificate previously gives you no priority. You’d think they’d prioritize members who requested an upgrade, but I suspect it’s a technology limitation of some sort.

I’d like to address the question of whether Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates are worth it both broadly, and more specifically to my situation.

I hear all the time from Atmos Rewards members who are frustrated by the lack of confirmable upgrade space. And indeed, compared to back in the day, upgrade space that can be confirmed is incredibly limited. At the same time, that’s true across airlines nowadays, given how much better airlines have become at actually selling their first class seats, rather than filling them with those upgrading.

For example, looking at the route between my home airport of Miami (MIA) and Seattle (SEA) as far out as the schedule opens, I don’t see a single date that has confirmable upgrade space. Now, you’ll sometimes find confirmable upgrade space up and down the West Coast, especially during off peak times, so I don’t want to suggest it’s impossible to find a confirmable upgrade.

But just broadly speaking, confirmable upgrades with “U” class available for transcontinental and Hawaii flights are exceedingly rare, and it’s like winning the lottery. So it’s really hard to get excited about that.

In theory, I of course love the idea of being able to upgrade a long haul flight with upgrade certificates. The catch is that an upgrade clearing at most 72 hours before departure really limits flexibility. I suppose you could always apply an upgrade, hope it clears, and then cancel your ticket if it doesn’t, but this would be a last minute scramble.

To me, that’s just too risky. It’s not that I’d be unwilling to fly economy on a long haul flight, but by strategically using points, it’s really not necessary in a vast majority of situations, at least based on my own travel patterns.

The thing is, it’s also important to view Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates in terms of the opportunity cost of selecting them.

For example, as I mentioned above, at 55,000 status points I can select two upgrade certificates or 5,000 bonus points. At an opportunity cost of 2,500 points per upgrade certificate, I think it might be worth selecting upgrade certificates. Based on my latest points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, so the opportunity cost per upgrade is $37.50. That’s a rate at which I’d probably be happy to gamble, because if the upgrades expire, it’s not the end of the world.

Meanwhile at 95,000 status points, the opportunity cost becomes 7,500 bonus points per upgrade, so that’s a value of $112.50 per upgrade. Then at 125,000 status points, the opportunity cost becomes 12,500 bonus points per upgrade, so that’s a value of $187.50. That’s the point at which I’m definitely more inclined to take the “sure thing,” rather than take my chances with an upgrade.

Atmos Rewards lets members select upgrade certificates as part of the milestone perks program. This always comes at an opportunity cost, and is a better value at some tiers than others.

Upgrade certificates can be used on Alaska and Hawaiian flights globally, with most one-ways requiring one upgrade certificate, though some global routes requiring two upgrade certificates. While upgrades within North America can be confirmed at the time of booking (pending upgrade availability), global upgrades can only be confirmed at most 72 hours before departure.

The big issue with upgrades is the lack of availability. Alaska is just really bad about making confirmed upgrades available, and upgrades clearing at most 72 hours before departure on global flights is less than ideal.

What do you make of the value of Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates?

It appears air travel is back on track after one of the most chaotic weekends we’ve seen at airports in years.

Flight schedules returned to normal this week after a rare nationwide ground stop created a nightmare weekend for flying. More than 18,000 flights were canceled between Friday and Sunday, affecting millions of travelers. It appears there will be no spillover from that meltdown into the big Thanksgiving travel week that’s on the horizon, though.

It’s not so much a safety question — industry experts steadfastly agree that air travel is still remarkably safe.

But there are plenty of worries about the possibility of another major air travel headache like we saw this weekend.

And that’s a stressful and costly reality whether you’re a passenger, a crew member, an airline executive or a front-line aviation worker.

In recent years, travelers have gotten one reminder after another about how strained our aviation infrastructure is.

For years, the Federal Aviation Administration has been plagued by both severely outdated technology and short staffing in air traffic control.

Those concerns have grown even louder in the wake of several recent incidents.

After 9/11, the U.S. went more than 20 years without a nationwide ground stop like the one we saw on Friday.

We’ve now seen two happen since 2023. Both instances involved outages to critical FAA systems.

Meanwhile, the vital air traffic control workforce that directs the flow of planes in our airspace has been chronically understaffed. Controllers routinely work six-day weeks and mandatory overtime.

Together, these problems have fueled several of the most high-profile air travel disruptions in recent memory.

Last fall, ATC staffing was a major factor in the mass flight cancellations and delays we saw at the height of the government shutdown.

In 2025, equipment outages plus undermanned air traffic control centers contributed to the weeks of chaos travelers endured at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR).

In the wake of the latest technology failure on Friday, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford was asked bluntly whether he could say for certain that there wouldn’t be a repeat of this past weekend’s chaos.

“I can say with certainty that the system is really, really old,” he told CBS News Tuesday.

“Let’s not kid ourselves,” Bedford added. “This system has been fragile, and it does go down.”

There has been momentum to fix both problems, which have festered for decades under the leadership of both political parties.

In recent years, the FAA has upped its air traffic control hiring efforts, in a push to reduce long-standing vacancies.

Meanwhile, Congress last year earmarked $12.5 billion for infrastructure upgrades.

The Department of Transportation has started that work, but says it needs a lot more money to make truly sweeping upgrades.

The travel sector has broadly supported that request: “They need to get to 100% staffing and to have the funds to modernize the technology,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby wrote in a social media post Sunday.

But securing that funding will hinge on political dealmaking in Washington, D.C., which in January will be led by a divided government.

And however that fight ends, these problems won’t be solved overnight.

It takes years to fully train air traffic controllers.

And to add to the complexity, overhauling aviation infrastructure while tens of thousands of flights operate each day is painstaking work with significant consequences — even if the money is there in the first place.

Look no further than last week’s FAA outage, where crews replacing a router apparently triggered a chain-reaction outage that upended air travel in the U.S. for days — a disruption American Airlines now counts among the most significant in its 100-year history.

“The transition itself needs to be carefully analyzed and tested,” said Capt. Shem Malmquist, a longtime Boeing 777 captain and visiting professor at the Florida Institute of Technology’s College of Aeronautics. “Otherwise, an upgrade intended to solve one problem can introduce another."

Despite all the concerning headlines, industry experts largely agree:

“Both things can be true,” Malmquist said, pointing to the many safety layers that allow planes to safely operate even when problems arise.

Keep in mind: Every plane that was in the sky during last week’s FAA disruption landed safely.

And the move to halt thousands of flights? That was ultimately meant to protect travelers, leaders have emphasized.

"Passengers experience delays and cancellations, but those restrictions help keep the system safe," Malmquist said. “That doesn’t mean the underlying vulnerabilities are acceptable.”

#6095. Wow: Lufthansa Adds Premium Business Seats On Some Short Haul A320 Flights!

Lufthansa has just announced plans to introduce “real” business class seats on some of its narrow body planes, and that’s a really exciting development, given the typical business class standard on narrow body aircraft in Europe!

Interestingly, this is a concept that was initially trialed on Lufthansa Group low cost subsidiary Eurowings, and we knew at the time it was being used as a test for a more widespread implementation across the airline group. I’m delighted to see this become more widespread, and I hope this is just the start of a bigger trend.

Lufthansa has revealed that it will expand its premium offering on short and medium haul routes. With the introduction of the new Premium Business Seat, passengers will get more personal space than they’re used to on short haul aircraft.

Historically, business class on Airbus A320-family aircraft has consisted of standard economy seats with a blocked middle. So that means with the 3-3 layout, four seats were only sold per row. What’s happening is that the first three rows on some aircraft are being replaced with two rows of recliner seats, meaning the per-seat footprint is around 50% bigger than in standard business class.

At launch, the new Lufthansa Premium Business Seat will be available on six Airbus A320 aircraft (and these planes will also be equipped with Starlink). The seat will feature significantly more space, with nearly one meter of legroom, plus extra recline. This doesn’t replace the standard business class product, but instead, is an upsell option.

This new product is now available for sale for flights as of March 1, 2027, on routes between Frankfurt (FRA) and Athens (ATH), Cairo (CAI), and Nice (NCE). However, the first plane with the seats will already be in service as of December 16, 2026, and as of February 2027, it’ll be deployed on the above routes (but tickets are only on sale as of March as of now).

If a flight has this product available, you’ll see the “Premium Business Seat” designator during the booking process.

The process of actually booking a Premium Business Seat is essentially an upgrade cost on top of the standard business class fare. For example, looking at a Frankfurt to Athens route, I see an upgrade cost of €139, which frankly seems quite reasonable for a flight of this length.

Lufthansa is for the time being describing this as a commercial test, with the aim of examining demand for additional comfort on these routes, and the results will form the basis for deciding whether to expand the offering.

You’ll see many people refer to short haul business class in Europe as a “scam” (I don’t agree, but people say that), and they’re shocked to find economy seats with blocked middles. Admittedly product standards differ vastly around the globe.

The reason that airlines in Europe can get away with this product is threefold:

Keep in mind that most of the network carriers in Europe don’t make much money on short haul flights (or even lose a lot of money), given high costs and fierce competition from ultra low cost carriers.

With that in mind, I think Lufthansa is going about this exactly right:

I’d love to see more airlines introduce something similar. In particular, Air France, as Europe’s most premium airline, seems best positioned to do this, and could do it with very little opportunity cost. Why?

Honestly, if I were Air France, I’d just introduce this throughout the A220 fleet, and it would be a major point of differentiation, competitively. No airline could do it as efficiently as Air France, and every A220 flight has at least two rows of business class, so the opportunity cost is minimal.

Lufthansa will be introducing “real” business class seats on a subfleet of its Airbus A320s. As of the spring of 2027, expect these planes to be flying from Frankfurt to Athens, Cairo, and Nice. This Premium Business Seat concept will complement the existing business class, and will be available as a buy-up for business class passengers.

I’m very happy to finally see some more comfort on flights within Europe, and I imagine this will prove successful. If it doesn’t, I suspect it would be due to a lack of people knowing about this, rather than there not actually being demand.

What do you make of the Lufthansa Premium Business Seat concept?

#6094. New Resy Rewards Program Offers 4x Bonus Amex Points For Dining Out

Resy has just launched the Resy Rewards program, which lets American Express card members in the United States earn an extra 4x points per dollar spent at participating Resy restaurants, on top of their credit card rewards. As you’d expect, it’s not quite that straightforward, but I’d still consider this to be pretty exciting!

American Express owns both Resy and Tock (which is now being integrated into Resy), as part of its larger “lifestyle” play for attracting card members. So along with that, Resy is leaning more into the rewards program side of things, with the new Resy Rewards program offering an extra 4x Amex points per dollar spent at eligible Resy restaurants.

Resy Rewards is first launching in New York City, where users will see a new “Rewards” tab within the Resy iOS app, where they can browse and book eligible restaurants. Restaurants participating in the Resy Rewards launch include Carne Mare, Le Crocodile, Hearth, Kiko, OPTO, Le Pavillon, and more. In 2027, Resy Rewards plans to expand to additional U.S. cities, and select Tock venues will become eligible to participate in the program.

So, how exactly does Resy Rewards work? Card members need to enroll a US-based Membership Rewards program eligible card in Resy Rewards, then book a Resy Rewards reservation through the “Rewards” tab in the Resy iOS app, and then pay the bill for the dining experience with the enrolled card. So this requires a little more jumping through hoops than just using an Amex card Resy credit, for example.

These rewards are in addition to whatever the standard rewards are on an Amex card. For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) ordinarily earns 4x points at restaurants globally, so if you dined at a restaurant eligible for Resy Rewards, you could be earning 8x points per dollar spent, which is pretty awesome.

Here’s how Pablo Rivero, CEO of Resy and SVP of American Express Global Dining, describes this:

“For the first time, we’re bringing American Express’s industry-leading Rewards program into the Resy iOS app and connecting two things our Card Members value deeply: great dining experiences and meaningful rewards. As we’ve seen with the success of the Resy Credit, rewarding diners while driving demand and revenue to Resy restaurants is a win on both sides of the table.”

I’m delighted to see Amex introduce an opportunity to earn points for dining out, beyond the bonus categories already offered on some of the issuer’s most popular cards. For the time being, this is rather niche, given that it’s limited to select restaurants in New York City, but the expectation is that it will expand more broadly in 2027 (though it remains to be seen how broadly).

Essentially think of this as being similar to a dining rewards program, as the idea is that restaurants have to opt-in to participate in this, with the hope being that this drums up business for them (and presumably they pay Amex and Resy something extra in exchange for that).

Furthermore, you do have to specifically reserve your reservation through Resy to qualify for this, so if you don’t have a reservation made through the “Rewards” tab on Resy, then you won’t earn bonus points.

I’m happy to see this, as earning 8x points on dining when paying with the Amex Gold Card is quite a great deal. Then again, so much of my dining out is through InKind, which is my favorite dining rewards program, given the excellent selection of restaurants the program has in Miami, and it’s tough to compete with the rewards offered by the program.

The new Resy Rewards program offers bonus Amex points when you make a reservation at an eligible restaurant and then pay with your eligible Amex card. The idea is that you can earn an extra 4x points per dollar spent on purchases at eligible restaurants, which is pretty awesome.

The catch is that this is initially launching in New York City, only “eligible” restaurants qualify, and you need to reserve through Resy and then pay with the same linked card in order to earn the bonus points. It’s nice to see this launch, and I look forward to it expanding to more markets.

#6093. Why Southwest Airlines Might Change Its Cabin Interior Again

Southwest Airlines completed the fleet-wide reconfiguration of its cabins to add extra legroom seating earlier this year. The 737 MAX 8s and 737-800s left the shop essentially the same as when they entered, but with the seat pitch adjusted to add the extra legroom section, while the 737-700s have lost one row to make room for the extra legroom seats.

The project was massive in scope, but the work itself was light and was even completed a week ahead of schedule. The reconfigurations represent the start of a new era at Southwest, in which the famous 'open seating' policy has been discontinued.

Today, there are now premium seating options, and passengers are paying to select specific seats online. The final Southwest flight with open seating, operating from Honolulu to LAX, departed on January 26, and when it arrived the following morning, Southwest was just like everyone else. However, could another interior modification be on the cards?

Southwest has recently changed the configurations of its entire 800+ Boeing 737 fleet. The primary change was to adjust the seat pitches of each aircraft to create a dedicated section of extra legroom seats. While the newest Boeing 737 MAX 8 deliveries feature Recaro R2 seats with special seat covers to denote that they offer added space, these seats will be largely indistinguishable on most aircraft.

This is because special seat covers have not been applied to the Collins Meridian or Innovator II seats found on older aircraft. The 737-800s and 737 MAX 8s are maintaining their maximum capacity of 175 seats, but 45 of these seats now feature 36 inches (91.44 cm) of legroom, per aeroLOPA.

The 737-700s, previously configured with 143 seats, will now feature 137 seats, as the thickness of the older Innovator II seats meant that a row had to be sacrificed to make room for the extra legroom seats. 40 of these are extra legroom seats, boasting an exceptional seat pitch of 38 inches (96.52 cm). Currently, only new 737 MAX 8s, along with some reconfigured 737-800s, feature the Recaro R2 seats.

The rest of the 737 MAX 8 fleet and most of the 737-800 fleet are equipped with the Collins Meridian. Meanwhile, some 737-800s, along with all 737-700s, are equipped with the B/E Aerospace (now part of Collins) Innovator II. Some 737-700s will be retrofitted with Collins Meridian seats, and all 737-800s with the Innovator II seats will receive the Recaro R2. All planes with the R2 feature in-seat power, and all aircraft with the Collins Meridian will be retrofitted with in-seat power.

Southwest's CEO Bob Jordan has confirmed that his company is seriously looking into adding a first class cabin onto its planes. No official announcement has been made since Jordan commented on this idea in January, and looking into a new cabin is hardly the same as a confirmation

However, in the current state of the US market, as well as Southwest's trajectory, Jordan's comments are essentially a confirmation that a first class cabin on Southwest is a matter of when, not if. Naturally, any details as to what this could look like are pure speculation. The company is partnering with Recaro for its newest economy seats, so the Recaro R4 or R5 would be the frontrunners.

Southwest is retrofitting its aircraft with in-seat power as well as Wi-Fi, so you can expect these amenities, but seatback entertainment is extremely unlikely. The carrier's pitch for extra legroom seats is among the best in the industry, so some inches would likely be taken out to make room for first class seats. Southwest Airlines traditionally positioned itself as a hybrid carrier, blurring the lines between a low-cost carrier and a legacy airline.

Now, however, budget airlines are increasingly moving upmarket as that's where the money is. Spirit long offered a stripped-down first class product called 'Big Front Seat' before its collapse, and Frontier is now also preparing to debut a new first class product. JetBlue, meanwhile, is working on a domestic first class product titled 'Mini Mint.'

Southwest Airlines once pulled off the impossible, using an ambitious strategy to save the company.

In any industry, premium products generally sell for high margins, but of course, face a smaller market than mainstream products. In the US airline industry, however, the market for premium seating has increased dramatically. As such, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and Alaska Airlines have been making all of the money.

Meanwhile, the rest (including American, which strategically moved downmarket before COVID) have been left behind. This is tied to the increasing importance of loyalty programs, which are the primary profit centers at Delta, United, and Alaska. Customers want to earn miles and use airline-sponsored credit cards so that they can then fly in Delta One, travel to Cape Town with United, or book an award ticket with an Alaska Atmos partner.

Earning Southwest Rapid Rewards points for redemptions in economy within the US simply doesn't have the same appeal, and so consumers are moving to the legacies. Adding a first class product increases the appeal of Southwest's Rapid Rewards program and gives potential loyalists more incentive to build status with the carrier.

First class seats are also higher-margin products than economy seats as a whole. Being cheap no longer sells, which is why the ultra-low-cost carriers are adding premium products, and Southwest's previous brand image of being a quirky airline with a uniform onboard product at largely affordable prices also doesn't cut it today.

There can be no denying that after Elliott Investment first boarded the airline in June 2024, it fundamentally changed Southwest's business model. Before Elliott, Southwest did not offer premium seating, it gave two checked bags for free, there were no airline partnerships, bookings could only be made on Southwest's website, there were no assigned seats, and no redeye flights.

Elliott aggressively argued that this needed to change. It is true that Southwest's finances greatly lagged behind industry leaders coming out of the COVID-19 pandemic, and the carrier had also been suffering from antiquated systems as well as outdated practices. Southwest's operational and sales changes, as such, have been a net positive.

However, many of the customer-facing changes have been controversial, to say the least. Southwest is now charging for previously complimentary services like checked bags, and it now assigns seats to passengers. Under Elliott, Southwest has been chasing ancillary revenue and attempting to move up-market with its premium seating options.

However, before the COVID-19 pandemic, Southwest had recorded nearly half a century of straight profits. This was possible because Southwest's unique attributes, such as open seating and two free checked bags, garnered it a cult following. This customer base kept Southwest in the green during previous downturns, but Southwest, under Elliott, has decided to shun its most loyal followers in favor of following industry trends.

Here's the latest in a long series of changes aimed at transforming Southwest into an entirely new, more profitable airline.

Southwest is now just like every other airline in the US, and the former loyalists now have no reason to stick with the carrier. Instead, the carrier is targeting a wider audience and offering an increasingly diverse selection of seating options to cater to a more premium clientele. It's competing mainly on price, schedule, and network.

While boosting ancillary revenue has increased the carrier's short-term financials, it's not sustainable to rely on this long-term. Without Southwest's former cult following, the carrier has to commit fully to its premium shift, even once Elliott Investment has left the company. First class is as popular with travelers as ever, and delaying Southwest's entry into this market space simply leaves money on the table.

Furthermore, the presence and availability of the product will make Rapid Rewards a more desirable loyalty program, a goal that Southwest has already been working towards with its foreign airline partnerships and changes to its credit cards. It's unclear when Southwest will commit to this move or how the product will look.

​​​​​​​However, the US airline industry is shifting towards one dominated by premium products and loyalty programs. Southwest, looking to emulate the profits made by the nation's most successful airlines, is adapting to emulate their business models. As such, first class could be the next logical step.

#6092. What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

"I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson plan?

Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”

Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

Mary C. Curtis has worked at The New York Times, The Baltimore Sun, The Charlotte Observer, as national correspondent for Politics Daily, and is a senior facilitator with The OpEd Project. She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on X @mcurtisnc3.
