#6091. Delta SkyMiles & World Of Hyatt Partnership Live: Dual Earning, Milestone Rewards, & Linking Accounts

In September 2026, Delta SkyMiles and World of Hyatt unveiled plans to launch a new, long term strategic partnership. This announcement came just shortly after American AAdvantage and World of Hyatt announced that they will be ending their partnership.

At the time, we didn’t actually have any details as to what the partnership would entail, but that has now changed, as additional information has been revealed. Parts of the partnership are even now live, and members can already link their accounts.

Delta and Hyatt are launching a new loyalty program collaboration, which comes with a “shared ambition to create additional value, recognition and engagement opportunities across more of the travel journey.” This includes reciprocal opportunities to earn rewards, and also reciprocal opportunities to select perks with the partner brand.

Here’s how Laurie Blair, Hyatt’s SVP of Global Marketing and Loyalty, describes this:

“World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles were each built to make travel more meaningful and rewarding, which makes this collaboration feel meant to be. By connecting the Delta flight and Hyatt stay, we are helping members get more from the journeys they are already taking while opening the door to new experiences, destinations and memories. It is an exciting next step in our commitment to caring for members throughout the full travel journey, from takeoff to check out.”

Here’s how Dwight James, Delta’s SVP of Customer Engagement & Loyalty, describes this:

“At Delta, we know loyalty is something we earn by delivering meaningful value and experiences that make our Members want to keep choosing us. Our relationship with World of Hyatt gives us another way to do that by recognizing and rewarding Members across more of their travel, while creating new ways to earn, engage and experience both brands.”

Effective immediately (as of November 17, 2026), elite members of both loyalty programs can earn simultaneously with the new “Dual Earn” benefit. Members must link their accounts, and can then earn additional rewards.

World of Hyatt members can earn bonus points on eligible Delta flights (which includes Delta Comfort, Delta Premium Select, Delta First Class, and Delta One), as follows:

Delta SkyMiles members can earn bonus miles on eligible Hyatt stays (which includes qualifying room rates, qualifying incidental spend, and qualifying non-stay charges at participating Hyatt properties, eligible Mr & Mrs Smith spend booked through Hyatt, and eligible spend at The Venetian booked through Hyatt):

As of 2027, eligible elite members of both World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles will gain access to new milestone reward choices, giving people more ways to earn, and more flexibility in how they use their loyalty benefits. This would apply to World of Hyatt Milestone Rewards, and Delta SkyMiles Choice Benefits.

As of January 1, 2027, World of Hyatt members will be able to choose Delta awards as they reach qualifying Milestone Rewards thresholds. The first Delta award choice will become available at 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 base points, with additional choices as members progress through the program, including:

As of February 1, 2027, Delta SkyMiles members will be able to choose Hyatt awards as they reach qualifying Choice Benefits thresholds. Members will be able to select free night awards, as follows:

To celebrate the start of this partnership, Hyatt and Delta are offering limited time offers for members who link their accounts.

First, from November 17 through December 31, 2026, linked members can register to earn one additional World of Hyatt elite night after completing their first qualifying Hyatt stay during the offer period. Taking advantage of this should be a no-brainer.

Next, from January 4 through February 15, 2027, linked members can:

Basically, Hyatt has dumped American in favor of Delta. Admittedly the partnership between American and Hyatt had already been scaled back over time. The two programs used to offer a dual accrual opportunity as well, but that was eventually cut.

After all, companies only want to offer perks like that if they’re driving incremental business, and I imagine at some point it’s hard to justify that expense, when you feel like there’s not much upside left:

Now the Delta and Hyatt partnership is starting out in a similar way to how the American one did, with one major exception. On the dual accrual front, SkyMiles elite members are lucky, as they earn rewards on all qualifying Hyatt spending. Meanwhile World of Hyatt members only earn rewards when booking premium tickets, which is a bit disappointing. And here I was thinking that all seats on Delta aircraft are premium!!

I do have to say, as much as I’m a World of Hyatt loyalist, the program has certainly become less differentiated over time. While Delta can argue all it wants about how premium it is, SkyMiles simply isn’t as good of a loyalty program as AAdvantage. So perhaps this swap reflects the direction Hyatt is trying to head on loyalty… I dunno.

Delta and Hyatt have launched an exclusive new partnership, which explains why American and Hyatt cut ties. The partnership is now live, and it includes dual points accrual opportunities, reciprocal milestone perks, and some limited time opportunities.

At a minimum, it’s definitely worth linking accounts. And if you’re a World of Hyatt member with a stay planned before the end of the year, be sure to register for an extra elite night, as there’s no reason not to take advantage of that.

What do you make of this new Delta and Hyatt partnership, and American being dumped?

#6090. Standing Athwart Pumpkin Tyranny

Through October and November, this mediocre flavor and scent are in everything everywhere all the time.

A display of Trader Joe’s pumpkin and fall-themed products at a grocery store in Lafayette, Calif., September 25, 2026.

A pumpkin spice latte is on the menu at every coffee shop. Sometimes, the drink is served in a pumpkin-shaped mug. To lure in customers for brunch, quaint cafes serving pumpkin pancakes put a chalkboard sign on the sidewalk saying, “COME IN FOR GOURD VIBRATIONS!” Each bakery has pumpkin scones, pumpkin pie, pumpkin banana bread, and pumpkin coffee cake. An attempt to order an old fashioned will be met with an invitation from the demoralized bartender, “Do you want to try our pumpkin spice old fashioned?” The pen at the bank is topped with a rubber pumpkin; this way, customers know that all the money is kept safe. Little plastic pumpkins are in the windows displays at clothing shops, or beside the cashiers (who work in front of pumpkin-flavored nicotine patches). Squashes are piled high in cardboard bins by the entrance of every grocery store. I reach for what I think is my favorite chai tea blend on the shelves — but alas! It is now pumpkin chai with an orange label.

Through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time. Anything edible is infused, swirled, drizzled, and dusted with pumpkin. You cannot escape the flavor: pumpkin cereal, pumpkin protein powder, pumpkin bagels with pumpkin cream cheese. The Asian aisle has frozen Kung Pao-mpkin Dumplings. Dog treats are flavored like a pumpkin spice latte because everyone must participate, no exceptions. Longstanding favorites are replaced, so French fries are now pumpkin fries. That peculiar squash always sneaks its way into a dish, and so the stuffed raviolis have a little bit of pumpkin. Despite its omnipresence, the pumpkin surprises you: The waiter arrives at the table with a salad that is topped — just for this week — with toasted pumpkin seeds. (Of course, the utensils are wrapped in a flimsy brown napkin dotted with little orange pumpkins.) Even things we thought were reliably mint, like gum and the dentist’s fluoride, are pumpkin spice.

Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

#6089. Earning World Of Hyatt Elite Nights & Status With Credit Cards: Worth It?

Chase and Hyatt have two co-branded credit cards — the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more). I’d consider these to be among the more lucrative hotel credit cards out there, particularly the personal version of the card.

One of the awesome things about Hyatt’s two credit cards is that they can earn you elite nights, making it easier to qualify for status in the World of Hyatt program. In this post, I’d like to get into the nitty-gritty of how earning Hyatt elite status with credit cards works, and discuss whether it’s worth it.

Chase and Hyatt have both the World of Hyatt Credit Card (a personal card) and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (a business card). Both cards have valuable benefits, though I think the personal card is considerably more compelling than the business card. Let me start by just briefly recapping the perks of the two cards.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card has a $95 annual fee and offers:

This means that you’re getting five elite nights toward status and a Category 1-4 free night award every year just for having the card. To me that more than justifies the annual fee, by a long shot (I consistently get $250+ of value out of the free night certificate alone). That doesn’t even factor in the incremental perks you can get for spending on the card.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card has a $199 annual fee and offers:

The business version of the card isn’t quite as rewarding as the personal version of the card, especially if you’re not a big spender. However, for businesses that spend quite a bit on credit cards, this can be the best card for earning elite status.

Both the World of Hyatt Credit Card and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offer the ability to earn elite nights. However, the ways in which you earn elite nights differ between the two cards, so let’s go over those details.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers qualifying nights toward Hyatt status in two ways. First of all, the World of Hyatt Card offers five elite nights annually just for having the card. There’s no spending required to earn these five elite nights, and you receive them for each calendar year in which you have the card, including the year in which you open the card.

Beyond that, the World of Hyatt Card offers two elite nights for every $5,000 spent on the card (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,500 of spending). There’s no limit to how many elite nights you can earn this way, and the elite nights earned through spending on this card aren’t in any way tied to the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $2,500 on the card in 2026 and then spend $2,500 on the card in 2027, you’d earn two elite nights at that point.

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offers five elite nights for every $10,000 spent on the card in a calendar year (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,000 of spending). On this card, the spending counter resets at the beginning of the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $8,000 on the card in 2026, you’d still have to spend a full $10,000 in 2027 to earn five elite nights.

As you can see, this card offers elite nights for spending at an accelerated rate, though unlike the personal card, it doesn’t offer the five elite nights annually just for having the card.

How soon do elite nights post from the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card?

While the above covers the basics, I’d like to now analyze the overall value proposition of earning World of Hyatt elite status by spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, including addressing some of the most common questions and scenarios that come up.

With Hyatt, not all elite perks are tied directly to having status, but rather some require earning a certain number of elite nights in a year, known as the Milestone Rewards program. The Milestone Rewards program is how you earn perks like suite upgrade awards, club access awards, Guest of Honor awards, and more.

Hyatt elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards would count toward Milestone Rewards the same as any hotel stays would, which adds further value to credit card spending.

One of the perks of both Hyatt credit cards is that you receive Discoverist status for as long as you have the card. Discoverist status ordinarily requires 10 elite qualifying nights or 25,000 base points per year. As a reminder, here are World of Hyatt’s elite thresholds:

One common point of confusion is that people assume these cards really come with up to 15 elite nights per year. They assume you already get Discoverist status, and that any elite nights are on top of that. Note that while these cards offer Discoverist status, you don’t get the elite nights that correspond to that.

This means that if you have a Hyatt credit card, you’ll receive Discoverist status on an ongoing basis (and five elite nights every year if you have the personal card), but you’ll still need to qualify for Explorist or Globalist status based on the full criteria.

Hyatt’s lifetime Globalist status is based on earning one million base points in the program. World of Hyatt members earn five base points per dollar spent on Hyatt stays, meaning you essentially have to spend $200,000 at Hyatts to earn lifetime Globalist status.

Credit card spending, and any elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards, won’t count toward lifetime Globalist status. That’s because the qualification criteria is based solely on base points, and not based on elite qualifying nights (in which case it would count).

World of Hyatt Globalist is my favorite top tier hotel status, and what I love is that Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards make it easier to earn that. Let’s look at the best strategy for earning Globalist status with the card. Hyatt Globalist status ordinarily requires earning 60 qualifying nights in a year. So how much would you have to spend on a Hyatt credit card to earn that status?

On the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you’d need to spend $140,000 to earn Globalist status:

Meanwhile on the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you’d need to spend $120,000 to earn Globalist status:

As you can see, the personal credit card offers more elite nights upfront, while the business credit card offers elite nights at a faster pace for spending (assuming you can reach the thresholds).

When you’re analyzing the value of spending your way toward status, don’t forget that even beyond the general status perks, the Milestone Rewards perks could really add up. For example, if you make it to 60 elite nights, you could select five suite upgrade awards and four club access awards, and would also receive a Category 1-7 free night award, a Category 1-4 free night award, and three Guest of Honor awards.

Then on the personal version of the card, you also receive an additional Category 1-4 free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a year. The value of all of those perks really adds up.

Hyatt counts award nights toward status, and just for having the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you get a free night every year, plus the opportunity to earn a further three free nights for spending $15,000, earning Explorist status, and earning Globalist status.

On top of that, presumably you want to earn Globalist status because you actually intend to stay at Hyatts with some frequency. Hotel status is worthless if you don’t actually stay at that brand.

To be realistic, let’s assume that long term you’re earning 30 elite nights per year through actual stays. There are so many great Globalist benefits to use (like suite upgrade awards and free night awards), so if you’re staying at Hyatts less than that I question whether Globalist is worth it for you.

If you earned 30 of the required 60 elite nights through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following:

Given all the incremental perks you’re picking up with Milestone Rewards, I’d say the math could really check out.

When deciding if it makes sense to spend money on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, consider the opportunity cost of the spending. For easy math purposes, I tend to consider the opportunity cost of credit card spending to be around 3.4%.

That’s because based on my valuation of miles & points, most transferable points currencies are worth 1.7 cents each, and you have some cards offering 2x points per dollar spent. Meanwhile I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

If we were to theoretically assume you’re spending $60,000 on a Hyatt credit card per year (give or take) in order to earn Globalist status, what’s the opportunity cost of that spending? By my math, you’re looking at an opportunity cost of up to 2% (the spread between a 3.4% return and 1.4% return). That’s around $1,200, if you value things the way that I do. But that’s not factoring in the value of all the other perks mentioned above:

For many, I think the above perks could more than justify the difference in return on spending otherwise.

There are many things to love about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, though the ability to get a fast track toward status is probably my favorite perk. I absolutely love Hyatt Globalist status, and credit cards have historically helped me requalify for status. If you’re a Hyatt loyalist and don’t yet have the hotel group’s co-branded credit cards, they’re seriously worth considering.

What has your experience been using World of Hyatt Credit Cards to earn elite status?

#6088. Tulum Is Losing Airlines Fast: Why The Hyped New Airport Is Failing

In late 2023, we saw the opening of the Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport (TQO), in Tulum, Mexico. For those not familiar, Tulum is located on the eastern coast of the Yucatan Peninsula, and for years, it was a growing tourist destination.

While it could previously be accessed via Cancun International Airport (CUN), the hope was that by opening a new international airport, visitor numbers would expand massively. Unfortunately what has actually happened is exactly the opposite, as airline after airline has pulled out. What exactly is going on here? I think it makes for an interesting story, and thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this.

In 2023, we saw airline after airline announce flights to Tulum. Among US carriers, we saw American, Delta, JetBlue, and United, all launch flights to Tulum, while Spirit announced flights, but never launched them.

That was only a small part of the overall international service to the airport, as we also saw flights to Tulum on Air Canada, Air Transat, Avianca, Copa, Discover, and WestJet, along with flights on domestic carriers like Aeromexico, Mexicana de Aviacion, Viva, and Volaris.

Less than three years after the airport opened, where do things stand? When it comes to international year-round service, we’ve now gone from service to 12 airports, to service to four airports, which is an absolutely massive reduction:

Just to put this into numbers, in the first half of 2026, the airport saw a 33.2% reduction in passengers. June 2026 was the worst month to date, with a 44.8% drop, as there were just 47,600 passengers, compared to 86,200 passengers the year prior.

It goes without saying that for a newly built airport, this is rather catastrophic, and not what you hope to see.

In some ways, it feels like the whole concept behind Tulum Airport was sort of unnecessary. That’s also easily explained by the fact that the airport was well over a decade in the making, so while I can see how it might’ve seemed like a good idea at some point, tourism trends do evolve over time.

The reality is that there was a point where Tulum was cool, edgy, and a bit off the beaten path, compared to… whatever it is now. But when it comes to the struggles that airlines have had with flying to Tulum, it seems like the problems have been endless:

It’ll be interesting to see if Tulum can reverse any of these trends, and regain visitors…

A few years ago Tulum Airport opened to some fanfare, as a good number of airlines rushed to add service there. Unfortunately the excitement didn’t last long, as the airport has gone from a dozen year-round international routes, to just four.

This reduction in demand particularly evident from the United States, as soon there will just be nonstop service on American and Delta, and even that will be with reduced frequencies and routes.

Tulum Airport is facing endless challenges, not the least of which is a decline in visitors to Mexico from the United States, combined with increasing competition for those fewer visitors. Mexico just isn’t a value destination in the way that it used to be in places like Cancun, Tulum, Los Cabos, etc., and that’s understandably impacting demand.

I’m curious if Tulum can find a way to turn things around, but it’s not a good situation.

What do you make of the Tulum Airport demand problem?

An airport lounge membership, hotel perks and a handful of statement credits used to be enough to set a premium travel rewards card apart. These days, that sounds like the starting point.

The faces competition from the (see rates and fees), Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card and (see rates and fees). All four offer transferable rewards and airport lounge access, along with benefits designed to offset their high annual fees.

Still, the Platinum makes a compelling case for a place in a frequent traveler's wallet. Its strengths include extensive lounge access, generous earnings on flights booked directly with airlines and hotel benefits that can make a stay considerably more comfortable.

At $895 a year (see rates and fees), it's also the most expensive of these four cards.

Here's where the Platinum stands out — and where another premium card might be a better fit.

Complimentary Priority Pass lounge access is a shared benefit across these cards (enrollment required). What makes the stand out is the additional lounges available through the American Express Global Lounge Collection.

The American Express Global Lounge Collection includes Centurion Lounges, eligible Delta Sky Clubs and other participating partner lounge networks.

The Centurion network has a larger footprint than either Capital One’s or Chase’s own branded lounge network. Citi doesn't operate its own network, although cardholders receive four Admirals Club passes per calendar year.

For me, the Centurion Lounges at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) and George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston are particularly useful when connecting to and from Austin. I enjoy the food at the lounges, but after an international flight, the opportunity to shower before my final flight of the day is what I appreciate most.

Delta Sky Club access is another reason to consider the Platinum. Cardmembers receive 10 visits per benefit year when flying on eligible itineraries. (Basic economy tickets don't qualify, and unlimited visits require $75,000 in eligible annual spending.)

There are other limits to consider. Centurion guest access costs extra unless you meet a spending requirement, and the biggest network won't necessarily be the most useful at your home airport.

Check the lounges along your regular routes before choosing a card based on access alone.

Related: My 5 top travel credit cards — and how they elevate my trips

The offers up to $600 in annual lodging statement credits, split into two allowances of up to $300: one from January through June and another from July through December.

Eligible purchases include prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection bookings through American Express Travel®, plus qualifying prepaid Airbnb Luxe stays booked through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel App™.

THC and eligible Airbnb Luxe bookings require stays of at least two nights. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, FHR bookings will also require a two-night stay to qualify for the lodging credit.

I tend to use my credit for THC stays because I often find lower prices than at FHR properties. For January, I've booked two nights at The Standard, Bangkok Mahanakhon for $362. After applying the $300 credit, the stay will cost me $62 out of pocket.

My stay includes daily breakfast for two and a $100 credit toward eligible on-property charges, which I plan to use at an on-site restaurant or for room service. I'll also be eligible for early check-in, late checkout and a room upgrade (subject to availability). Breakfast is an additional benefit at this particular property; it isn't standard across THC.

FHR offers a more consistent package, including daily breakfast for two and guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout. That last benefit can be especially useful before an evening flight.

Competing premium cards have their own hotel programs. The Platinum's appeal is the combination of its credit and booking benefits. Just make sure to compare the total price with other available rates before deciding how much you're saving.

Related: A comparison of luxury hotel programs from credit card issuers

The earns 5 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through Amex Travel (on up to $500,000 of airfare purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The ability to book directly is a meaningful advantage. You can earn generously while dealing with the airline directly if you need to change your reservation or something goes wrong.

The earns 4 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly. It earns a higher 8 points per dollar through Chase Travel℠, while the earns 6 points per dollar spent on flights through Citi Travel.

Here's an example of earnings on a $500 flight:

The Platinum also earns 5 points per dollar spent on eligible prepaid hotels through Amex Travel and prepaid Airbnb bookings through AmexTravel.com or the Amex Travel app. The Airbnb earning rate applies beyond the Luxe properties eligible for the lodging credit.

Those points offer plenty of redemption options.

Membership Rewards airline partners provide access to Oneworld, SkyTeam and Star Alliance flights through programs such as British Airways Club, Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Air Canada Aeroplan. Hotel partners include Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy.

All four cards have useful transfer partners, so consider which programs you actually use. A strong earning rate matters more when it earns points you know how to redeem.

Related: The best premium credit cards: A side-by-side comparison

Eligible applicants can find out their offer and see if they are eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Based on our valuations, the maximum 175,000-point offer is worth up to $3,500 — the highest value among the current publicly advertised offers on these four cards.

The high spending requirement deserves attention. Make sure you can meet it through purchases you already planned to make, and assess the card's ongoing value separately from its first-year bonus.

The 's long list of credits makes more sense when you focus on the ones that fit your existing spending.

Its up to $300 annual digital entertainment credit is one I particularly like. It provides up to $25 monthly toward eligible purchases with participating providers.† I use it for YouTube Premium and Disney+/Hulu; the monthly allowance is shared across eligible subscriptions.

Uber users have two benefits to consider. The card provides up to $200 in annual Uber Cash for eligible U.S. rides and orders (up to $15 monthly, plus an extra $20 in December; you must add the Platinum to your Uber account and use an Amex card to pay). A separate credit provides up to $120 annually toward an eligible auto-renewing Uber One membership.

The up to $400 annual Resy statement credit (available in quarterly allowances of up to $100) can also be straightforward to use if you already dine at qualifying U.S. restaurants.†

There’s also an up to $300 annual Equinox statement credit for eligible Equinox memberships or an Equinox+ digital subscription (subject to auto-renewal).† I use mine for the digital subscription.

These benefits can help cover the annual fee, but only assign them the value they have to you. Signing up for a service you won't use doesn't save money. Monthly expiration dates and U.S. restrictions also make some credits less useful for certain cardmembers.

Related: The gift card trick that helps me maximize my US restaurant credits while I'm abroad

cardmembers receive complimentary Hilton Honors Gold, Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite and Leaders Club Sterling status.† The benefits vary by program, but having status without meeting the usual stay or spending requirements is a useful starting point.

Perks with Avis, Hertz and National† can also improve the experience of renting a car.

The card provides up to $219 in statement credits per calendar year toward a Clear+ membership (subject to auto-renewal),† plus either a $120 Global Entry application fee credit or an up to $85 TSA PreCheck application fee credit (every four years) when you pay with your Platinum.

Clear+ handles identity verification at participating airport checkpoints, while TSA PreCheck provides expedited security screening. Global Entry expedites eligible arrivals into the U.S. and includes TSA PreCheck.

You can also select one qualifying airline to receive up to $200 in statement credits for eligible incidental fees† charged to your Platinum card each calendar year. (Note that it isn't a general airfare credit.)

Outside its limited bonus categories, the earns just 1 point per dollar spent. Dining and everyday purchases are usually better placed on another card.

The Venture X offers a simpler alternative: a $395 annual fee, at least 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases, a $300 annual Capital One Travel credit and 10,000 anniversary miles. There are fewer credits to track to make the annual fee worthwhile.

#6086. Delta CEO: “Customers Are Not Choosing Airlines Based On Wi-Fi”

I’ve gotta be honest, I don’t envy the situation that Delta CEO Ed Bastian is in. Unlike most other carriers in the United States, Delta hasn’t opted for SpaceX Starlink Wi-Fi, and has instead gone with Amazon Leo.

In theory that’s fine, except Amazon Leo is years behind Starlink, and just faced a new setback, due to a rocket failure. Elon Musk has also repeatedly publicly ridiculed Bastian, regarding what Bastian reportedly said about Musk to employees.

There’s now an interesting update, as Bastian made some comments about the carrier’s Wi-Fi choice, and overall customer preferences. It sure is amazing how narratives can change, based on what’s convenient…

This week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum 2026, Delta’s CEO was asked about the carrier’s decision not to choose Starlink, plus the public spat with Musk. Here’s what Bastian had to say about this:

“We’ve been the leader in Wi-Fi, and in free and fast Wi-Fi, and we’ve been at it for five years. I’ve got a long history with Elon on that. We’ve looked at Starlink, we actually helped them started in aviation, we gave them our planes to use during COVID, when we weren’t flying, and they tested the system out. We just couldn’t come to agreement on a business model.”

“We’ve been the leader in free, fast Wi-Fi. We are confident there will be more than one LEO product in the world other than Starlink, and I’m confident Amazon has the capability to do a great job. Customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi. We’ve been out with a great product from Viasat, which we’ve got two new satellites in the sky. It’s not Starlink caliber but it’s pretty darn close.”

“This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”At the #F500Innovation Forum, @Delta CEO Ed Bastian told @ajs that the airline helped Elon Musk’s satellite Wi-Fi “get started in aviation,” but the two sides “just couldn’t come to… pic.twitter.com/xmSERJNjjH

Look, before I get too deep into this, let me make several points that I think no one reasonable will disagree with (which is not to say some commenters won’t disagree!):

When Bastian formally unveiled plans for free Wi-Fi at CES 2023 in Las Vegas, he said the following:

“At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different. Our vision has long been to deliver an experience at 30,000 feet that feels similar to what our customers have available on the ground.”

“We didn’t just want free Wi-Fi to offer base-level service – we wanted it to be transformative for the entire onboard experience. It is imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home, and we’ve put this system through meticulous tests to make that possible.”

Earlier this year, when announcing plans to partner with Amazon Leo for connectivity, Bastian said that “we need to stay the leader” in inflight connectivity. Obviously that won’t be the case for a long time.

As I see it, Delta’s problem here is pretty simple. Customers absolutely notice a difference between Viasat and Starlink. The issue isn’t that people will stop flying Delta altogether. The issue is that Delta has built its entire brand on being the industry leader, and on being on the forefront of technology.

There’s no denying that this sentiment among the public changes over time, because inflight Wi-Fi is easily one of the top amenities that passengers notice nowadays. Seriously, I can’t count the number of people I’ve heard from or just overheard talking about their first Starlink experience, and how blown away they were.

I guess to look at it from another angle, there’s no airline that loves talking about how premium it is more than Delta. What makes Delta premium? If we’re going to believe that Delta is premium, it’s not based on any one single thing, but rather, it’s based on the sum of the experience. And I think anyone who thinks a major Wi-Fi disadvantage lasting for years isn’t part of what contributes to consumer sentiment is lying to themselves.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is now downplaying the importance of inflight Wi-Fi. He’s arguing that “customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi,” which in isolation, is probably true. But he’s also arguing that Viasat is “pretty darn close” to Starlink, which is most definitely not true, as I see it.

I wouldn’t be so critical of these statements if it weren’t for Bastian spending years hyping up how it’s “imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home,” while also saying “we need to stay the leader.” And for that matter, Delta has of course also long hyped how premium it is — if that’s to be believed, it’s not about any one feature, but instead, it’s about the sum of the experience.

What do you make of Bastian’s inflight connectivity comments?

#6085. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#6084. An Airline You’ve Never Heard Of Will Fly From Seoul Incheon To Los Angeles

A very small international airline plans to add long haul, international flights to the United States as of next spring, and I feel pretty confident in saying that 99% of people have never heard of this airline (I had to look it up after seeing one of their planes at an airport several weeks back, and I know a thing or two about identifying airplanes). 😉

As reported by AeroRoutes, as of May 1, 2027, Parata Air will launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Los Angeles (LAX). The flight will operate with the following schedule:

WE301 Incheon to Los Angeles departing 12:00PM arriving 7:20AMWE302 Los Angeles to Incheon departing 9:50AM arriving 3:20PM (+1 days)

Parata Air will operate the route with an Airbus A330-200, featuring 260 seats, including 18 business class seats and 242 economy seats. The 5,944-mile flight is blocked at 11hr40min eastbound and 13hr30min westbound.

Tickets on the flight are now on sale, and I see fares starting at around $670 one-way in economy, and around $2,500 one-way in business class. Those aren’t exactly terribly attractive fares for a newcomer that appears to have a pretty lackluster onboard product.

For those not familiar with Parata Air, the airline launched operations back in 2019, but it has a fleet of just a handful of planes, including three Airbus A330s and two Airbus A320s. This will be the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. As I hinted at in the headline, I imagine this is a fully unknown player to most people, and I had never heard of the airline until a few weeks ago.

Random thought — can anyone think of a smaller international airline (in terms of fleet size) that added long haul flights to the United States? I know that’s very specific, but I can’t think of another one… it’s possible I’m missing something, though!

The airline acquired its three A330s secondhand from different sources, with the planes having flown for Garuda Indonesia, Hainan Airlines, and Thomas Cook (though that plane doesn’t have business class).

The Seoul Incheon to Los Angeles market is pretty well served in terms of capacity, but not so well served in terms of competition. That’s because no US carrier flies between Los Angeles and Seoul Incheon, and with Korean Air having acquired Asiana, there’s now only one South Korean flag carrier.

If you look at the market, you’ll see that Korean Air operates up to four daily flights, and Air Premia operates up to two daily flights. Now we’ll see a third airline from the country operating in the market, though with the lowest capacity, and arguably the worst product.

It’ll be interesting to see when we see some competition here on the US side. Delta might operate the route eventually, but that doesn’t actually increase competition, since the airline has a joint venture with Korean Air. American has (smartly, probably) given up on Los Angeles as a long haul hub. So that leaves United, and I could definitely see the airline eventually adding service in the market, as a competitive response against Delta and Korean Air, if nothing else.

As of May 2027, Parata Air will be launching a new nonstop route between Seoul Incheon and Los Angeles, representing the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. The airline will be operating daily in the market with Airbus A330s. With this, there will be three South Korean carriers flying this route, though no airlines from the United States.

What do you make of this new Parata Air service?

#6083. Why Boeing Added New Engines To 1 Of Its 2 Longest-Running Aircraft In Production

Wikimedia Commons, Andreas Zeitler | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Inside Boeing's gigantic Washington plants, two of the longest-running jets in commercial aviation history are headed toward very different destinations. Workers in Renton installed huge 69-inch CFM LEAP-1B turbofans on the 737 MAX to bring the 1960s airframe up to 21st-century standards. However, thirty miles north in Everett, Boeing is winding down production of its twin-aisle 767 in 2027, despite being decades newer with its 1980s-era engineering.

Still, the doors have not shuttered yet, and thanks to a lifeline from Congress, the classic widebody is continuing to roll off the line with the same engines. Inside those historic walls, Boeing’s engineers constantly push the cutting edge of aerospace technology. Yet they applied that innovation unevenly between their two oldest active product lines, pouring $3 billion into modernizing the 737 while letting the veteran 767 face its looming sunset.

Boeing's decision to abandon the 767 results from both significant changes in the global cargo industry and commercial realities. The 737 MAX's extensive wing and engine redesigns were justified by thousands of airline orders, but the 767's niche cargo demand could never justify a similar overhaul, particularly since shippers are shifting their focus to the upcoming 777-8F freighter and the 777-200F passenger-to-freighter conversions are being slowed down by a severe shortage of used donor airframes.

Boeing scrapped plans for a brand-new single-aisle aircraft after Airbus received over 1,000 bookings for its A320neo and former exclusive customer American Airlines threatened to defect, as Leeham News wrote. Rather, the 737 airframe, whose fundamental cabin cross-section dates back to the 1954 Dash 80 prototype, was modified with CFM LEAP-1B turbofans at a cost of almost $3 billion. In order to preserve single-aisle market dominance, the 737 MAX upgrade served as a crucial stopgap. It quickly compensated for itself with hundreds of airline orders and allowed Boeing to develop a future clean-sheet replacement.

While building the next-generation 777-8F and awaiting the availability of used passenger 777 donor airframes for P2F conversions, Boeing continued to operate the twin-aisle 767-300F as a temporary freight bridge. Freighter sales were restricted to a few dozen aircraft a year since commercial airlines switched from ordering passenger 767s to the lightweight, composite 787 Dreamliner in 2014.

As global e-commerce and pandemic-era cargo demand increased, the 767-300F, powered by its reliable but thirsty 1980s-era General Electric CF6-80C2 or Pratt & Whitney PW4062 engines, performed adequately as a temporary stopgap. However, the International Civil Aviation Organization's carbon emission regulations, which go into effect on January 1, 2028, cannot be met by those older engines. After that cutoff, a temporary cargo stopgap would become a permanent commercial closure because the 767 could not lawfully comply with international routes without contemporary engines.

With the 737 MAX, massive narrowbody order volume turned an aging fuselage into a multi-decade cash engine that absorbed billions in engineering upgrades. With the 767-300F, low production rates meant Boeing treated the jet purely as a low-cost bridge to hold cargo customers until the 777-8F arrived and P2F conversion lines ramped up, willingly letting regulatory deadlines retire the commercial airframe rather than sinking new capital into a sunsetting program.

By enacting a rule that exempted freight jets weighing between 396,832 and 529,109 pounds from new carbon restrictions until 2033, Congress attempted to give Boeing a crutch. This effectively shielded the 412,000-pound 767-300F. However, Stephanie Pope and Kelly Ortberg, Boeing executives, declined to rely on a complete legislative rescue. Foreign authorities in Europe and Asia could prohibit the aircraft from landing because a US exemption has no power outside the US, keeping brand-new freighters behind American borders and damaging their resale value for international carriers like FedEx and UPS.

Instead of leaning on political life support, Boeing chose to shut down commercial 767 production in 2027 and absorb a $400 million charge. Unlike the 737 MAX, where massive passenger volume easily funded complex structural and engine upgrades, the low-volume 767 could never justify a multi-billion-dollar overhaul. Boeing recognized that stretching an outdated freighter through domestic loopholes made far less sense than focusing its engineering muscle on programs with real global demand.

Everett's widebody engineers are advancing the next-generation 777X family toward final FAA certification in early 2027, opening the door for the new 777-8F freighter, while the 737 MAX line continues to produce the high-volume revenue flow required to finance ongoing enhancements. Instead of producing geographically limited 767s, Boeing allowed the commercial line to shut down on time, keeping Everett's equipment focused on military KC-46 tankers while its new widebodies get ready to take over international cargo routes.

The demise of the sawtooth jet engines in the era of next-gen turbofans.

Putting new engines on the 737 was no simple bolt-on modification despite the appearance to a casual observer. The modern LEAP-1B engine featured a huge 69-inch fan, forcing engineers to stretch the 737’s nose landing gear by eight inches and mount the engines further forward and higher on its low-slung 1960s wing. Applying the same MAX upgrade formula to the 767 seemed promising on paper because both aircraft have similar profiles and basic construction, though the 767 has a larger fuselage.

Boeing’s engineering resources and factory tooling were already locked onto far bigger, future-ready platforms than the 767. Instead of pouring capital into a temporary bridge, Boeing preserved its engineering capacity for the next-generation 777-8F and more popular 777-200F, letting the 767 finish its final bridge run before handing its crucial air freight mission over to its successors.

The engineering compromises that brought a 1960s jet into the 21st Century.

Bolting a modern engine onto the 767 would require gutting the airplane’s internal structures and essentially changing every aspect. Its legacy aluminum wings were engineered to carry older engines weighing roughly 9,800 pounds each. Swapping in an advanced turbofan like the GEnx-1B would add over 3,700 pounds of extra dead weight per side. Supporting that heavy overhang would force Boeing to rebuild the wing’s internal ribs, spars, and titanium mounts, triggering a multi-billion-dollar safety certification that niche cargo sales could never pay back.

The technology gap inside the engines was just as wide. 21st-century jets squeeze every drop of energy from fuel by running at extreme pressures and blistering heat, using space-age ceramic parts and single-crystal metal blades that survive temperatures above 3,000 degrees. That intense efficiency lets new engines burn far less fuel and easily pass tough global pollution rules.

By contrast, the 767’s 1980s-era engines run at much lower pressures with traditional metal blades that cannot handle extreme heat. Those older thermal limits mean higher fuel burn and heavier exhaust that fail modern clean-air standards. Faced with rebuilding the entire wing just to carry heavier, hotter engines, Boeing accepted that upgrading the 767 was an engineering dead end.

Analyzing why Atlas Air broke its all Boeing streak for the first time.

Before the 2028 carbon cutoff, the commercial 767's demise was cemented by a market squeeze. After FedEx Express took delivery of its 152nd and final new 767-300F in May 2026, only 15 civilian orders remained on Boeing’s books, including seven for UPS and eight for an undisclosed buyer. Once those final commercial jets leave Everett before the 2027 deadline, the civil 767 will vanish permanently from Boeing’s lineup.

By carrying 116,000 pounds of cargo across 3,255 nautical miles without burning as much fuel as larger widebodies, the 767-300F maintained a profitable middle ground for decades. That mid-size niche is mostly gone now. While extra-large twinjets like the Airbus A350F, Boeing 777F, and forthcoming 777-8F exceed the 767 in every parameter on long-haul international routes, upgraded single-aisle freighters increasingly dominate short domestic e-commerce flights.

However, a military lifeline has ensured that the Everett assembly line itself continues to operate well into the 2030s. To fulfill significant orders for the KC-46A Pegasus aerial refueling tanker for the US Air Force and allies like Japan and Israel, Boeing will keep its 767 tooling operational because defense aircraft are exempt from commercial pollution regulations. This will close a legendary commercial chapter while solidifying its future as a military powerhouse.

That military transformation sets the stage for the next chapter of this 1980s airframe’s remarkable survival. Outfitted with fly-by-wire refueling booms, defensive armor, and advanced cockpit displays borrowed from the 787 Dreamliner, the KC-46A Pegasus is quietly evolving far beyond its commercial roots. While the civilian 767 fades into history, its combat-ready twin is taking on high-stakes global refueling missions that will keep Everett’s assembly line vital for decades to come.

#6081. Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex Review: Is The No Annual Fee Card Worth It?

American Express and Delta have had a close relationship for many years, and as part of that, they issue seven co-branded Delta Amex cards. This is my in-depth Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card review, as this is the entry-level personal Delta credit card with no annual fee (Rates & Fees), and probably the least talked about card in the lineup. It’s far from the most rewarding Delta credit card, but if you want to earn Delta miles and only fly the airline occasionally, it could be worth a look.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card

Before I get into the full Delta Blue Amex Card review, here’s an overview of the card’s main features, from its welcome bonus and earning rates, to other benefits:

Beyond that, here are my thoughts on the pros and cons of the Delta Blue Amex:

When applying for a credit card, the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and fees, are obviously major factors that people consider. With that in mind, let’s take a look at those details for the Delta Blue Amex Card. As you’d expect for this card, the lack of fees largely comes at expense of a smaller welcome offer.

The Blue Delta SkyMiles Amex has a welcome offer of 10,000 bonus SkyMiles after spending $1,000 within the first six months of your card membership. Based on my latest points & miles valuations, Delta SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each, making this bonus worth $110. We’ve seen this card’s bonus go a bit higher, but not by a huge amount.

The bonuses on all other Delta Amex cards are significantly higher, which isn’t a surprise, since cards with annual fees often have better bonuses than cards without annual fees. It’s hard to get excited about that offer, but I guess something is better than nothing?

The welcome offer on the Delta Blue Amex Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. The rules go beyond that, though.

You’re actually not eligible for the bonus on the card if you have or have had any of the more premium versions of the Delta Amex card portfolio, at least among the personal cards. This is true across the portfolio, and the idea is that you’re always eligible for the bonus on a more premium card, but not eligible for the bonus on a less premium card.

So if you do want to pick up multiple Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to first apply for the Delta Blue Amex, then the Delta Gold Amex, then the Delta Platinum Amex, and then the Delta Reserve Amex (or at least you’ll want to move in that general order).

Beyond that, Amex’s general card application restrictions apply, including that you can typically have at most five credit cards from Amex at a time (that doesn’t include hybrid cards).

Let me emphasize once again that the Blue Delta Amex has no annual fee. It’s great to see a trend whereby we’re seeing more airline credit cards with no annual fees, since it’s a nice option for someone who wants a co-branded credit card, but doesn’t want to pay an annual fee.

You can also add additional users to the card at no extra cost.

There’s no doubt that card issuers are moving toward offering more no annual fee cards with no foreign transaction fees, though it’s still not the standard. The Blue Delta Amex has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), which is awesome, since most Amex no annual fee cards do still have these fees.

When it comes to earning rewards, the Blue Delta SkyMiles Credit Card offers:

For a no annual fee product, it’s nice to see a card offering a bonus on dining. While some bonus categories are better than none, I don’t find the bonuses to be particularly compelling, as there are still better cards out there for airfare purchases and restaurant purchases.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or on Delta’s SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

The Delta Blue Amex is a decent no annual fee card in the sense that it offers 2x miles at restaurants and has no foreign transaction fees, but how are the perks on the card? Not surprisingly, this is an area where the card lags, and where the cards with annual fees offer significantly more value.

Nonetheless, there are some perks to the card that may prove valuable to the occasional Delta flyer.

If you have the Blue Delta Amex, then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food or alcoholic beverages, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

Having the Blue Delta Amex makes you eligible for the Delta Pay With Miles program. What is that? This allows those with co-branded Delta Amex cards to redeem miles for one cent each towards a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles towards flights, and then they still earn elite miles for taking those flights.

In other words, the 10,000 miles available as part of the welcome offer can be redeemed for a minimum of $100 worth of travel on Delta. This is obviously the lowest cost option for unlocking that benefit.

The Delta Blue Amex includes access to dedicated entrance lanes and fast lanes at stadiums and arenas that participate in the Amex Venue Collection program. As part of this benefit, you can also get 10% back on qualifying concessions purchases, up to $250 back per calendar year. (Enrollment required)

Amex Offers is a program that offers discounts for purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

The ideal situation is to have a no annual fee card (like this one), so you can get access to these offers without paying an annual fee to get access to this.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page.

The Delta Blue Amex comes with some basic travel and purchase protection benefits:

There are some coverage limits and exclusions to be aware of, so you’ll want to review the full details in the card’s benefits guide before assuming you’re insured.

Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

Many people who like Delta as a brand may be tempted to pick up the Delta Blue Amex — it allows you to earn miles with Delta, it has no annual fee, and it offers some perks that could add value (20% off inflight purchases, Amex Offers, access to Delta Pay With Miles, etc.).

However, in general, I wouldn’t recommend outright applying for this card:

Let me address both of those points below.

If you’re considering the Delta SkyMiles Blue Amex, let me make the case for applying for the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (learn more) instead, which currently has the limited-time offer:

You can always get the Gold Delta Amex, and then if you don’t find it to be worth the annual fee, you can downgrade it to the Blue Delta Amex after a year. That would allow you to maintain the card account, and you wouldn’t pay the annual fee when you downgrade (and you’d still get the elevated perks and bigger bonus for the first year).

At a minimum, it really is worth trying the Delta Gold Amex to see if you like it and to take advantage of the better bonus, and then you can downgrade at a later point if you find it’s not worthwhile.

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. That’s because these points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year and then 1x), and 3x points on flights booked directly with airlines or at AmexTravel.com. That’s a much better return than you’ll get on this card, and it’s also quite easy to make the math on the card work.

If you’re absolutely committed to having a no annual fee card and want to maximize your return on spending, there are lots of excellent no annual fee cards to consider.

My favorite is the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card earns 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase (in the form of ThankYou points).

But it gets even better than that — rewards earned on this card can be converted into ThankYou points at a 1:1 ratio and can be moved to partner programs at the best possible ratio, assuming you have the card in conjunction with one earning premium ThankYou points, like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more).

That means the card earns two ThankYou points per dollar, and I value those points at 1.7 cents each, so that’s like a 3.4% return on everyday spending.

I appreciate that American Express and Delta offer a no annual fee option with the Delta Blue Amex. For someone absolutely committed to getting a Delta Amex Card and not paying an annual fee, this is the best/only option.

The card has no foreign transaction fees, offers 2x miles on dining, and gives you access to Pay With Miles and 20% discounts on inflight purchases.

However, for most people, I think it’s worth applying for the Delta Gold Amex. The card has a lot more perks and a much better bonus, and you can always downgrade the card to the Delta Blue Amex after at least a year.

There are six United credit cards, ranging from a no-annual-fee card to premium personal and business cards with United Club access. Fortunately, figuring out which ones you're eligible for is straightforward.

Holding one United card generally doesn't prevent you from opening another or earning its welcome bonus. Instead, welcome-offer restrictions are largely card-specific: You can’t apply for a card you already hold or earn its welcome bonus if you've received a bonus on that same card in the last 24 months.

Apply here for a limited-time offer on the — Earn up to 80,000 bonus miles: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening (see rates and fees).

All six United cards are currently offering elevated welcome bonuses.

The information for the United Club Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

As of November 2026, TPG valuations place United miles at 1.2 cents each, making these offers worth between $600 and $1,200, excluding the value of any PQPs.

For United cards, applicants need to clear three main hurdles:

Meeting these requirements doesn't guarantee approval, only that you are free to apply and are eligible for the welcome offer if approved.

Chase allows you to apply for multiple United cards, as long as they are separate cards.

For example, if you already hold an , you can also apply for a . However, you can't hold two of the same card, so if you have a Quest card, you can't get a second in order to double up on its benefits.

The Gateway, Explorer, Quest and Club offer different benefits, so holding more than one could make sense depending on your travel habits. Having two or more cards means you also have access to different bonus categories when earning miles and potentially multiple PQP deposits for being a cardholder, depending on which cards you have.

There's one exception: If you are an existing United Club Visa Signature cardmember (no longer available to new applicants), you are not eligible for the current United Club card.

You'll need to close the old card and apply for a new Club card 24 months after you received the initial bonus. Or, you can call the number on the back of your card to product change to the current Club card, which preserves your account history and 5/24 status but won't earn an introductory offer.

The information for the United Club Visa Signature Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: Which United credit card is right for you?

The  and United Club Business Card have similar product-specific restrictions.

You won't qualify if you currently hold the business card you're applying for or received its new-cardmember bonus within the past 24 months.

You don't need an LLC or a company with employees to apply. You may qualify with a legitimate sole proprietorship or side hustle, such as freelance work, consulting, pet sitting or reselling.

Chase generally requires business card applicants to be under 5/24. However, once you're approved, a Chase business card typically won't appear on your personal credit report or add another account to your 5/24 total.

Related: United Business Card vs. United Club Business Card: Which should you get?

Yes, you can have multiple United credit cards at one time. Unlike some other airline credit cards, United's cards don't have a broad restriction that prevents you from holding multiple cobranded cards.

You could hold a for its TravelBank Cash and 10,000-mile award discount, the for lounge access and a for business expenses.

There's also an incentive to pair a personal and business United card: Both United business cards offer 5,000 bonus miles each account anniversary if you're also the primary cardmember on a personal United card.

Holding multiple United cards won't make sense for infrequent flyers, since benefits like free checked bags and priority boarding overlap on multiple cards. However, for loyal customers, the collection of slightly different perks and cardholder PQP bonuses could justify the cost of paying multiple annual fees.

Yes, you can get the same United credit card more than once. However, you will only earn another welcome offer if you no longer hold that card and at least 24 months have passed since you received the new-cardmember bonus.

Remember, Chase counts from the date you receive the bonus, not from when you open or close the account.

If you are an authorized user on someone else's United card, Chase does not consider that being a current cardholder for the purposes of that card's bonus restrictions. In other words, you can still apply for your own version of that card and earn its welcome bonus.

However, an authorized-user account may appear on your credit report and increase your 5/24 count.

If you're denied because of an authorized-user account, you may be able to explain the situation to Chase by calling the reconsideration line, although approval isn't guaranteed.

If you're interested in both a personal and business United card, applying for the business card first often makes sense. That's because the business card won't add to your 5/24 limit and tip you over the edge.

However, if you're applying for multiple personal United cards, the order you apply shouldn't matter. Pick whichever card is your highest priority first, considering its benefits and how its current offer compares with past bonuses.

The best choice depends on how often you fly United and which benefits you'll actually use.

The is often a good starting point, since it offers strong benefits like a free checked bag and single-use lounge passes, and it has no annual fee in the first year. The offers TravelBank Cash and an annual award discount for more serious United loyalists, and the is best suited to frequent flyers who value ongoing lounge access.

United's eligibility rules are friendly to new applicants.

For the Gateway, Explorer, Quest, United Business and United Club Business cards, you're in a strong position if you don't currently hold the exact card and haven't received its welcome bonus within the past 24 months, while the United Club card has a minor caveat that won't impact most applicants.

For travelers looking to add to their United MileagePlus balance or take advantage of additional cardholder benefits, this can be an easy way to enhance your United experience.

#6079. Surprise: Aer Lingus Unveils First-Ever Premium Economy, Coming To 10 A330s

Aer Lingus is getting on the premium economy hype. The Irish flag carrier has today announced it will introduce the cabin for the first time on 10 of its Airbus A330s, which will also feature new business and economy cabins (the product won’t be coming to the Airbus A321LR/XLR fleet).

This is quite a big change, and one that should give it a leg up in the highly competitive trans-Atlantic market.

The cabin will feature just four rows with 28 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. That’s about average when compared to other premium economy cabins. The narrow fuselage of the A330 means there’s only room for three seats in the middle section, rather than the four many other airlines offer.

As for the soft product, Aer Lingus promises three-course dining, drinks throughout the flight, a pillow and blanket, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing (not noise-canceling) headphones.

I actually really like the design and color scheme. It’s modern, looks elegant and premium, and most importantly of all for the airline of the Emerald Isle, the colors are quintessentially Irish.

Aer Lingus says premium economy fares will start from 700 Euros one-way, putting a return trip at around 1,400 Euros. That works out to around $1,534, and a few hundred dollars cheaper than United’s nonstop fares from Newark (EWR) to Dublin (DUB).

We’ll have to wait until October 1 next year to try Aer Lingus’ new premium economy out for ourselves. The airline hasn’t yet announced which routes will get the product first, but we should find out in the coming months.

The good news is, they’ll operate on many of the airline’s 18 nonstop routes from Dublin to the United States.

As a small, almost boutique-style airline with just 63 aircraft, Aer Lingus must remain competitive, especially in the saturated transatlantic market in which it predominantly operates. The addition of premium economy bridges the large gap between economy and business, and should open the airline up to a potential new customer base who’ve never flown it before.

I’ll be attending an event in Dublin tonight, so I should be back with more images and extra info soon!

What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new premium economy?

#6078. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And the progressive also interned for former California state Rep. Rudy Salas, who made unsuccessful bids to unseat Valadao in 2022 and 2024.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

Jackie Wang and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

A previous version of this report misstated when Rudy Salas ran for office.
