#6063. Dear Tunisair: How About A Refund For My Downgrade, Please?

I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short. The airline industry is incredibly complex and low margin, and sometimes consumers have unrealistically high expectations, while not acknowledging the real cost and challenges of running an airline. Buying a ticket on a flight is more like buying a ticket on Amtrak than buying a night at a Four Seasons, and you should adjust expectations accordingly.

At the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft. Readers often share these stories with me, and I write about them when I can. Now I’d like to share my own story…

Several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS). A few days before the flight I received an email from Tunisair informing me that I had been downgraded. As it turns out, it was because my flight was swapped to a wet leased plane, in an all-economy layout.

The email informed me of this change without actually acknowledging it was a downgrade. Instead, the email was in French, and it translated to “we are writing to inform you that your flight reservation has undergone changes.” And the only reference to the downgrade was that the fare class only showed as being “Y,” which obviously isn’t business class.

There was zero other proactive communication from the airline about the incident, and I flew the flight in economy. The airline of course acted as if nothing happened, and there was no mention of how to request downgrade compensation, or anything like that.

After the flight, I submitted a request with customer service, asking for a refund for the fare difference. Making that request was a challenge in and of itself, because the customer service form is in French, and is not at all intuitive.

But anyway, it has been weeks, and I haven’t heard back. I’m a bit conflicted here. I try not to abuse credit card disputes, but you typically only have 60 days to file a dispute. So am I at the point where I should just file a dispute, or how would one handle that?

As I said above, I try to be pretty understanding of airlines, and recognize how many different scenarios there are. Just in terms of doing business ethically, I do feel like there should be a proactive refund offer if the airline is informing you in advance that you won’t be getting the product that you paid for. I mean, if you can inform me that I’ve been downgraded, you can also process some sort of a refund.

We’ve become desensitized to this kind of service level with airlines, but I’m trying to come up with a comparison. I guess it would be like buying premium tickets to a sporting event, being informed in advance that you’ll be given worse seats, and then customer service just not responding to you for weeks on end.

If you managed to take my money, surely you can also manage to give it back if you can’t give me the thing I paid for, no?

Tunisair informed me days before a flight that I had been downgraded (as it turns out, due to an aircraft swap), though there was no offer a refund for a fare difference, or anything. Weeks ago I sent an email to customer service asking for a refund for the fare difference, but I haven’t heard back.

It just strikes me as really unethical to take someone’s money for an experience you’re not going to offer, and then not have a way to get a refund in a reasonable timeframe. I know airlines hate when people file credit card disputes, but when you’re approaching the 60-day mark with no response, what is one supposed to do?

Am I the only one who thinks it’s ridiculous to proactively downgrade a customer, but then make getting a refund such a runaround?

#6062. Park Hyatt Brisbane Opening 2031, As Brand’s Fourth Australia Hotel

Hyatt will bring its luxury Park Hyatt brand to Brisbane, Australia. More Park Hyatt locations are always a good thing, but… well, let’s cover the details first.

Hyatt has announced plans for the Park Hyatt Brisbane, marking the brand’s debut in Queensland. The hotel is expected to open in 2031, and will be located on the shores of the Brisbane River, at the western edge of the city’s central business district.

The hotel will occupy the top floors of one of the two towers of the 309 North Quay, a mixed-use development also containing luxury homes and retail outlets. For what it’s worth, the two buildings will have 51 floors and 56 floors. The hotel will have 201 guest rooms and suites, offering views of the river and skyline, along with 50 serviced apartments, for extended residence.

There are no additional details about the property yet. I do appreciate that the hotel will at least be at the top of a building, as that should make for some very nice views (I hate when hotels are part of tall buildings, but then take up the bottom floors, as that’s becoming increasingly common).

While a 2031 opening is expected, I would definitely not count on that timeline sticking. Ground hasn’t even broken on this development, and these kinds of mixed-use developments tend to struggle with sticking to their planned timeline.

Here’s how Tamara Lohan, Hyatt’s Global Brand Leader for Luxury, describes this:

“The Park Hyatt calling cards have always been iconic design and extraordinary addresses. Brisbane has the confidence and growing global pull to make it a natural home for the brand. When it opens, Park Hyatt Brisbane will become the fifth Park Hyatt hotel in the Pacific, joining hotels in Sydney, Melbourne, Canberra and Auckland, and a deliberate next step in growing the brand in the right places.”

There are no renderings of the property yet, beyond the below one of the overall 309 North Quay development.

This will be the fourth Park Hyatt property in Australia, and the fifth in the South Pacific, complementing the properties in Auckland, Canberra, Melbourne, and Sydney. I don’t have the slightest clue what’s going on with the Canberra property, as my understanding is that it’s not up to Park Hyatt standards, so it’s marketed as “Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel.” So it is a Park Hyatt, or is it not a Park Hyatt?

World of Hyatt is my favorite major hotel loyalty program (though the lead is narrowing as of late), and Park Hyatt is probably my favorite Hyatt brand. 15 years ago, the brand got me really excited, because it had some really spectacular properties. But it just feels like the brand is sort of losing steam, especially when you compare the difference in trajectory between Park Hyatt and Waldorf Astoria. My frustration with Park Hyatt comes down to two things.

First, the brand just seemingly can’t pick up many “flagship” properties, or at least can’t maintain them. Look at the world’s biggest business markets and most iconic cities — we’re talking Hong Kong, London, New York, Paris, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, etc. There are no Park Hyatts in places like Hong Kong or Singapore, and the ones that have historically been pretty iconic just fall short of actually being the top properties in their cities:

The area where Park Hyatt has been doing well in recent times is in secondary cities, at least in comparison to the above. And this isn’t meant to be shade — I’d much rather hang out in Auckland or Kuala Lumpur than in London or New York (take your pitchforks elsewhere!), but there’s no denying that any true luxury hotel brand wants to have world class properties in those primary cities.

I just feel like as of late, Waldorf Astoria’s trajectory has been way more impressive than Park Hyatt’s, and I’m not sure what exactly is driving that. I feel like owners just aren’t as into developing Park Hyatts as they used to be. Is there a single Park Hyatt in the pipeline where I think “oh, this is going to be a best-in-class property in a major market?” I can’t think of any…

The Park Hyatt brand is coming to Brisbane, Australia, with a hotel expected to open in 2031. The 201-key property will be located on the top floors of a mixed-use development, which will also contain apartments and retail.

It’s cool to see more Park Hyatts in the pipeline, and I don’t want to knock the brand for expanding to more markets. I’m just disappointed that the Park Hyatt brand can’t pick up any steam in the biggest cities, in terms of delivering an actually competitive experience.

What do you make of plans for the Park Hyatt Brisbane?

#6061. Hyatt And Delta Launch Extra Points On Flights And Hotel Stays—But Standard Coach Tickets Don’t Qualify

Hyatt and Delta have launched extra points on flights and hotel stays, with airline status, lounge passes and hotel free night awards coming next year. But there’s a big restriction: even a Hyatt Globalist buying a regular Delta coach ticket earns no Hyatt points. That’s not ‘basic economy doesn’t count’ – it’s listerally standard main cabin coach that earns nothing. The companies announced their partnership in September. Now we know how the benefits actually work. This brings back some of what Hyatt members lost when American Airlines stopped reciprocal points earning at the end of 2024. But Delta excludes regular coach, gives Hyatt’s lowest elite tier half as many points, and pays hotel guests in a less valuable airline currency (SkyMiles). Who Earns Extra Points And Miles Start by linking your World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles accounts. Ongoing extra earning depends on your status: Your Status   Additional Earnings Delta Silver, Gold, Platinum or Diamond Medallion   1 SkyMile per eligible dollar spent with Hyatt, on top of Hyatt points Hyatt Discoverist   1 Hyatt point per $2 of eligible Delta premium cabin spending, on top of SkyMiles Hyatt Explorist, Globalist or Lifetime Globalist   1 Hyatt point per eligible dollar of Delta premium cabin spending, on top of SkyMiles Hyatt status qualifies you for Hyatt points on eligible Delta flights. Delta status qualifies you for SkyMiles on eligible Hyatt spending. For flights, Delta Comfort, Premium Select, First Class and Delta One qualify. Basic, Classic and Extra fare versions qualify when they’re sold in one of those cabins. So basic extra legroom coach qualifies, full fair regular coach doesn’t. . The flight earning rules also require: A Delta marketed and operated flight, with a Delta-issued ticket beginning 006. Your SkyMiles number attached before departure and Hyatt elite status when the flight is completed. A qualifying paid ticket. Eligible spending includes the base fare and airline imposed surcharges, but excludes government taxes, airport fees and amounts paid with miles. These are Hyatt bonus points. They don’t count as base points toward Hyatt status or lifetime Globalist. For hotel spending, eligible room charges, incidentals and qualifying purchases without an overnight stay can earn SkyMiles. Mr & Mrs Smith and The Venetian qualify when booked through Hyatt. Homes & Hideaways and FIND experiences are excluded. Hyatt Nights Can Earn Delta Credits, Lounge Visits And Status Beginning January 1, 2027, linked Hyatt members will have Delta options among their Milestone Rewards. These are choices, so you’ll need to compare them with the other rewards available at the same threshold. The specific awards are: Hyatt Qualification   Delta Reward Choice 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 base points   $25 Delta eCertificate 40 qualifying nights or 65,000 base points   $75 Delta eCertificate 60 qualifying nights or 100,000 base points   $100 Delta eCertificate 70, 80 or 90 qualifying nights   Two single visit Delta Sky Club passes 100 qualifying nights   Delta Gold Medallion status 150 qualifying nights   Delta Platinum Medallion status, without Choice Benefits The flight certificates and lounge passes expire one year after issuance. Each lounge pass covers one person for one visit with a qualifying same-day boarding pass (basic economy passengers excluded). The status awards are for your own account. They don’t provide anything extra if you already hold that tier or higher, and selecting the same status again doesn’t extend it. Platinum at 150 nights is potentially attractive, albeith without the Choice Benefits that normally come with that status (e.g. four Regional Upgrade Certificates). Delta Elites Can Choose Hyatt Free Nights Starting February 1, 2027, for the 2028 Medallion Year, Delta is adding: A Hyatt Category 1–4 free night as a Platinum Choice Benefit. A Hyatt Category 1–7 free night as a Diamond Choice Benefit. These aren’t extra certificates automatically handed to every Platinum and Diamond. You select one instead of another Choice Benefit. No new option to redeem SkyMiles directly for Hyatt free night certificates was announced, like we’d seen with the American partnership. Perhaps the biggest loss is Hyatt redemptions for American Airlines status for a day. Launch Bonuses Don’t Require Elite Status All linked members can participate in the launch offers: November 17–December 31, 2026: Register separately and complete a qualifying Hyatt stay to earn one additional qualifying night credit. That’s one bonus night total, not double nights for the entire stay. January 4–February 15, 2027: Complete your first eligible paid Delta Comfort-or-higher flight to earn 1,000 bonus Hyatt points. January 4–February 15, 2027: Complete your first qualifying Hyatt stay to earn 1,000 bonus SkyMiles. Paid and award stays qualify for the hotel promotions. Mr & Mrs Smith and The Venetian bookings through Hyatt qualify, while Homes & Hideaways doesn’t. The year-end stay must finish after registration and by December 31. For the January hotel offer, checkout must be by February 15. There’s also an Alila Mayakoba trip sweepstakes through November 23. Hyatt says reciprocal status challenges are coming. Is This Better Than Hyatt’s American Airlines Partnership? There are two different American partnerships to compare against. The original version, which ran through 2024, was better for everyday earning. Hyatt Discoverists earned the same one point per dollar on American airfare as Globalists, and regular coach counted. American elites earned a mile per eligible Hyatt dollar, and those miles also counted as Loyalty Points once that status system was introduced. Delta’s hotel earning has the same nominal mileage rate, but American miles are worth more. And there’s no status credit from those points. American’s final double earning terms also covered eligible FIND and Homes & Hideaways spending, both excluded here. On the flight side you’re earning Hyatt points either way, so the problem isn’t SkyMiles valuation. It’s the cabins that don’t qualify and the halved Discoverist rate. The 2025 American redesign removed double dipping and largely made members pay for partner benefits with their own points or by giving up another reward. Delta restores some actual additional earnings. The milestone comparison is mixed: Flight credits can be more useful than seat coupons. American offered two Preferred Seat coupons at 20 and 30 nights, then two Main Cabin Extra coupons at 40 and 50. Delta status starts later. American Gold was a choice at 70, 80 and 90 Hyatt nights. Delta offers lounge passes there, with its first announced status award at 100 nights. At 150 nights, Delta offers a higher tier. American’s offer topped out at Platinum. Delta Platinum is its third tier, although withholding Choice Benefits takes away a valuable part of the package. American also gave ConciergeKey members Hyatt Globalist and offered Hyatt status choices to other AAdvantage members. We’ll see what reciprocal status offers look like. It’s worth linking accounts and registering for the extra Hyatt night if there’s a stay coming up. #6060. New offers on Atmos Rewards credit cards: Earn up to 90,000 points, companion fares and more

Learn how to get started earning and redeeming rewards so you can make the most of your everyday spending.

Augusta Stone is a credit cards writer for TPG. She joined the TPG team in 2023 and is excited to take points and miles beginners with her on a journey toward maximizing rewards.

The Points Guy believes that credit cards can transform lives, helping you leverage everyday spending for cash back or travel experiences that might otherwise be out of reach. We publish editorial content and card reviews to help you find a great card to turn your goals into reality.

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

BEST FOR GROCERIES AND U.S. STREAMING CASH BACK

Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express

As High As $300 Cash Back. Find Out Your Offer.

Atmos Rewards is the loyalty program for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines, allowing members to earn and redeem points across both carriers. Atmos Rewards points can be used for flights on Alaska and Hawaiian, as well as a range of partner airlines, making it easier to turn everyday spending and travel into award trips around the world.

The program offers three cobranded credit cards: one business and two personal cards.

With strong welcome offers currently available on all three cards, now is a good time to consider applying if you regularly fly Alaska or Hawaiian.

Let's dig deeper into the bonuses available right now and whether they're worth applying for.

The features a valuable welcome bonus, useful earning rates and a solid suite of benefits.

Welcome offer: Earn 80,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,680 when you include the value of the 25,000-point Global Companion Award. While not the absolute top offer we've seen in the card's history, the current lower minimum spend requirement can still make it a great time to apply.

Why we like it: This welcome offer includes a Global Companion Award, which knocks up to 25,000 points off a companion’s award ticket when you book two award seats on Alaska, Hawaiian or a partner airline (including Oneworld members)in any class. The card also offers an ongoing 25,000-point Global Companion Award after each card anniversary.

Cardholders can also earn a 100,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $60,000 or more in a card anniversary year.

For frequent international travelers, earning 3 points per dollar spent on foreign transaction purchases is a major advantage and can help quickly accrue Atmos Rewards points. Matt Moffitt, TPG's contributing editor for credit cards, is based in Spain and uses this card for most of his everyday spending there since those purchases are charged in euros.

Welcome offer: Earn 70,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after spending $2,500 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening.

TPG's valuations place this offer at $1,120, plus the value of the Companion Fare. Like the Summit, this is a strong offer compared to the card's history considering its relatively easy spending requirements, but not the highest we've ever seen.

Why we like it: The Ascent offers a lower-cost way to earn Atmos Rewards points while receiving practical airline benefits. For travelers who fly Alaska or Hawaiian a few times each year, the free checked-bag benefit and preferred boarding could help justify the $95 annual fee.

The welcome offer also includes a Companion Fare, which can provide additional value for travelers who regularly fly with someone else.

Welcome offer: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening.

The points in this bonus are worth $1,440, per TPG's valuations. Unlike the personal cards, this represents the highest points offer we've ever seen on the card.

Annual fee: $195 per company (with free employee cards)

The refreshed card no longer includes the annual $99 Companion Fare or the $100 Alaska Lounge+ membership discount. Existing cardholders will retain their current benefits and won't automatically transition to the new version.

Why we like it: The 10-point earning rate is a standout benefit for businesses that frequently fly Alaska or Hawaiian Airlines, representing a 16% return on eligible flights booked through Atmos for Business based on TPG's November 2026 valuations.

Free employee cards extend perks like checked bags and preferred boarding to more travelers, while four annual lounge passes and waived same-day change fees add value for the primary cardholder. Together, these benefits make the card particularly appealing to businesses that frequently fly Alaska or Hawaiian.

#6059. Fun & Creative Airline Callsigns, From Shamrock To Starwalker

Here’s a fun topic for aviation geeks (so if you’re not one, feel free to skip this post)…

When pilots and air traffic controllers communicate, they have a callsign that they use to be identified.

In general aviation, that callsign is just the aircraft’s registration code, so it’s always the same for a particular aircraft. For example, if the plane has the registration code N111PG, it would be spoken as “November One One One Papa Golf.”

Meanwhile for commercial aircraft, the callsign consists of a company identifier plus the flight number. In some cases that company identifier is simply the company’s name, while in other cases, a different callsign is used. For example, for American, Delta, and United, the company identifier is simply the airline name, so American flight 100 would be spoken as “American 100.”

In some situations, airlines choose callsigns that are different from the company name, and this can be for a variety of reasons. Callsigns need to be approved by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), with some important considerations:

While most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, there are also some airlines that don’t, and there are some names that I find to be particularly fun. In this post, I’d like to share my favorite airline callsigns, with a little backstory on how they were chosen (as I understand it). In no particular order…

Aer Lingus’ callsign is “Shamrock,” and that’s because the shamrock is the national symbol of Ireland. It’s a key part of the airline’s corporate identity, down to the shamrock being featured on the tails of Aer Lingus planes.

British Airways’ callsign is “Speedbird,” and I’d argue it’s perhaps the most iconic callsign out there. The origin of this dates back to British Airways’ predecessor, Imperial Airways, which used the stylized bird logo. British Airways has been using the callsign since it was founded in 1974 (as a combination of predecessors).

While this is of course a creative callsign, it has a practical use as well. “British Airways” would’ve been too long of a callsign, and “British” would’ve likely been too generic. For example, British Midland (which ended up being merged into British Airways) used “Midland” as its callsign, to avoid confusion.

Republic Airways’ callsign is “Brickyard,” and it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The callsign is a tribute to the company’s headquarters in Indianapolis, also home to the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. The course was initially paved with three million bricks, and nicknamed “The Brickyard.”

For those not familiar, Republic operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is among the most common callsigns you’ll hear on air traffic control frequencies in the US.

PSA Airlines’ callsign is “Blue Streak,” and after Republic, it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The story behind this callsign is definitely a blast from the past. In the 1980s, PSA’s predecessor was Jetstream International Airlines, and it operated commuter flights as a Piedmont Commuter feeder carrier.

The carrier’s planes had a white fuselage with a prominent blue stripe along it, intended to match Piedmont Airlines’ livery, and that’s where it all started.

For those not familiar, PSA operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is also a very common callsign that you’ll hear. Given the lack of blue stripes nowadays, the callsign does tend to cause some confusion!

China Airlines’ callsign is “Dynasty.” It’s my understanding that the Taiwan-based carrier had to choose a non-obvious callsign both to avoid confusion (given the number of airlines with “China” in their name), and also with the intent of differentiating it from mainland China.

So, where did the dynasty term come from? China Airlines uses this branding pretty widely, with its frequent flyer program even being named Dynasty Flyer, and it’s intended to reflect the history of Taiwan.

Starlux Airlines’ callsign is “Starwalker.” The reason is because the “Starlux” callsign was already taken by Comlux Aruba, a tiny charter airline, before the Taiwanese airline was founded. Now, don’t ask me why Comlux Aruba has “Starlux” as its callsign, though!

The reason Starlux ended up with “Starwalker” is presumably because the company’s founder is a huge Star Wars fan, which is why many things about the airline have space branding. He’s also of course a huge aviation geek, and operates flights as a captain!

South African Airways’ callsign is “Springbok.” The reason is because “South African” would be too long of a callsign, so they selected the springbok, which is the national animal of South Africa. The carrier has also used this in its branding over the years. For example, back in the 1950s, the airline used “Springbok Service” to describe its long haul, flagship flights.

Atlas Air’s callsign is “Giant.” Huh, say what? For those not familiar, Atlas Air is a cargo and charter airline, and while it doesn’t operate regularly scheduled commercial flights, it is a big operation.

The callsign is presumably a reflection of the company’s name coming from Greek mythology, where “Atlas” was a titan of great strength, so that may also explain the “giant” callsign. Now, it’s worth mentioning that Atlas also flies some pretty “giant” planes, as the world’s largest Boeing 747 operator, but I don’t think that’s the primary motivation.

Kalitta Air’s callsign is “Connie.” For those not familiar, Kalitta Air is a cargo airline with a few dozen planes (most of which are Boeing 747s!). The callsign is named after the company’s founder, Conrad “Connie” Kalitta, who started the airline back in 1967, as Connie Kalitta Services.

European Air Transport’s callsign is “Postman.” For context, this is one of DHL’s European subsidiaries operating cargo flights, so it’s a pretty fitting callsign, eh?

Airlines have callsigns that they use to communicate with air traffic control. While most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, that’s not always the case. In some situations a different name has to be chosen for practical reasons, while in some cases airlines want to get creative. I love when airlines have some fun with this, so I figured it was worth a post.

Some of my favourites during my time as a controller in the UK in the late 90s/early 2000s: "Jambo" - Alliance Air (South Africa) "Zebra" - African Safari (Kenya) "Shuttle" - Certain BA Domestic routes (UK) "Jetset" - Air2000 (UK) "Elite" - Canada3000 (Canada) "Viking" - Premiar at the time, since retained by Thomas Cook Scandinavia and Sunclass Airlines (Scandinavia) "Nitro" - TNT Airways (Belgium, Cargo) "Zap" - Titan Airways (UK - still in use) "Funjet" - LTE International (Spain) "Rubens" - VLM Airways (Belgium) "Red Dragon" - Air Wales (UK) "Relax" - Sky Europe (Czech Rep) "Top Jet" - Thomas Cook Airlines (UK) Briefly used after JMC rebranded into Thomas Cook and after the airline used "Globe" and prior to "Kestrel" "Dagobert" Quick Jet (Germany) "Snoopy" Air Traffic Gmbh (Germany) These still stick in my mind even now all these years later

#6058. Chase Adds Qantas And Cathay Pacific Transfers—More Access To Premium Award Seats

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Chase is adding Qantas and Cathay Pacific as 1:1 transfer partners on November 18. For me, the biggest value is access to business and first class award seats that these airlines don’t make available to members of other frequent flyer programs.

These are Chase’s first new airline transfer partners in more than five years. And they’re an unambiguously positive addition, even if neither becomes the program most cardmembers use most often.

Eligible cards include Chase Sapphire Reserve, Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve for Business, Ink Business Preferred and J.P. Morgan Reserve. Both new partners transfer at 1:1. Hyatt transfers are now less generous for Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred: 4 Chase points become 3 Hyatt points, while the Reserve cards retain 1:1. That distinction doesn’t apply to these new airline partners. Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) is a strong card for actual spending, with 4 points per dollar on flights and hotels booked directly and 3 points per dollar on dining. Adding more transfer partners makes the value of those points even greater. Why I Want Qantas Points Chase already had ways to book oneworld flights through programs like British Airways and Iberia. But being able to book an airline doesn’t mean having access to all of its award seats. Airlines increasingly keep more of their premium cabin availability for their own members. As I explained when Rove added Qantas transfers, Qantas offers its members award space that American AAdvantage, Alaska and British Airways members can’t book. I have family in Australia and have had real success finding Qantas business class awards when there’s flexibility over the U.S. gateway and travel date. I’ll set alerts across several flights rather than insist on one. Some flight between Australia and the U.S. will inevitably open up with a couple of business class awards, usually around 60 days out. Qantas can also be useful for Emirates redemptions. I’d generally rather book the same available Emirates business class seat through Copa ConnectMiles, though. Copa charges 80,000 miles one way between the U.S. and Dubai in business class without fuel surcharges. And Qantas is no longer an unrestricted way around Emirates’ first class award limits. Booking Emirates first class with Qantas points requires Qantas Silver status or higher, and passengers must be at least nine years old. Cathay Offers More Award Space And Lower British Airways Surcharges Cathay Pacific is similar. Its own members get access to far more premium cabin award space than members of partner programs. Asia Miles prices can be high, though. I also like Asia Miles for reducing fuel surcharges on British Airways awards, particularly compared with booking through American AAdvantage. It’s also notable that Chase’s Cathay transfer rate is better than American Express’s. American Express transfers 1,000 Membership Rewards points to just 800 Asia Miles. An award requiring 100,000 Asia Miles takes 100,000 Chase points versus 125,000 Amex points (without transfer bonus). American Express, Citi, Capital One and Rove already partner with both Qantas and Cathay. Chase is catching up with these. I wouldn’t transfer points just because these options have been added. Chase Is Finally Adding Airline Partners Again Chase’s last new transfer partner was Wyndham Rewards in February 2026. Its last new airline partner was Air Canada Aeroplan on August 3, 2021. I welcomed Wyndham because it showed Chase was building out Ultimate Rewards, even though I had little interest in transferring points there. Qantas and Cathay are programs I can see myself using. They bring Chase to 12 airline transfer programs and four hotel programs. I also wonder whether these relationships could lead to more Points Boost opportunities. With Points Boost, Chase can use discounts it negotiates on paid tickets to offer more value per point through its travel portal. More airline relationships could help them offer more flights, more dates, or better redemption values. Qantas has already appeared in Points Boost, and American Airlines has participated without being a Chase transfer partner. But I’d love to see deeper relationships produce more opportunities to redeem at 2 cents per point for premium cabin tickets in the future. #6057. Privatize Air Traffic Control

A plane takes off from Hollywood Burbank Airport in Burbank, Calif., October 7, 2025.

Thank goodness we’re still two weeks away from Thanksgiving. Otherwise, Steve Martin and John Candy’s long trek home would have become a near-universal experience.

Over the weekend, more than 18,000 flights were canceled when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the agency that oversees America’s air traffic control system, ordered a nationwide ground stop. No plane was allowed to take off from a U.S. airport for over four hours. The stoppage was necessary when the FAA’s telecommunications network suddenly failed, apparently caused by a faulty update to its decades-old tangle of copper wiring.

This was the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11. The previous one happened less than four years ago, in January 2023, and was also caused by technical difficulties. Republican lawmakers blamed the Biden administration last time; now, Democrats are faulting the Trump administration. But the FAA’s antiquated infrastructure isn’t a partisan issue. It’s the institutional consequence of having an unaccountable bureaucracy manage the skies.

Unlike almost every other major country, the U.S. federal government funds and operates air traffic control directly. Congress must appropriate its budget each year, and controllers must work without pay when the government shuts down. Infrastructure investments are subject to political timetables. Meanwhile, the FAA is expected to regulate the very system that it runs.

Usually, it wastes no time in dodging responsibility. Immediately after the grounding, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy — who oversees the FAA as part of his department — placed the blame on Congress and past administrations for not adequately funding upgrades to the agency’s aging infrastructure. Yet the FAA received $12.5 billion from last year’s reconciliation law for that purpose. Earlier this month, it requested $30 billion more. Now, Duffy claims that he really needs $50 billion to get the job done. And we thought airlines’ add-on fees were bad.

Improvements don’t have to be so costly. The FAA has spent a quarter century trying to switch its network from copper wires to fiber-optic cables. Its counterpart up north, Nav Canada, completed most of the same transition in just 18 months.

The fundamental difference? Nav Canada was spun off from the national government in 1996 as a nonprofit corporation. The organization is funded entirely by user fees from the airlines and private aircraft that rely on its systems, not general taxes, and it’s structured to be accountable to both private stakeholders and the government. When it needs to finance capital projects, Nav Canada doesn’t have to wait for approval. It can simply issue bonds and recoup the cost over the long run.

The results are impressive. Research finds that privatization lowered costs and boosted productivity for the aviation sector, especially compared with the FAA. Safety has greatly improved, and Nav Canada leads in technological advancement. Dozens of countries have since followed Canada’s lead toward an independent, commercial operator.

Passengers wait at a terminal after the FAA issued a national ground stop following the agency’s earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues, at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Atlanta, Ga., November 13, 2026.

America almost joined that list in 2017. That year, legislation gained traction in Congress that would have transferred air traffic control to an independent entity while retaining the FAA’s oversight role. Regrettably, the plan was shot down by the labor union representing controllers, which feared losing the federal government’s generous protections and benefits. Private aircraft owners also opposed it to avoid paying user fees they are currently exempt from, keeping the revenue burden on commercial flyers.

Aside from placating these entrenched interests, there is no good reason to keep air traffic control in government hands. The public utility model has proven safe and effective elsewhere, and the FAA has shown once again that it can’t measure up. Free the aviation system from political gamesmanship, and watch dependability soar.

#6056. LATAM Unveils New Airbus A321XLR Business Class Suites, Coming March 2027

LATAM has just unveiled the full interiors for its upcoming Airbus A321XLRs, which will make it the first carrier in South America to offer fully flat suites with direct aisle access on a narrow body aircraft. These planes are expected to enter service in the coming months, so we won’t have to wait much longer to fly them!

LATAM has 13 Airbus A321XLRs are on order, which are expected to enter service as of March 2027. The A321XLR is the new long range, narrow body aircraft from Airbus, which stretches the capabilities of the A321 family.

The airline intends to use these planes to open up new long haul markets, though it’s not yet clear out of which LATAM hubs the planes will fly. I suspect these planes will primarily be used for service to North America, or possibly for service from secondary cities in Brazil to Europe. Officially, for now the airline just claims these planes will be used to “strengthen connectivity between South America and more distant destinations.”

Earlier this year, LATAM’s CEO did drop some hints that the plane could fly from Lima (LIM) and Brasilia (BSB) to the United States, and from Fortaleza (FOR) to Europe, though no final decisions have been announced.

We can expect LATAM to offer an all-new passenger experience (by the carrier’s standards) onboard the Airbus A321XLRs. The airline plans to configure the planes with a total of 174 seats, including:

Throughout the plane, passengers can expect the Panasonic Astrova entertainment system, with over 2,300 hours of content, including 330 movies and 1,200 TV shows. Bluetooth audio will also be available at all seats, so that passengers can connect to their own headphones. The A321XLR will also be equipped with SES Wi-Fi, with LATAM Pass members getting complimentary browsing or messaging, depending on their membership tier and ticket type.

LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product. So there will be 12 herringbone seats in a 1-1 configuration, with seats spread across six rows. This means all seats will have direct aisle access and doors. Business class seats will feature 19″ 4K OLED screens, AC power outlets, USB-C charging, and wireless charging.

It also looks like the front row seats will be pretty special, as they’ll feature quite a bit of extra space, including a closet and wardrobe. It remains to be seen how the airline will monetize that extra space, if at all (maybe they’ll just be reserved for certain types of passengers?).

LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Recaro R3 product. So there will be 162 seats in a 3-3 configuration, with six rows having extra legroom, and 21 rows having standard legroom. Economy class seats will feature 13″ 4K OLED screens, as well as USB-C outlets.

The A321XLR is impressive for its range, and it’s understandable that the economics of such a small plane for long haul flying can be challenging. As a result, we’re really seeing airlines try to maximize capacity as much as possible, and this is also leading to so many airlines having very similar premium products on planes.

LATAM will have herringbone seats on the A321XLR, just like… well, all current operators that use this primarily as a long haul aircraft, with the exception of Aer Lingus.

For those keeping track at home, the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product is what you’ll find in JetBlue’s Mint business class on select A321neo/LR aircraft, and it’s also what you’ll find in Iberia’s A321XLR business class.

While American’s A321XLR business class looks similar, it’s based on the Collins Aerospace Aurora seating platform, and that’s also what Air Canada has selected. Meanwhile United’s A321XLR business class also looks similar, but is based on the Elevate Altitude platform.

Admittedly these planes all have better business class products than we found on long haul Boeing 757s years ago (the most direct replacement), and the tech is also greatly updated. That being said, as a passenger experience geek, this sure is a boring plane… “you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, everyone gets a herringbone seat!”

While not quite A321XLRs, credit to ITA Airways’ A321neo business class and Etihad’s A321LR business class for having reverse herringbone seats.

To LATAM’s credit, I will say that the cabin finishes look gorgeous, so I hope they look as nice in real life as they do in renderings.

In early 2027, LATAM expects to start taking delivery of the Airbus A321XLR, which the airline plans to use to grow into new markets. The airline has now revealed what we can expect onboard these planes, and it includes herringbone seats with direct aisle access and doors in business class.

Ultimately the cabin looks sleek, and it’s cool to see this in South America, where no other airline is currently offering such an experience. But still, it’s hard to get too excited when so many airlines are introducing a similar product.

LATAM in general deserves credit for the extent to which it’s elevating the passenger experience in Latin America, as we’ve seen the airline introduce two new wide body business class products over the past several years.

What do you make of LATAM’s new A321XLR business class?

#6055. Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

Leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she said. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

“A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”

Several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”

Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

#6054. World Of Hyatt Status Revamps For 2027—Award Stacking And New Benefit Choices, But Cuts Come Also

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Hyatt will finally let members combine a free night certificate with a confirmed suite upgrade starting January 1, 2027. I’ve wanted that for years. They’re also extending milestone free night certificates from 180 days to a year, and adding rewards after just 10 qualifying nights.

This isn’t an across the board improvement. Suite upgrades will expire sooner. The suite upgrade choice at 50 nights gets cut in half. And My Hyatt Concierge becomes something you select alongside other rewards, rather than something everyone automatically receives at 60 nights. Free parking will no longer be an automatic benefit on award stays for Globalists.

When I covered Hyatt’s last major status benefit refresh in November 2023, I liked it overall. They made awards transferable, added choices, and let members try Globalist benefits before earning Globalist. Guest of Honor became limited, but the Milestone Rewards themselves mostly got better.

This time there are new and better options. I genuinely like a lot of the choices, but there are real tradeoffs. Hyatt is pitching the changes as more choice and flexibility, based on listening to members. That’s actually fair for much of this, though I don’t think members told them what they really wanted was for suite upgrade to expire up to a year earlier.

Hyatt will allow members to combine eligible awards on the same reservation, including Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards and the new Free Parking Awards. This fixes one of the problems I’ve been complaining about for years. A free night certificate is something you often want to use on a special leisure stay. That’s also when a suite may matter most, especially traveling with family. When I didn’t want to use a free night certificate was a work trip by myself. Free night awards had a lot less value to me because I had to give up a confirmed suite to use them. But being able to use the two awards together makes both more valuable. Combining Guest of Honor with a suite upgrade is useful, too. You can give someone Globalist treatment and confirm their suite ahead of time, rather than leaving the room upgrade to availability when they arrive. Hyatt also promises an enhanced Pay My Way experience, letting members mix awards, points, cash and Points + Cash by night. Online selection, gifting and redemption will be available for eligible awards. Pay My Way and stacking, by the way, really do all work together. Hyatt offers me this illustration, Let’s say a member is making a three night booking. Assuming both the Standard Suite was available for the duration, and there is award inventory available on the selected dates (just like today) – yes, a member could apply a Suite Upgrade Award to the whole stay, a Free Parking award to the whole stay, a Guest of Honor Award to the whole stay, and then pay for the reservation using points on one night, a promotional Free Night Award on another night, and cash on the third night.

Milestone Rewards currently begin at 20 qualifying nights. Next year they’ll start at 10 nights or 20,000 base points. Here’s the new chart through 50 nights. Qualifying nights / base points   What you receive 10 / 20,000   Choose one: 1 qualifying night credit, $25 FIND experience credit, or $30 Inclusive Collection spa credit. 20 / 35,000   Choose one: 2 qualifying night credits, $30 spa credit, $25 Delta certificate, 2K Next Stay Award, or 2 Club Access Awards. 30 / 50,000   Choose 10,000 bonus points or a Category 1–4 free night. Also choose one: 2 qualifying night credits, $30 spa credit, $25 Delta certificate, 2K Next Stay Award, or 2 Club Access Awards. 40 / 65,000   Receive 1 Guest of Honor Award. Also choose one: 5 qualifying night credits, $200 Thompson Hotels credit, $75 Delta certificate, 5,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. 50 / 80,000   Choose one: $200 Thompson Hotels credit, $75 Delta certificate, 5,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. The qualifying night choices add up to 10 nights: one at the first milestone, two at the next, two at 30 nights and five at 40 nights. These count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. That creates a path to Globalist with 50 qualifying nights from other sources, if you select all four night rewards. The requirement remains 60, but 10 can come from these choices. And you earn qualifying nights with the The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) too – 5 qualifying night credits every year and 2 qualifying night every time you spend $5,000 on the card. The 30 night option to take 10,000 points instead of a Category 1–4 certificate is useful for someone who struggles to use the certificate. A good Category 4 redemption can be worth more, and the certificate will become easier to use with the longer expiration and ability to add a suite upgrade. One Fewer Suite Upgrade, And A Choice About Your Concierge The reduction at 50 nights is easy to miss. The current choice is two Suite Upgrade Awards. The new chart offers one. At 60 nights or 100,000 base points, members will receive: 2 Guest of Honor Awards. A choice of free nights: 2 Category 1–4 awards or 1 Category 1–7 award. Two selections from this menu: 7,500 bonus points, a Free Parking Award, a $100 Delta certificate, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, or My Hyatt Concierge. You can still select the two suite upgrades and concierge access, keeping the existing 60 night package. But if you want points or parking, something else has to go. And you can’t make the same two choices at 60 nights – you can’t have four upgrades, 15,000 points or two parking awards. You don’t have o select all of your awards at once, though you do have to make these two selections at the same time. Hyatt explains to me that you’ll still have 90 days to make your choices, and: In milestones where there are separate choices, such as 30 nights, the member can make those choices at different points within the 90 day selection window (e.g., could choose the Free Night Award one day, and the HIC Spa credit on a different day.) At 60 nights, the member can choose their free night award choice on a different day from the other selection, but the two selections within “Choose Two” must be made together at the same time. I do plan to keep the concierge benefit, even though mine has never been very responsive. I won’t give up the ability to email someone to address issues. I just wish I would hear back more quickly, and didn’t need to follow up so often. Maybe that’s actually coming? Hyatt tells me they do plan greater investment in the concierge program: [B]y shifting to a choice, we will be able to further invest in My Hyatt Concierge and deliver even more proactive and personalized care. We will share more when available.

At 60 nights, the member can choose their free night award choice on a different day from the other selection, but the two selections within “Choose Two” must be made together at the same time.

I do plan to keep the concierge benefit, even though mine has never been very responsive. I won’t give up the ability to email someone to address issues. I just wish I would hear back more quickly, and didn’t need to follow up so often. Maybe that’s actually coming? Hyatt tells me they do plan greater investment in the concierge program:

[B]y shifting to a choice, we will be able to further invest in My Hyatt Concierge and deliver even more proactive and personalized care. We will share more when available.

As before, lifetime Globalists retain their concierge without having to stay 60 nights.

The new parking award covers a qualifying paid or award stay of up to seven nights, and can be gifted. It appears among the choices at 60, 70, 80 and 90 nights. However it’s no longer simply a benefit for Globalists redeeming points for free nights. I wrote in that Hyatt was surveying turning automatic benefits into awards you could choose and they’ve done that with this one. The benefit is no longer unlimited It comes with a tradeoff – the benefit is instead of something else And you have to plan ahead, one more thing to track and manage, rather than something that’s just ‘taken care of’ in recognition of your loyalty. Hyatt explains the decision to me as, [T]his decision was made as 70% of Globalists did not use the free parking benefit in 2025; 95% used it 4 times or less, and moving this to a choice allowed the program to retain it for members who value it and introduce other exciting new awards like the $200 Thompson Hotels Credit and the $500 Premium Suite Credit. If the benefit wasn’t being used, it actually wasn’t that expensive to offer! And not using it regularly doesn’t mean the option isn’t valued. It may not have been the most valuable benefit of Globalist for most people, but I wouldn’t personally make the tradeoff (in fairness, I’m someone that did use and get value from it). Of course, a parking award will be eligible for use a paid stay while it previously was only available on points. However, at 70, 80 or 90 nights where you can claim it you’re passing up 10,000 points or a suite upgrade to select it. A Year To Use Every Award Is Both An Improvement And A Cut Hyatt’s release presents the new expiration policy as giving members extra time. That’s true for some awards, but the effect runs in both directions. Hyatt tells me, For all awards issued on January 1, 2027 or later, expiration dates will be 365 days from the date of issuance. Milestone free night awards that currently expire after 180 days will get substantially more time. But suite upgrades, ordinary Milestone Guest of Honor awards and club access awards currently have much longer lives, generally through the end of the year earned plus another 14 months under Hyatt’s existing rules. A suite upgrade selected January 1, 2026 remained valid through February 2028. Under a 365 day rule, the same issuance date would produce a January 1, 2027 expiration. That’s more than a year of usefulness gone. Shortening the window makes it harder to hold upgrades for a major trip, to book far ahead, or to save awards from a heavy travel year for a quieter one. Note that this change applies to Milestone Rewards earned starting in 2027. So any that you earn at the end of 2026, and redeem in 2027, follow the old rules. Hyatt confirms, Only awards earned and selected after January 1, 2027 follow the new 365 expiration from issuance. So, a 2026 award (even if selected in 2027) would carry the current 2026 expiration rules. More Free Night Choices And Delta Status At Higher Milestones Here’s the rest of the 2027 chart: Qualifying nights   What you receive 70, 80 and 90, at each milestone   1 Guest of Honor Award, plus choose one: a Free Parking Award, 2 single visit Delta Sky Club passes, 10,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. 100   Choose 1 Category 1–7 night, 2 Category 1–4 nights, or a $500 premium suite credit. Also choose one: Delta Gold Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. 110, 120, 130 and 140, at each milestone   1 Guest of Honor Award, plus choose one: Delta Gold Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. 150   Choose 2 Category 1–7 nights or an Ultimate Free Night Award. Also choose one: Delta Platinum Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. The Ultimate Free Night at 150 nights isn’t going away. The two Category 1–7 nights are an alternative. Someone who wants two nights at less expensive hotels can choose those, while someone planning one especially expensive night can retain the Ultimate award, which covers participating Category 1–8 hotels, Category A–F all-inclusives and Miraval. The new hotel credits are more restrictive than points: $30 Inclusive Collection spa credit: for spa treatments at participating all-inclusive resorts. $200 Thompson Hotels credit: toward an eligible paid stay. $500 premium suite credit: toward an eligible paid premium suite stay of at least two nights. I’ve wanted a way to use two suite upgrades to confirm a premium suite. A discount on buying a premium suite isn’t as attractive to me. But there are times I might use it. Delta Gold starting at 100 nights and Platinum at 150 nights are interesting choices for someone who flies Delta without status. I still preferred the American partnership. The ability to redeem Hyatt points for American status for a trip was useful for people who didn’t have American status. And the earlier version earned American miles on Hyatt stays. I’d rather earn those than Delta miles. FIND credits are being pared back sharply. The $25 choices at 20 and 30 nights disappear, as do $150 choices at 40 and 50 nights and $300 choices at 70, 80 and 90. A $25 FIND choice appears at the new 10 night milestone. What Hyatt Gets From These Changes The strongest improvements are award stacking, more time to use free night certificates, an earlier first reward, and choices that let members avoid awards they won’t use. A member who doesn’t value concierge access can get something else, while someone who prefers two less expensive hotel nights can choose them. I expect members approaching Globalist will like the qualifying night choices. People who lose free night certificates to expiration should come out ahead, too. Existing Globalists who use all their suite upgrades, plan trips far ahead, or regularly choose FIND experiences have more to lose. Hyatt also gets more ways to influence where members spend. A Thompson credit encourages a paid Thompson stay. A spa credit encourages a treatment that may cost much more than the credit. The premium suite credit encourages someone to buy a room they might otherwise try to upgrade into. Shorter suite award validity should leave fewer outstanding upgrades available for future use. Making concierge elective lets members reveal whether they value the service more than points or another reward. And offering status credits makes the next milestone feel closer, encouraging someone with a modest number of Hyatt nights to keep going. For me, being able to confirm a suite on a free night certificate is the biggest improvement. I care much more about that than a spa coupon. There really is more choice and the ability to earn status faster with these changes. Stacking and combining rewards is great. So is longer expiration of free night awards, though sadly at the cost of shorter expiration for suite upgrade awards. The most consequential change for me might be something that isn’t really being announced. If changing My Hyatt Concierge to a choice benefit really does entail greater investment in the program, it would make the experience far more premium and secure even greater loyalty. Of course, a parking award will be eligible for use a paid stay while it previously was only available on points. However, at 70, 80 or 90 nights where you can claim it you’re passing up 10,000 points or a suite upgrade to select it.

Hyatt’s release presents the new expiration policy as giving members extra time. That’s true for some awards, but the effect runs in both directions. Hyatt tells me, For all awards issued on January 1, 2027 or later, expiration dates will be 365 days from the date of issuance. Milestone free night awards that currently expire after 180 days will get substantially more time. But suite upgrades, ordinary Milestone Guest of Honor awards and club access awards currently have much longer lives, generally through the end of the year earned plus another 14 months under Hyatt’s existing rules. A suite upgrade selected January 1, 2026 remained valid through February 2028. Under a 365 day rule, the same issuance date would produce a January 1, 2027 expiration. That’s more than a year of usefulness gone. Shortening the window makes it harder to hold upgrades for a major trip, to book far ahead, or to save awards from a heavy travel year for a quieter one. Note that this change applies to Milestone Rewards earned starting in 2027. So any that you earn at the end of 2026, and redeem in 2027, follow the old rules. Hyatt confirms, Only awards earned and selected after January 1, 2027 follow the new 365 expiration from issuance. So, a 2026 award (even if selected in 2027) would carry the current 2026 expiration rules.

Here’s the rest of the 2027 chart: Qualifying nights   What you receive 70, 80 and 90, at each milestone   1 Guest of Honor Award, plus choose one: a Free Parking Award, 2 single visit Delta Sky Club passes, 10,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. 100   Choose 1 Category 1–7 night, 2 Category 1–4 nights, or a $500 premium suite credit. Also choose one: Delta Gold Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. 110, 120, 130 and 140, at each milestone   1 Guest of Honor Award, plus choose one: Delta Gold Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. 150   Choose 2 Category 1–7 nights or an Ultimate Free Night Award. Also choose one: Delta Platinum Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. The Ultimate Free Night at 150 nights isn’t going away. The two Category 1–7 nights are an alternative. Someone who wants two nights at less expensive hotels can choose those, while someone planning one especially expensive night can retain the Ultimate award, which covers participating Category 1–8 hotels, Category A–F all-inclusives and Miraval. The new hotel credits are more restrictive than points: $30 Inclusive Collection spa credit: for spa treatments at participating all-inclusive resorts. $200 Thompson Hotels credit: toward an eligible paid stay. $500 premium suite credit: toward an eligible paid premium suite stay of at least two nights. I’ve wanted a way to use two suite upgrades to confirm a premium suite. A discount on buying a premium suite isn’t as attractive to me. But there are times I might use it. Delta Gold starting at 100 nights and Platinum at 150 nights are interesting choices for someone who flies Delta without status. I still preferred the American partnership. The ability to redeem Hyatt points for American status for a trip was useful for people who didn’t have American status. And the earlier version earned American miles on Hyatt stays. I’d rather earn those than Delta miles. FIND credits are being pared back sharply. The $25 choices at 20 and 30 nights disappear, as do $150 choices at 40 and 50 nights and $300 choices at 70, 80 and 90. A $25 FIND choice appears at the new 10 night milestone. What Hyatt Gets From These Changes The strongest improvements are award stacking, more time to use free night certificates, an earlier first reward, and choices that let members avoid awards they won’t use. A member who doesn’t value concierge access can get something else, while someone who prefers two less expensive hotel nights can choose them. I expect members approaching Globalist will like the qualifying night choices. People who lose free night certificates to expiration should come out ahead, too. Existing Globalists who use all their suite upgrades, plan trips far ahead, or regularly choose FIND experiences have more to lose. Hyatt also gets more ways to influence where members spend. A Thompson credit encourages a paid Thompson stay. A spa credit encourages a treatment that may cost much more than the credit. The premium suite credit encourages someone to buy a room they might otherwise try to upgrade into. Shorter suite award validity should leave fewer outstanding upgrades available for future use. Making concierge elective lets members reveal whether they value the service more than points or another reward. And offering status credits makes the next milestone feel closer, encouraging someone with a modest number of Hyatt nights to keep going. For me, being able to confirm a suite on a free night certificate is the biggest improvement. I care much more about that than a spa coupon. There really is more choice and the ability to earn status faster with these changes. Stacking and combining rewards is great. So is longer expiration of free night awards, though sadly at the cost of shorter expiration for suite upgrade awards. The most consequential change for me might be something that isn’t really being announced. If changing My Hyatt Concierge to a choice benefit really does entail greater investment in the program, it would make the experience far more premium and secure even greater loyalty. The strongest improvements are award stacking, more time to use free night certificates, an earlier first reward, and choices that let members avoid awards they won’t use. A member who doesn’t value concierge access can get something else, while someone who prefers two less expensive hotel nights can choose them.

I expect members approaching Globalist will like the qualifying night choices. People who lose free night certificates to expiration should come out ahead, too. Existing Globalists who use all their suite upgrades, plan trips far ahead, or regularly choose FIND experiences have more to lose.

Hyatt also gets more ways to influence where members spend. A Thompson credit encourages a paid Thompson stay. A spa credit encourages a treatment that may cost much more than the credit. The premium suite credit encourages someone to buy a room they might otherwise try to upgrade into.

Shorter suite award validity should leave fewer outstanding upgrades available for future use. Making concierge elective lets members reveal whether they value the service more than points or another reward. And offering status credits makes the next milestone feel closer, encouraging someone with a modest number of Hyatt nights to keep going.

For me, being able to confirm a suite on a free night certificate is the biggest improvement. I care much more about that than a spa coupon.

There really is more choice and the ability to earn status faster with these changes. Stacking and combining rewards is great. So is longer expiration of free night awards, though sadly at the cost of shorter expiration for suite upgrade awards.

The most consequential change for me might be something that isn’t really being announced. If changing My Hyatt Concierge to a choice benefit really does entail greater investment in the program, it would make the experience far more premium and secure even greater loyalty.
